title: Two Sum
statement: You get an array of integers nums and an integer target. Return the indices of the two numbers in nums that add up to target. Each input has exactly one solution. You may not use the same element twice, so the two indices must be different. Two different indices can hold equal values. You can return the two indices in any order. The array is not necessarily sorted. It can contain negative numbers, zero and duplicates.
follow_up: Can you come up with an algorithm that is less than O(n^2) time complexity?
signals: The task asks for a pair of elements that satisfy an exact relation, such as a sum or difference equal to a target. One element then fixes the exact value of its partner.
The output is original indices, not values. Sorting the values loses those indices, so a hash map from value to index fits better.
The input has no order and the follow-up asks for less than O(n^2) time. This points to one linear scan with constant-time lookups.
Values range up to 10^9 in magnitude. A direct-address array is too large, so a hash map replaces it.
memory_hook: Ask the map for the partner, then add yourself.
approach: One-pass hash map of seen values. Walk the array once. For each value, look up its partner target - value in the map. If the partner is there, return both indices. If not, store the value with its index.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty dict seen that maps a value to its index.
Loop with i, x in enumerate(nums).
Compute need = target - x.
If need is in seen, return [seen[need], i].
Else store seen[x] = i and continue.
After the loop, return [] (the constraints make this unreachable).
key_insight: When a pair must satisfy an exact relation, one element determines the exact value of its partner. So you do not search for the partner. You look it up in a hash map of the elements you have already seen.
ladder: Brute force over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort indices by value, then binary search: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Sort indices by value, then converging two pointers: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Two-pass hash map: O(n) time, O(n) space
One-pass hash map of seen values (optimal): O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Inserting the current value before the lookup lets an element pair with itself. For [3,2,4] and target 6, that returns [0,0].
In the two-pass version, you must check that the stored index is different from the current index.
Equal values such as [3,3] with target 6 must give two different indices. Lookup-before-insert handles this with no special case.

title: Add Two Numbers
statement: You get two non-empty singly linked lists. Each list represents a non-negative integer. The digits are stored in reverse order, so the head holds the least significant digit. Each node holds a single digit from 0 to 9. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list in the same reverse-digit format. The two numbers have no leading zeros, except the number 0 itself. The two lists can have different lengths.
constraints: The number of nodes in each linked list is in the range [1, 100].
It is guaranteed that the list represents a number that does not have leading zeros.
signals: A number is given as a sequence of digits, so the task is digit-by-digit arithmetic, not native integer math.
The digits come least significant first. This matches the order of column addition, so one forward pass is enough.
The digit count can exceed the range of a 64-bit integer. Here, 100 digits is far above the 19 digits that fit, so native integer math fails in most languages.
The output is a new linked list of unknown length that you build one node at a time. This points to a dummy head and a tail pointer.
memory_hook: Add digits plus carry while anything is left; write mod 10, carry div 10.
approach: Column addition with a carry. Walk both lists together. At each position, add the two digits and the carry. Use 0 for a list that has ended. Append the sum mod 10 as a new node after a dummy head. Pass the sum div 10 on as the carry.
rebuild_steps: Make dummy = ListNode(), set tail = dummy and carry = 0.
Loop while l1 or l2 or carry.
Set total = carry. If l1 exists, add l1.val and move l1. Do the same for l2.
Set carry, digit = divmod(total, 10).
Append ListNode(digit) at tail.next and move tail forward.
Return dummy.next.
key_insight: When a number is stored as a digit sequence, simulate column arithmetic. Process one position at a time, add the digits and the carry, emit the total mod base, and pass the total div base forward. A least-significant-first order lets one forward pass do the whole job. The carry stays small, so each position costs O(1).
ladder: Convert to integers and back: O(m + n) arithmetic steps, about O((m + n)^2) digit work with big integers time, O(m + n) space
Digit-by-digit addition with carry (optimal): O(max(m, n)) time, O(1) extra, O(max(m, n)) for the output list space
Recursive digit addition: O(max(m, n)) time, O(max(m, n)) call stack space
In-place reuse of an input list: O(max(m, n)) time, O(1) extra space
pitfalls: Stopping the loop when both lists end drops a final carry, so [9] + [1] returns [0] instead of [0,1].
Reading .val or .next on an ended list raises an AttributeError when the lists have different lengths. Check each list for None first.
Writing separate loops for the leftover tail of the longer list duplicates logic and often forgets the carry.
solution:
class Solution:
    def addTwoNumbers(self, l1: Optional[ListNode], l2: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode()
        tail = dummy
        carry = 0
        while l1 or l2 or carry:
            total = carry
            if l1:
                total += l1.val
                l1 = l1.next
            if l2:
                total += l2.val
                l2 = l2.next
            carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
            tail.next = ListNode(digit)
            tail = tail.next
        return dummy.next

title: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters
statement: Given a string s, return the length of the longest substring of s that has no duplicate characters. A substring is a contiguous, non-empty run of characters in s. A subsequence that skips characters does not count. If s is empty, the answer is 0. Characters are case-sensitive, and spaces, digits and symbols count as characters.
constraints: s consists of English letters, digits, symbols and spaces.
signals: The problem asks for the longest or shortest contiguous substring or subarray.
The validity rule is monotone: if a window is valid, every smaller window inside it is also valid.
The validity check depends only on the contents of the window, which a set, map or counter can track as elements enter and leave.
The input length is up to 10^5, so an O(n^2) scan of all substrings is too slow and a linear pass is the target.
memory_hook: Drop from the left until the new character is unique, then add it on the right.
approach: Sliding window with a set (shrink step by step). Grow the window one character at a time on the right. While the new character is already in the set, remove the leftmost character and move left forward.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty set called window, and set left = 0 and best = 0.
Loop with for right, ch in enumerate(s).
While ch is in window, remove s[left] from window and add 1 to left.
Add ch to window. Now the window s[left..right] has no duplicates.
Set best = max(best, right - left + 1), and return best after the loop.
key_insight: For each right end, the best valid left end never moves backward. So a window that grows on the right and shrinks on the left covers all candidate substrings in linear time, because every element enters and leaves the window at most once.
ladder: Brute force over all substrings: O(n^3) time, O(min(n, k)) space (too slow)
Extend from each start with a set: O(n * min(n, k)) time, O(min(n, k)) space (too slow)
Sliding window with a set (shrink step by step): O(n) time, O(min(n, k)) space
Sliding window with last-seen index map (jump left): O(n) time, O(min(n, k)) space
Sliding window with a fixed array of size 128: O(n) time, O(1) (128 slots) space
pitfalls: The empty string must return 0, so initialize best to 0 and do not assume s[0] exists.
Remove s[left] from the set before you increase left, and remove characters one at a time until the duplicate leaves the window.
Add s[right] to the set only after the while loop, otherwise the loop condition is always true.
solution:
class Solution:
    def lengthOfLongestSubstring(self, s: str) -> int:
        window = set()          # characters inside s[left..right]
        left = 0
        best = 0
        for right, ch in enumerate(s):
            while ch in window:         # shrink until ch is unique
                window.remove(s[left])
                left += 1
            window.add(ch)              # expand
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

title: Median of Two Sorted Arrays
statement: You get two arrays nums1 and nums2. Each array is sorted in non-decreasing order. Their sizes are m and n. One array can be empty, but the total size m + n is at least 1. Return the median of all m + n values together. If m + n is odd, the median is the middle value of the merged sorted order. If m + n is even, the median is the average of the two middle values. Return the result as a float. The overall run time complexity should be O(log (m+n)).
signals: The input is two or more sorted arrays and the question asks for an order statistic, such as the median or the k-th smallest value.
The statement demands a logarithmic run time, so a linear merge is not allowed even if it fits the size limits.
The answer depends only on where a split line falls, not on the full merged order.
A check at a candidate split tells you if the split is correct, too far left or too far right, so the search space is monotonic.
memory_hook: Cut the shorter array so the left half is full: too many from A, go left; too few, go right; just right, read the borders.
approach: Binary search on the cut in the shorter array: too many, too few, just right. The left half has a fixed size. You take i values from the shorter array A and the rest from B. You move i until every left value is <= every right value.
rebuild_steps: Swap so A is the shorter array. Set m, n = len(A), len(B) and half = (m + n + 1) // 2.
Write at(arr, k). It returns -inf for k < 0, +inf for k >= len(arr), else arr[k].
Set lo, hi = 0, m. While lo <= hi, set i = (lo + hi) // 2 and j = half - i.
If at(A, i-1) > at(B, j), you took too many from A. Set hi = i - 1.
Elif at(B, j-1) > at(A, i), you took too few from A. Set lo = i + 1.
Else the cut is just right. Set left_max = max(at(A, i-1), at(B, j-1)).
For an odd total, return float(left_max). For an even total, return (left_max + min(at(A, i), at(B, j))) / 2.
key_insight: A median is a split, not a value: the left half has a fixed size, so choosing how many elements come from one array forces the count from the other. That reduces the problem to a one-variable binary search where you check a split with only the border elements.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same as solution_code. Only the border reads differ. solution_code reads the four borders inline with conditional expressions, and this version calls the at helper. Both run in O(log(min(m, n))) time and O(1) extra space.
ladder: Merge then sort: O((m+n) log(m+n)) time, O(m+n) space (too slow)
Two-pointer merge walk: O(m+n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
k-th smallest by halving k: O(log(m+n)) time, O(1) iterative, O(log(m+n)) recursive space
Binary search on the partition of the shorter array: O(log(min(m, n))) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Binary searching the longer array lets j go negative or past n, which causes index errors or wrong answers.
Forgetting the sentinels for i = 0, i = m, j = 0 or j = n breaks the cases where one array is empty or fully on one side.
In Python, A[i - 1] with i = 0 reads the last element instead of raising an error, so you must guard every border read with a range check.

title: Longest Palindromic Substring
statement: You get a string s. Return the longest substring of s that is a palindrome. A substring is a contiguous, non-empty run of characters of s. A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. If more than one substring has the maximum length, you can return any of them. The string has at least one character, so the answer always has at least one character.
constraints: s consist of only digits and English letters.
signals: The task asks for the longest contiguous substring with a symmetric property, such as a palindrome.
The length limit is about 10^3. O(n^2) is about 10^6 steps and is safe. O(n^3) is about 10^8 steps and is too slow or borderline.
The property of a window depends only on its two end items and on the smaller window just inside it.
The property is symmetric around a middle point, so each candidate can grow outward from a center, one pair of ends at a time.
memory_hook: Every palindrome grows from a center: try each character and each gap, expand while the ends match, keep the longest.
approach: Use expand around center. Try every center: one character for odd length and two neighbors for even length. Grow outward while the two ends match. The helper returns the palindrome string, and the main loop keeps the longest one.
rebuild_steps: Inside longestPalindrome, define a helper expand(left, right).
In the helper, loop while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]. In each step, move left down by 1 and right up by 1.
After the loop, return s[left + 1:right]. The loop stops one step too far on each side.
In the main body, set best to the empty string.
For each center in range(len(s)), set odd = expand(center, center) and even = expand(center, center + 1).
In the same loop, set best = max(best, odd, even, key=len).
After the loop, return best.
key_insight: A palindrome is defined by its center. If the inner window around a center is a palindrome and the two new ends match, the outer window is also a palindrome. If the ends do not match, no larger window on that center is a palindrome. So you grow each of the 2n-1 centers outward until the first mismatch, instead of checking every substring from scratch.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses the same expand-around-center algorithm. It keeps only a start index and a length through nonlocal and slices once at the end, so it uses O(1) extra space. The intuitive version builds two slices per center. Each slice costs no more than the expansion that found it, so both versions are O(n^2) time. The difference does not matter for n <= 1000. Use Manacher's algorithm only when a statement requires O(n) time on much longer strings.
ladder: Brute force over all substrings: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Interval DP table: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
Expand around center: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
Binary search on length with rolling hash: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Manacher's algorithm: O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Forgetting even-length centers. The string "cbbd" then returns "c" instead of "bb".
Off-by-one after expansion. The loop exits one step past the palindrome, so the answer is s[left+1:right], with length right - left - 1.
Checking s[left] and s[right] before the bounds checks. Python allows s[-1], so a missing left >= 0 check silently compares the wrong character. A missing right < n check raises IndexError.

title: Reverse Integer
statement: You get a signed 32-bit integer x. Return x with its digits reversed. The sign stays the same. Leading zeros of the result disappear, so 120 becomes 21. If the reversed value is outside the signed 32-bit range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1], return 0. Assume the environment cannot store 64-bit integers, signed or unsigned. This means you must detect overflow before it happens, not after you compute a wider value.
signals: The task changes the digit order of a number. Pop the last digit with modulo 10 and integer division by 10. Push a digit onto a result with res * 10 + digit.
The statement names a fixed-width range and says you cannot use a wider type. Guard each arithmetic step before the value can overflow.
The statement says to return a sentinel such as 0 on overflow. Return early from inside the loop at the first step that would overflow.
The input has at most 10 digits. Any digit-by-digit loop is effectively constant time, so the challenge is correctness, not speed.
memory_hook: Put the sign aside. Pop a digit, solve res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX for res, and push only if it holds.
approach: Digit pop and push with a one-line guard. Pop each digit with divmod by 10 and push it with res * 10 + digit. Before each push, solve res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX for res and return 0 if res > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10.
rebuild_steps: Set INT_MAX = 2**31 - 1. Store the sign, set x = abs(x), and set res = 0.
While x is not 0, pop the last digit with x, digit = divmod(x, 10).
Write the push condition res * 10 + digit <= INT_MAX. Solve it for res: res <= (INT_MAX - digit) // 10. Floor division is exact here because res is an integer.
If res > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10, return 0.
Push with res = res * 10 + digit.
After the loop, return sign * res.
key_insight: Check for overflow before the operation, not after it. Rearrange the condition res * 10 + digit > LIMIT into res > LIMIT // 10, or res == LIMIT // 10 and digit > LIMIT % 10. Then every value you compute stays inside the allowed range.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same: pop, guard before the push, push, with a stored sign. Only the guard expression differs. The record solution_code uses the classic two-part guard: res > INT_MAX // 10, or res == INT_MAX // 10 and digit > INT_MAX % 10. Both guards are equivalent for every res >= 0 and digit from 0 to 9, and both have O(log|x|) time and O(1) space. Learn to read the two-part form, because most C and Java references use it. In a fixed-width language, keep x signed (approach 4), because abs(INT_MIN) does not fit a signed 32-bit int.
ladder: String reversal with a range check after: O(log|x|) time, O(log|x|) space (too slow)
Digit pop and push with a check after the loop: O(log|x|) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Digit pop and push with an overflow guard before each push (optimal): O(log|x|) time, O(1) space
Signed truncation without abs (C/Java style, NeetCode reference): O(log|x|) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Python // rounds toward negative infinity, and % takes the sign of the divisor. So -123 % 10 is 7 and -123 // 10 is -13. Work on the magnitude with a stored sign, or use truncating division.
A range check only after the loop gives correct answers in Python but breaks the no-64-bit rule. In Java the value wraps silently and gives a wrong answer. In C signed overflow is undefined behavior.
The magnitude of INT_MIN is 2^31, which does not fit a signed 32-bit int in C or Java. Python handles it, but in fixed-width languages keep x signed.

title: Regular Expression Matching
statement: You get an input string s and a pattern p. Implement regular expression matching that supports '.' and '*'. The character '.' matches any single character. The character '*' matches zero or more of the preceding element. Return a boolean that tells if the pattern matches the entire input string, not only a part of it. s contains only lowercase English letters. p contains only lowercase English letters, '.', and '*'. The input guarantees that each '*' has a previous valid character (a letter or '.') to repeat.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
p contains only lowercase English letters, '.', and '*'.
signals: Two strings and a yes or no question about whether one fully matches or turns into the other. This points to a DP over a pair of indices (i, j).
A pattern symbol matches a variable number of characters, including zero. Each such symbol creates a choice, and different choices reach the same pair of positions again.
The words 'entire string' or 'not partial' mean the base case needs both indices at the end at the same time.
A brute force branches at each choice, but its whole state is only a few indices. Many branches reach the same indices again. This overlap means you can memoize on those indices or fill a table.
memory_hook: Peek for a star: skip it, or eat one and stay.
approach: Top-down memoized DFS on (i, j). dfs(i, j) asks if s[i:] matches p[j:]. A unit "x*" has two moves: skip it, or eat one matching character and stay on it.
rebuild_steps: Import cache from functools.
Inside isMatch, define dfs(i, j) that tells if s[i:] matches p[j:], and put @cache on it.
Base case: if j == len(p), return i == len(s).
Set first = i < len(s) and p[j] in (s[i], '.').
If j + 1 < len(p) and p[j + 1] == '*', return dfs(i, j + 2) or (first and dfs(i + 1, j)).
Else return first and dfs(i + 1, j + 1).
Return dfs(0, 0).
key_insight: Treat a repeat operator and its element as one token with two moves: skip the token, or consume one matching character and stay on the same token. The self-loop turns 'zero or more' into a finite recurrence over two indices, so you never enumerate repeat counts.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code fills the same states bottom-up in a table dp[i][j], with i from m down to 0 and j from n - 1 down to 0. It has the same O(m * n) time and space. It uses no recursion and no function calls per state. It is also the start point for the two-row O(n) space version. Use it when the input is long enough to hit the recursion limit, or when you need O(n) space. With lengths up to 20, the memoized DFS is enough.
ladder: Plain recursion (backtracking): O((m + n) * 2^(m + n/2)) worst case time, O(m + n) recursion depth (O((m + n)^2) with string slicing) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS on (i, j): O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Bottom-up 2D table over suffixes: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Two-row rolling table: O(m * n) time, O(n) space
NFA simulation (Thompson style): O(m * n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Checking for '*' at p[j] instead of p[j + 1]. Then you consume x once before you know it is optional, and "aab" with "c*a*b" fails.
Forgetting that "x*" can match zero characters. The row for the empty suffix of s (i = m) must be computed, because "a*b*" matches the empty string.
Reading s[i] or dp[i + 1] when i == m. Test i < m first, and put first before dp[i + 1] so that short-circuit evaluation skips the read.

title: Container With Most Water
statement: You get an integer array height of length n. There are n vertical lines. The two endpoints of line i are (i, 0) and (i, height[i]). Find two lines that, together with the x-axis, form a container that holds the most water. Return the maximum amount of water that a container can store. You may not slant the container. For two lines i < j, the amount of water is min(height[i], height[j]) * (j - i).
signals: The task asks for the best pair (i, j) in an array, and n up to 10^5 rules out checking all pairs.
The score of a pair is a product of a width (j - i) and a limiting value (the minimum of the two endpoints).
The width term is largest at the two ends, so you can start with the widest pair and shrink inward.
The pair score depends only on the two endpoints, not on the elements between them.
memory_hook: Start widest, keep the best area, and move the shorter wall in.
approach: Use two pointers that start at both ends. Record the area of the current pair. Then move the pointer at the shorter line one step inward. Stop when the pointers meet.
rebuild_steps: Set left = 0, right = len(height) - 1, and best = 0.
Loop while left < right.
Compute area = min(height[left], height[right]) * (right - left). Set best = max(best, area).
If height[left] < height[right], move left one step right. Else move right one step left.
Return best after the pointers meet.
key_insight: When a pair score is capped by the smaller endpoint and grows with the distance between the endpoints, the smaller endpoint meets its best partner in the widest remaining window. So you can discard it safely and remove one candidate per step instead of checking all pairs.
ladder: Brute force over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort indices by height (each line as the shorter side): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Two pointers converging from both ends: O(n) time, O(1) space
Two pointers with skip of short lines: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Do not move the taller pointer. That can skip the optimal pair, because the shorter line still limits the height.
Do not confuse this with Trapping Rain Water. Here only the two chosen lines matter, and the inner lines do not hold or block water.
Width is r - l, not r - l + 1.

title: 3Sum
statement: You get an integer array nums. Return all triplets [nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]] where i, j and k are three different indices and nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0. The result must not contain duplicate triplets. Two triplets are duplicates when they hold the same values, even if they come from different indices or list the values in a different order. The order of the triplets in the output and the order of values inside a triplet do not matter. Return an empty list when no triplet sums to zero.
signals: The task asks for all groups of k elements (k >= 3) whose sum equals a target. Fix k - 2 elements and solve a pair problem on the rest.
The output needs values, not indices, and order does not matter. This means you are free to sort the input.
The task forbids duplicate groups in the output. Sorting puts equal values next to each other, so you can skip repeats instead of filtering with a set.
n is at most a few thousand. This allows O(n^2) work (about 9e6 steps for n = 3000) but not O(n^3).
memory_hook: Sort, fix one, squeeze two pointers, skip repeats.
approach: Sort, fix one anchor, converging two pointers. Sort the array, then for each distinct anchor run Two Sum with two pointers on the suffix, and skip any value equal to the previous one at the same level.
rebuild_steps: Sort nums and create an empty result list.
Loop anchor i over range(n - 2) and set a = nums[i]. Break when a > 0. Continue when i > 0 and a == nums[i - 1].
Set l = i + 1 and r = n - 1, and loop while l < r.
Compute total. If total < 0, move l right. If total > 0, move r left.
If total == 0, append the triplet, move l right and r left, then move l right while l < r and nums[l] == nums[l - 1].
Return the result list.
key_insight: Fixing one element turns a k-sum problem into a (k-1)-sum problem. On a sorted array, a pair-sum search is a linear two-pointer scan, because each comparison rules out a whole row or column of pairs. Sorting also makes duplicate removal cheap: equal values sit next to each other, so you skip them instead of storing and filtering results.
ladder: Brute force with a set of sorted tuples: O(n^3) time, O(t) for the set, where t is the number of distinct triplets space (too slow)
Sort, fix two, binary search the third: O(n^2 log n) time, O(1) extra besides the sort and the output space (too slow)
Fix one, hash-set Two Sum: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Sort, fix one, converging two pointers (optimal, standard): O(n^2) time, O(1) extra besides the output; Python's Timsort can use O(n) temporary memory space
Value counting over distinct values: O(n + d^2), where d is the number of distinct values time, O(d) space
pitfalls: Skipping the anchor when nums[i] == nums[i + 1] instead of nums[i - 1] loses triplets that reuse a value, such as [-1, -1, 2].
Forgetting to skip repeated anchors or repeated left values after a match produces duplicate triplets.
Not moving a pointer after a match causes an infinite loop.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
statement: You get a string digits that contains only digits from 2 to 9 inclusive. Return all possible letter combinations that the number can represent. You can return the answer in any order. The digits map to letters as on telephone buttons: 2 -> abc, 3 -> def, 4 -> ghi, 5 -> jkl, 6 -> mno, 7 -> pqrs, 8 -> tuv, 9 -> wxyz. The digit 1 does not map to any letters. Each combination takes one letter for each digit, in the order of the digits.
constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range ['2', '9'].
signals: The task says return all possible combinations, so the output size is exponential and you must enumerate every item.
The input length is tiny (at most 4 here), so an exponential number of results is acceptable.
Each position has its own fixed list of options, and you pick exactly one option for each position.
The number of positions depends on the input, so a fixed number of nested loops cannot solve it.
memory_hook: Start with one empty string, and grow every prefix by every letter of the next digit.
approach: Layer expansion (iterative Cartesian product). Start with a list that holds one empty string. For each digit, replace the list with every old prefix extended by every letter of that digit.
rebuild_steps: If digits is empty, return an empty list.
Write the keypad dict from 2 to 9, and give 7 and 9 four letters.
Set combos to a list that holds one empty string.
For each digit d, set combos to [prefix + ch for prefix in combos for ch in letters[d]].
Return combos.
key_insight: A variable number of nested loops is a recursion with one level per position. Each level chooses one option for its position, and a leaf is one complete combination.
optimal_note: The record solution uses backtracking with an index, a path list, append, recurse and pop. Both forms have the same time, O(4^n * n), and both fit the constraints. Backtracking keeps only O(n) extra memory besides the output, and it lets you prune a branch inside the loop. Use the backtracking form when the choices depend on each other, for example in Generate Parentheses, N-Queens or Word Search, or when you must stop early. For a plain product with no pruning, layer expansion is enough.
ladder: Fixed nested loops: O(4^n * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Backtracking (DFS over digits): O(4^n * n) time, O(n) auxiliary, O(4^n * n) output space
Iterative BFS layer expansion: O(4^n * n) time, O(4^n * n) space
itertools.product: O(4^n * n) time, O(4^n * n) space
pitfalls: Empty input: the current constraints exclude it, but an older version expects [] for an empty string. Without a guard, the recursion returns [""]. Return [] first.
Digits 7 and 9 have four letters, not three. A wrong keypad table gives missing or wrong combinations.
Appending the mutable path list directly stores a shared reference. Append a joined string or a copy.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
statement: You get the head of a singly linked list and an integer n. Remove the nth node counted from the end of the list. The last node is the 1st node from the end. Return the head of the changed list. The list has sz nodes, with 1 <= sz <= 30, and n is always between 1 and sz. If the removed node is the head, the new head is the second node, or the list is empty when sz is 1.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is sz.
follow_up: Could you do this in one pass?
signals: The problem gives a position relative to the end of a sequence, but you can only walk forward from the start.
The problem asks for one pass over a list of unknown length, so you cannot count the length first and then walk again.
A fixed distance k from the end suggests two pointers that keep a constant gap of k.
You must delete or insert in a singly linked list, so you need the node before the target and must stop one node early.
memory_hook: Line up the nodes behind a dummy, then nodes[-n - 1] skips its next.
approach: Copy to array with a dummy node. Walk the list once and store every node, with a dummy node in front, in a Python list. Python negative indexes count from the end, so nodes[-n - 1] is the node before the target, and you link it past the target.
rebuild_steps: Make dummy = ListNode(0, head) so that the head has a predecessor.
Walk from the dummy to the end and append every node to a list called nodes.
nodes[-n] is the target, so set prev = nodes[-n - 1], the node before it.
Skip the target: prev.next = prev.next.next.
Return dummy.next, because the head can be the removed node.
key_insight: To find the kth item from the end in one forward pass, keep two pointers k nodes apart. When the lead pointer steps past the last item, the trail pointer is on the target. To delete, stop one step earlier so that the trail pointer is on the predecessor.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses fast and slow pointers that keep a gap of n nodes. It finds the predecessor in one pass with O(1) extra memory and no list of nodes. The array version is also one pass, but it uses O(sz) extra memory. Use the gap pointers when the task asks for one pass and constant extra space, or when the list is too long to copy. The same gap finds the kth node from the end and the cut point when you rotate a list.
ladder: Copy to array: O(sz) time, O(sz) space
Two passes with length count: O(sz) time, O(1) space
Recursion counting from the end: O(sz) time, O(sz) space
One pass with fast and slow pointers and a dummy node: O(sz) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: If both pointers start at the dummy and the loop runs until fast is past the last node, slow stops on the target, not on its predecessor. Stop when fast is on the last node. Or start slow at the dummy and fast at the head, and run until fast is past the last node.

Without a dummy node, removal of the head (n equals sz) needs special code. If you start both pointers at the head, fast becomes None after n steps and the loop condition fails with an AttributeError.
If you return the original head and not the node after the dummy, the result is wrong when the head is removed.
solution:
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        # Line up every node, with the dummy in front.
        nodes = []
        node = dummy
        while node:
            nodes.append(node)
            node = node.next
        # nodes[-n] is the target, so nodes[-n - 1] is the node before it.
        prev = nodes[-n - 1]
        prev.next = prev.next.next
        return dummy.next

title: Valid Parentheses
statement: Given a string s that contains only the characters '(', ')', '{', '}', '[' and ']', determine if the input string is valid. The string is valid if all three rules hold. Rule 1: open brackets must be closed by brackets of the same type. Rule 2: open brackets must be closed in the correct order. Rule 3: every close bracket has a corresponding open bracket of the same type. Return true if s is valid. Otherwise, return false.
signals: The input has items that open and items that close. Each closer must pair with an earlier opener.
Pairs nest inside each other but must not cross, as in balanced brackets, HTML tags or start and end logs of function calls.
The most recent unmatched opener is always the only legal partner for the next closer. This is last in, first out order.
There are several pair types. One balance counter cannot work, because you must remember the order of the open items.
memory_hook: Push openers. Each closer must pop its own opener off the top. End with an empty stack.
approach: Stack of open brackets. Push every opener. When a closer arrives, the top of the stack must be its opener, so pop it. At the end, the stack must be empty.
rebuild_steps: Make a map opener_of from each closer to its opener. Make an empty list stack.
Loop over each character c of s.
If c is a key of opener_of, c is a closer. Return False if the stack is empty or the top is not opener_of[c].
If the closer passes that check, pop the top, because the closer matches it.
Else c is an opener. Append c to the stack.
After the loop, return not stack, because leftover openers make the string invalid.
key_insight: When pairs nest and must not cross, the next closer can only match the most recent unmatched opener. A stack holds exactly the unmatched openers in order, so each match check is O(1) at the top.
ladder: Repeated removal of adjacent pairs: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Stack of open brackets with a closer-to-opener map (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
Stack of expected closers: O(n) time, O(n) space
Odd-length early exit (add-on): O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: A closer can arrive when the stack is empty, as in ")" or "]". Return false in that case. Check that the stack is not empty before you peek or pop.
At the end, return whether the stack is empty. Do not return a constant true. Leftover openers, as in "((", make the string invalid.
Separate counters per bracket type, or equal counts of each type, are not enough. They accept crossed pairs such as "([)]", because the order of the openers matters.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
statement: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists, list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted list. Make the merged list by splicing together the nodes of the two input lists. Return the head of the merged linked list.
constraints: The number of nodes in both lists is in the range [0, 50].
Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order.
signals: Two or more inputs are already sorted, and the output must be sorted too. This points to a linear merge with one pointer per input, not a new sort.
The output is a linked list that you build from the input nodes. This points to pointer rewiring with a tail pointer.
The first output node depends on a comparison, or the output can be empty. This points to a dummy (sentinel) head node. The dummy removes the special case for the first node.
memory_hook: Dummy and tail. Take the smaller head, move the tail. Glue the rest.
approach: Zipper merge with a dummy head and a tail pointer. Compare the two current heads. Link the smaller head after the tail, and move forward in that list. Then move the tail. When one list runs out, link the rest of the other list after the tail.
rebuild_steps: Create one dummy node and point tail at it: dummy = tail = ListNode().
Loop while list1 and list2 both have nodes.
If list1.val <= list2.val, link list1 after tail and move list1 to list1.next. The <= keeps list1 first on equal values.
Else, link list2 after tail and move list2 to list2.next.
At the end of each loop step, move tail to tail.next.
After the loop, at most one list has nodes left. Set tail.next = list1 or list2.
Return dummy.next.
key_insight: When inputs are already sorted, the next output element is always the smallest of the current fronts. One comparison per step builds the full sorted result in linear time. A dummy head node lets you append to the output without a special case for the first node.
ladder: Collect values, sort, rebuild: O((m + n) log(m + n)) time, O(m + n) space
Collect nodes, sort by value, relink: O((m + n) log(m + n)) time, O(m + n) space
Recursive merge: O(m + n) time, O(m + n) space
Iterative merge with dummy node and tail pointer (optimal): O(m + n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to advance the tail after linking a node. Each link then overwrites the dummy's next. The result then holds only the leftover part of one list.
Forgetting to attach the leftover list after the loop. The result then loses the remaining nodes of the list that is not empty.
Returning the dummy instead of the node after it. The result then starts with an extra 0 node.

title: Generate Parentheses
statement: You get n pairs of parentheses. Generate all combinations of well-formed parentheses. Each combination is a string of exactly n '(' and n ')' characters, so its length is 2n. A string is well-formed when, during a scan from left to right, the count of ')' never exceeds the count of '(', and the two counts are equal at the end. The output order is not fixed, and the judge accepts the strings in any order.
signals: The task says generate all or return all combinations. The output size is the cost, so an exhaustive search that builds each answer once is the target.
The input bound is tiny (n <= 8). Exponential output is acceptable.
Each position of the answer has a small fixed set of choices (here two characters).
The validity rule can be checked on a partial answer (a prefix). This points to backtracking with pruning instead of generate-then-filter.
memory_hook: Open while opens remain. Close only what is open. Save at length 2n.
approach: Use backtracking and pass the string down. Grow the string one character at a time. Add '(' while opens < n. Add ')' while closes < opens. When the length is 2n, save the string.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty result list and a helper build(text, opens, closes).
If len(text) == 2 * n, append text to the result and return.
If opens < n, call build(text + '(', opens + 1, closes).
If closes < opens, call build(text + ')', opens, closes + 1).
Call build('', 0, 0) and return the result.
key_insight: When the validity rule must hold for every prefix of a valid answer, make only moves that keep the prefix completable. For one bracket type, a prefix is completable exactly when opens <= n and closes <= opens hold after every step. With exact pruning, every branch of the search ends in a valid answer, so the work is proportional to the output size.
optimal_note: The optimal code uses the same search and the same two rules. It keeps one shared list as the path. It does append, recurse, and pop, and it joins the list only at a leaf. This avoids an O(n) string copy at each node. The gain is only a constant factor here. The pruned tree has about 5 C(n) nodes, so both versions run in O(n C(n)) = O(4^n / sqrt(n)). Use the shared path when the search tree has many more nodes than answers, for example when most branches die before a leaf. Then a copy at each node costs much more than the output.
ladder: Brute force: enumerate all strings and filter: O(n * 4^n) time, O(n) extra, plus the output space
Backtracking with count pruning (optimal, standard): O(4^n / sqrt(n)) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and path, plus the output space
Closure-number DP (Catalan decomposition): O(4^n / sqrt(n)) time, O(4^n / sqrt(n)) to store the lists for all smaller sizes space
Iterative search with an explicit stack of states: O(4^n / sqrt(n)) time, O(n^2) for the pending states (each state holds a prefix string), plus the output space
pitfalls: Using close_count < n instead of close_count < open_count lets ')' come before its '(' and produces invalid strings.
Forgetting to pop after the recursive call corrupts the shared path for later branches.
Appending the path list itself instead of a joined copy stores a reference that later changes.

title: Merge k Sorted Lists
statement: You get an array lists of k singly linked lists. Each linked list is sorted in ascending order. Merge all the linked lists into one linked list that is sorted in ascending order, and return its head. The array can be empty, and any list in it can be empty (None). If there are no nodes at all, return None. Values can repeat across lists and inside a list.
signals: Several inputs are each sorted, and the output must be one sorted sequence. This points to a k-way merge.
Each step needs the minimum of a set of candidates, and the set changes by one remove and one add per step. This points to a min-heap.
Only the front element of each sorted source can be the next output. So the candidate set has at most one item per source.
Both the number of sources k and the total size N can reach 10^4. O(N*k) is about 10^8 steps and is too slow. O(N log k) is the target.
memory_hook: Heap the fronts; pop the smallest, push its next.
approach: Min-heap of list fronts (k-way merge). Put the head of every non-empty list in a min-heap. Pop the smallest node, append it to the result, and push the next node of the same list.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq.
Build heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]. The index i breaks ties, so Python never compares two nodes.
Call heapq.heapify(heap).
Make dummy = tail = ListNode().
While heap is not empty, pop (_, i, node) with heapq.heappop. Set tail.next = node, then set tail = node.
If node.next exists, push (node.next.val, i, node.next) with heapq.heappush.
Return dummy.next.
key_insight: When you merge several sorted sources, the next output is always the minimum among the current fronts of the sources. Keep only those fronts in a min-heap, so each step costs O(log k) instead of O(k). After you take a front, replace it with the next item from the same source.
ladder: Collect values, sort, rebuild: O(k + N log N) time, O(N) space
Scan all heads for the minimum each step: O(N*k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sequential fold with merge-two-lists: O(N*k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Min-heap of current heads (k-way merge): O(k + N log k) time, O(k) space
Divide and conquer pairwise merging: O(k + N log k) time, O(k) space
Counting sort on the bounded value range: O(N + V) time, O(V) space
pitfalls: Pushing (val, node) without a tie-breaker raises TypeError when two values are equal.
Pushing None for an empty list breaks the heap. Filter out empty heads first.
lists = [] and lists = [[]] must both return None. A divide-and-conquer version that returns lists[0] without a guard fails on an empty array.
solution:
import heapq
from typing import List, Optional


# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def mergeKLists(self, lists: List[Optional[ListNode]]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Heap holds (value, list index, node). The index breaks ties so
        # Python never compares two ListNode objects.
        heap = [(node.val, i, node) for i, node in enumerate(lists) if node]
        heapq.heapify(heap)

        dummy = tail = ListNode()
        while heap:
            _, i, node = heapq.heappop(heap)
            tail.next = node
            tail = node
            if node.next:
                heapq.heappush(heap, (node.next.val, i, node.next))
        return dummy.next

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
statement: You get the head of a singly linked list and a positive integer k. Reverse the nodes of the list k at a time and return the head of the modified list. k is less than or equal to the length of the list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k, the nodes left over at the end keep their original order. You must not change the values in the nodes. You may only change the nodes themselves, that is, rewire the next pointers.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is n.
follow_up: Can you solve the problem in O(1) extra memory space?
signals: The statement asks you to reverse or reorder a linked list in fixed-size blocks.
The statement forbids changing node values, so you must rewire pointers instead of swapping data.
A partial last block has a different rule, so you must look ahead and confirm a full block before you change it.
The first node of the result can differ from the original head. This points to a dummy node before the head.
memory_hook: Before, first, last, after: probe k, reverse with prev = after, link before to last, step to first.
approach: Probe, reverse, splice (iterative, in place, with a dummy node). For each group, walk k steps to find its last node, reverse the k nodes with the standard prev/curr loop where prev starts at the node after the group, then link the node before the group to the old last node.
rebuild_steps: Make dummy = ListNode(0, head) and set before = dummy.
In a while True loop, set last = before and move last forward k times. If last becomes None, return dummy.next.
Save first = before.next and after = last.next.
Reverse from first until curr is after, with prev starting at after (save nxt, point curr.next to prev, move prev and curr).
Splice with before.next = last, then move before = first and repeat.
key_insight: A block reversal inside a linked list is a normal reversal plus two splice points. Record the node before the block and the node after the block before you reverse. Start the reversal with prev set to the node after the block, so the reversed block is already attached at its tail. Then attach its new head to the node before the block.
ladder: Copy values to an array and rebuild: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Copy node references to an array and relink: O(n) time, O(n) space
Stack per group: O(n) time, O(k) space
Recursion by group: O(n) time, O(n/k) space
Iterative in-place reversal with a dummy node (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
Count first, then head insertion: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Reversing a short last group. You must confirm that k nodes exist before you change any pointer.
Losing the rest of the list. Save group_next = kth.next before the reversal starts.
Moving group_prev to kth after the splice. kth is now the head of the group, so the next group would start in the wrong place. Move group_prev to the old first node, which is now the tail.
solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, next=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.next = next
class Solution:
    def reverseKGroup(self, head: Optional[ListNode], k: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        before = dummy  # tail of the finished part
        while True:
            # 1. Probe: walk k steps to find the last node of the group.
            last = before
            for _ in range(k):
                last = last.next
                if last is None:
                    return dummy.next  # short group: leave it as is
            first, after = before.next, last.next

            # 2. Reverse first..last. Start prev at after, so first ends up pointing to after.
            prev, curr = after, first
            while curr is not after:
                nxt = curr.next
                curr.next = prev
                prev = curr
                curr = nxt

            # 3. Splice: before -> last ... first -> after. Then first is the new before.
            before.next = last
            before = first

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: You get an integer array nums. The array was sorted in ascending order and all values are distinct. Before you get it, nums is possibly left rotated at an unknown index k (1 <= k < nums.length). The result is [nums[k], nums[k+1], ..., nums[n-1], nums[0], nums[1], ..., nums[k-1]] (0-indexed). For example, [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] left rotated by 3 becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2]. You also get an integer target. Return the index of target if it is in nums. Otherwise return -1. Your algorithm must run in O(log n) time.
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
nums is an ascending array that is possibly rotated.
signals: The input is a sorted array that was rotated or shifted. Sorted order breaks at one point only.
The statement demands O(log n) time. A linear scan is not allowed, so think binary search.
The values are distinct. Then one comparison of an end value with nums[mid] tells you which half is sorted. Duplicates break this test.
You look for one exact value and return its index, or -1. This is a match search with an early return at nums[mid] == target, not a lower-bound search.
memory_hook: Find the drop, then binary search the side that can hold target.
approach: Find the drop, then search one sorted side. Use one first-true binary search template twice: first to find the minimum (the first value <= nums[-1]), then as a normal lower-bound search in the sorted side where target belongs.
rebuild_steps: Write first_true(lo, hi, ok): while lo < hi, set mid = (lo + hi) // 2; if ok(mid) set hi = mid, else set lo = mid + 1; return lo.
Set n = len(nums) and last = nums[-1]. Find pivot = first_true(0, n, nums[i] <= last). The pivot is the index of the minimum.
If target <= last, search the right side [pivot, n). Else search the left side [0, pivot).
Find i = first_true(lo, hi, nums[i] >= target), which is a normal lower bound in that sorted side.
Return i if i < hi and nums[i] == target, else return -1.
key_insight: When an array is sorted except for one break, any cut at mid leaves at least one half fully sorted. You can only trust a range check on a sorted part. So decide with the sorted half: if target fits its value range, go there; else go to the other half.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code does one binary search pass instead of two. At each step it finds the sorted half with nums[lo] <= nums[mid] and keeps that half only if target is inside its value range. Both versions are O(log n) time and O(1) space, so the two-pass version fully meets the O(log n) demand. At n = 5000 the one-pass version runs at most 13 loop steps, and the two-pass version runs at most 26. In CPython the one-pass version is about two times faster per call (about 4 microseconds against about 7). Both are far below any time limit. The one-pass version is the form that many people expect to see. Learn it when you want the shortest code, or for Search in Rotated Sorted Array II, where the one-pass form extends with lo += 1 for duplicates. The pivot search of the two-pass form does not work with duplicates, because the test nums[i] <= nums[-1] is then not monotone.
ladder: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Find pivot, then binary search one sorted segment: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Single-pass binary search on the sorted half: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Virtual unrotated index: O(log n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Use nums[lo] <= nums[mid], not <. When lo == mid the left half is one element and is sorted. A strict test sends a two-element range like [3,1] down the wrong branch.
Use the correct strict and non-strict bounds. Since nums[mid] != target at that point, the left check is nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid] and the right check is nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi].

Take the range-check bounds from the half that you proved sorted. If the sorted test uses nums[lo], check target against nums[lo] and nums[hi]. A mix such as nums[lo] for the test and nums[0] for the range fails, for example on [6,8,10,0,2,4] with target 0. The global ends nums[0] and nums[n-1] work only when the sorted test also uses nums[0].

title: Valid Sudoku
statement: You get a 9 x 9 Sudoku board as a list of lists of one-character strings. Each cell is a digit '1' to '9' or '.' for an empty cell. Return true if the filled cells obey three rules, else return false. Rule 1: each row contains each digit 1-9 at most once. Rule 2: each column contains each digit 1-9 at most once. Rule 3: each of the nine 3 x 3 sub-boxes contains each digit 1-9 at most once. Only the filled cells need validation. Empty cells do not matter. A partially filled board can be valid but not solvable. Do not check solvability.
signals: The task asks whether a value repeats inside a group. A 'no duplicates' rule points to a hash set of seen values per group.
Each item belongs to several groups at the same time, such as a row, a column and a box. Keep one seen-set per group and check every group of the item.
The groups are fixed rectangular blocks of a grid. Integer division of the cell coordinates by the block size gives the block of a cell.
The task asks only to validate, not to solve or to count solutions. One pass with an early exit at the first conflict is enough. No search or backtracking is necessary.
memory_hook: Each digit checks in at its row, its column and its box (r // 3, c // 3). A second check-in at any of the three fails.
approach: Seen-sets keyed by group, with the box as a pair key. Keep a dict of sets for the rows, a dict for the columns and a dict for the boxes. Use the pair (r // 3, c // 3) as the box key. Scan every filled cell once. If its digit is already in one of its three sets, return false. Otherwise add the digit to all three sets.
rebuild_steps: Import defaultdict from collections.
Make three defaultdict(set): rows, cols and boxes.
Loop r over range(9) and c over range(9).
Read digit = board[r][c]. Skip the cell if the digit is '.'.
Set box = (r // 3, c // 3).
If the digit is in rows[r], cols[c] or boxes[box], return False.
Otherwise add the digit to rows[r], cols[c] and boxes[box].
After the loops, return True.
key_insight: Each filled cell belongs to several groups at the same time. Give every group its own seen-set. Map each cell to its group ids with simple arithmetic on its coordinates. Then one pass finds every duplicate, because a duplicate is a value that is already in one of the sets of its cell.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same one-pass seen-set scan. The optimal code flattens the box to the id (r // 3) * 3 + c // 3 and stores all groups in plain lists of 9 sets. This avoids the import and the dict hashing of a tuple key, but the gain is only a constant factor on an 81-cell board. Use the flattened id when you need array indexes, for example with bitmasks or boolean arrays in the Sudoku Solver.
ladder: Rescan per cell (brute force): O(n^2 * n) = O(n^3) for an n x n board; about 81 * 24 checks for 9 x 9 time, O(1) space
Check each of the 27 units separately: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
One pass with a seen-set per row, column and box (optimal, standard): O(n^2), which is O(81) = O(1) for the fixed board time, O(n^2), which is O(81) = O(1) for the fixed board space
One pass with a single set of encoded tuples: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
One pass with bitmasks: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: A wrong box index gives wrong answers. The sum r // 3 + c // 3 puts different boxes on the same id, for example box (0, 1) and box (1, 0). The formula with c % 3 uses the position inside the box, not the box column.
If you forget to add the digit to one of the three sets, a later duplicate in that group stays hidden.
Do not treat '.' as a value. Empty cells can repeat freely.

title: Combination Sum
statement: You get an array candidates of distinct integers and an integer target. Return a list of all unique combinations of candidates where the chosen numbers sum to target. You may return the combinations in any order. You may choose the same number from candidates an unlimited number of times. Two combinations are different if the count of at least one chosen number is different. Thus the order inside a combination does not matter. The test cases guarantee that fewer than 150 unique combinations sum to target for the given input.
constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct.
signals: The task asks you to return all combinations, not to count them. The output can be exponential, so enumerate with backtracking.
Order inside an answer does not matter, and answers differ only by the count of each value. Treat each answer as a multiset and build it in one canonical order. Do not remove duplicates afterward.
An element may be used an unlimited number of times. Recurse with the same index. If each element may be used once, recurse with the next index.
The input values are distinct. You do not need logic to skip equal siblings.
memory_hook: Sort first. In dfs, save a copy at zero, then loop j from start: break if too big, pick, recurse with the same j, pop.
approach: Sorted start-index backtracking. Sort the candidates. Then dfs(start, remain) tries each candidate from index start onward and stops the loop at the first candidate that is larger than remain. It recurses with the same index so the value can repeat, and it records a copy of the path when remain reaches 0.
rebuild_steps: Sort candidates and make empty lists res and path.
Define dfs(start, remain). If remain is 0, append a copy of path to res and return.
Loop j from start to the end of candidates. Let c = candidates[j]. Break when c > remain.
Append c to path, call dfs(j, remain - c), then pop.
Call dfs(0, target) and return res.
key_insight: To list multisets without duplicates, build each one in a fixed canonical order. A start index forces non-decreasing index order, so every multiset has exactly one path. Recursing with the same index allows unlimited reuse, and recursing with the next index allows single use. With positive values, sorting lets you break the loop once a value exceeds the remaining sum.
ladder: Ordered sequences plus deduplication: O(n^(T/m) * (T/m) log(T/m)) where T = target and m = min(candidates) time, O(S * T/m) for the set, where S is the number of answers space (too slow)
Enumerate count vectors: O(n * product over c of (T // c + 1)) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Include or exclude backtracking (NeetCode): O(2^(n + T/m)) loose bound time, O(n + T/m) recursion depth space

Sorted start-index backtracking with break (chosen): O(M + S * T/m), where M is the number of multisets of candidates with sum at most T and S is the number of answers. Loose bound: O(n^(T/m)). time, O(T/m) recursion depth and path, excluding the output space
Unbounded knapsack DP that builds lists: O(n * T + W * T/m) where W is the total number of partial combinations stored time, O(W * T/m) space
pitfalls: Appending path instead of a copy stores one shared list many times, and every stored entry ends as an empty list.
Looping from 0 instead of start produces every ordering of the same multiset, so the output has duplicates.
Recursing with j + 1 forbids reuse and misses answers such as [2,2,3].

title: Combination Sum II
statement: You get an integer array candidates and an integer target. Find all unique combinations of elements of candidates whose sum equals target. Each element (each index) can be used at most once in one combination. The candidates array can contain duplicate values. The result must not contain duplicate combinations: two combinations that are the same multiset of values count as one. All values are positive. The statement fixes no output order, and the judge accepts the combinations in any order.
signals: The task asks for all combinations, not a count or a best value. Enumeration means backtracking.
Each element is usable once, so the recursion moves to the next index after a pick.
The input can contain duplicate values, but the output must not contain duplicate combinations. This calls for sorting plus a same-level skip.
All values are positive and the target is small. A running sum that exceeds the target can never recover, so the branch can stop early.
memory_hook: Sort, then each level tries each value once.
approach: Sort + start-index backtracking with a same-level skip. Sort so that equal values sit together. Loop from start. Skip a value that this loop already tried. Stop at the first value that is larger than the remaining sum. Recurse on i + 1, because each index is usable once.
rebuild_steps: Sort candidates and create res and path.
Write backtrack(start, remain). If remain is 0, append path[:] and return.
Loop i from start to the end of the array.
If i > start and candidates[i] equals candidates[i - 1], continue. If candidates[i] > remain, break.
Append candidates[i], call backtrack(i + 1, remain - candidates[i]), then pop.
Call backtrack(0, target) and return res.
key_insight: Sort the input so equal values are adjacent. Duplicate combinations come only from putting equal values at the same position of the path. So at each recursion level, try each distinct value at most once as the next choice. This removes duplicates during the search, without a set.
ladder: All subsets plus set of sorted tuples: O(2^n * n) time, O(2^n * n) space (too slow)
Backtracking without dedup, then a set: O(2^n * n) time, O(n) plus output space (too slow)
Sort + include/exclude backtracking with run skip: O(2^n * n) upper bound, much less with pruning time, O(n) recursion depth, excluding output space

Sort + for-loop backtracking with same-level skip and break (optimal, standard): O(P * n), where P is the number of distinct multisets with sum at most target. P is at most 28,629 for target 30, because each call holds a different such multiset. Each call scans at most n indices. Each recorded result costs O(target) to copy. Without a small target the general bound is O(2^n * n). time, O(min(n, target)) recursion depth, excluding output space
Counter of distinct values, choose a count per value: O(product of (freq + 1)) upper bound, pruned by the target time, O(d) for d distinct values, excluding output space

Knapsack-style DP over sums storing combination sets: O(n * target * C * target), where C is the number of stored combinations per sum and each tuple copy costs O(target) time, O(target * C * target) space
pitfalls: Skipping a value whenever it equals the previous array element, not only when the previous element is inside the same loop. That blocks valid combinations such as [1,1,6] that use equal values at different depths.
Forgetting to sort. The skip check only works when equal values are adjacent.
Recursing on the same index instead of the next one. That reuses one element many times, which is the Combination Sum I rule.

title: Trapping Rain Water
statement: You get n non-negative integers in the list height. They represent an elevation map. The width of each bar is 1. Compute how much water the map can trap after it rains. Return the total amount of trapped water.
signals: The answer is a sum of per-index amounts. Each amount depends on the maximum on the left and the maximum on the right of that index.
The array models bars, walls or terrain, and the problem asks how much fills the gaps between them.
A per-index formula uses min(best on left, best on right). The smaller side is the binding side, so you can decide that side early.
n is up to about 10^4 or more. An O(n^2) rescan per index is too slow in Python, so you need O(n) with precomputed or running maxima.
memory_hook: Water at i is the lower wall minus the bar: min(left max, right max) - height.
approach: Prefix max and suffix max arrays. Each index fills up to the lower of two walls: the tallest bar on its left and the tallest bar on its right. Precompute both walls in two passes. Then sum min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i].
rebuild_steps: Write the formula: water[i] = min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i].
Set n = len(height). Make left_max = [0] * n and set left_max[0] = height[0]. For i from 1 to n - 1, set left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], height[i]).
Make right_max = [0] * n and set right_max[n - 1] = height[n - 1]. For i from n - 2 down to 0, set right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], height[i]).
Set water = 0. Loop over every index and add min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i] to water.
Return water. Each max includes height[i], so every term is zero or more and the end bars add zero.
key_insight: The amount at an index depends only on the smaller of two boundary values. If you know one side is smaller than some lower bound for the other side, you can settle that side now without knowing the exact other side. So you process from the side whose bound is smaller and never need the full arrays.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses two converging pointers with running maxima. It replaces the two O(n) arrays with two variables. So it uses O(1) extra space with the same O(n) time. Use it only when a problem asks for constant extra space. To get there from this solution, note that only the smaller maximum matters. If left_max < right_max, the true right maximum for the next left index is at least right_max. So left_max alone sets the level of that index. Settle the side with the smaller running maximum and move that pointer inward.
ladder: Brute force per index: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Prefix max and suffix max arrays: O(n) time, O(n) space
Monotonic decreasing stack: O(n) time, O(n) space
Two pointers with running maxima: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: You can compare height[l] < height[r] instead of the running maxima. That version is also correct.

Match the loop condition to the loop style. In the move-then-settle style, use l < r. In the settle-then-move style with running maxima that start at 0, use l <= r, because the index where the pointers meet is not settled yet.
Adding water before you update the running maximum can add a negative amount. Update the maximum first, then add maximum minus height.
solution:
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def trap(self, height: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(height)

        # left_max[i] = tallest bar in height[0..i]
        left_max = [0] * n
        left_max[0] = height[0]
        for i in range(1, n):
            left_max[i] = max(left_max[i - 1], height[i])

        # right_max[i] = tallest bar in height[i..n-1]
        right_max = [0] * n
        right_max[n - 1] = height[n - 1]
        for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):
            right_max[i] = max(right_max[i + 1], height[i])

        # water level at i = the lower of the two walls
        water = 0
        for i in range(n):
            water += min(left_max[i], right_max[i]) - height[i]
        return water

title: Multiply Strings
statement: You get two non-negative integers num1 and num2 as decimal strings. Return their product, also as a decimal string. You must not use a built-in BigInteger library. You must not convert the inputs to integers directly. Each string has 1 to 200 digits. The strings have no leading zeros, except the number 0 itself. The expected answer has no leading zeros, so a zero product is "0".
constraints: num1 and num2 consist of digits only.
Both num1 and num2 do not contain any leading zero, except the number 0 itself.
signals: Numbers arrive as strings and can have hundreds of digits, so they do not fit in a 64-bit integer.
The statement forbids big-integer libraries and direct conversion, so you must do the arithmetic digit by digit.
The task is a basic arithmetic operation (add, multiply, subtract) on digit sequences, which signals a grade-school simulation with carries.
Small lengths (a few hundred) allow an O(m * n) pairwise loop over digits.
memory_hook: Reverse so index is the power, drop a[i] * b[j] into slot i + j, then carry once.
approach: Reverse, multiply into slots, then carry once. Reverse both digit lists so index k is place 10^k, add every product a[i] * b[j] into slot i + j, and then fix all carries in one low-to-high pass like Add Strings.
rebuild_steps: Turn each string into a reversed digit list, so index k is place 10^k.
Make slots = [0] * (len(a) + len(b)), because the product has at most m + n digits.
Double loop: slots[i + j] += a[i] * b[j], with no carry yet.
Set carry = 0. Then for k from 0 up, do carry, slots[k] = divmod(slots[k] + carry, 10).
Pop top zeros while more than one digit remains, so zero stays "0".
Reverse the slots and join them as a string.
key_insight: In positional notation, the digit at place a times the digit at place b contributes to place a + b. So multiplication is a convolution of digit lists into a fixed-size array of m + n slots, followed by carry propagation.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code has the same O(m * n) time and O(m + n) space. It keeps the original left-to-right order, so it uses slot i + j + 1. It also carries inside the inner loop and checks for zero first. This keeps every slot small at all times and avoids the reverse step. The lazy carry is also safe here. Before the carry pass, a slot holds at most min(m, n) * 81, which is 16200 for these sizes. That value fits in a 32-bit integer, so the lazy form works in any language. Both forms pass all tests.
ladder: Convert to int and multiply: O(m * n) time, O(m + n) space (too slow)
Repeated addition: O(10^n * (m + n)) time, O(m + n) space (too slow)
Sum of shifted partial products: O(n * (m + n)) time, O(m + n) space
Place-value array with carry (optimal, standard): O(m * n) time, O(m + n) space
Lazy carry (convolution then one carry pass): O(m * n) time, O(m + n) space
Karatsuba or FFT/NTT convolution: O(L^1.585) for Karatsuba and O(L log L) for FFT, where L = m + n time, O(m + n) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the zero case. A zero product gives all-zero slots, and a strip of leading zeros then returns an empty string instead of "0".
Using slot i + j instead of i + j + 1 with left-to-right indices. This shifts the result by one place.
Stripping too much. A nonzero product has m + n - 1 or m + n digits, so the array has at most one leading zero. If you do not check for zero first, the strip must still keep one digit.

title: Jump Game II
statement: You get a 0-indexed integer array nums of length n. You start at index 0. The value nums[i] is the maximum length of a forward jump from index i. From index i you can jump to any index i + j where 0 <= j <= nums[i] and i + j < n. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach index n - 1. The test cases guarantee that index n - 1 is reachable.
constraints: It's guaranteed that you can reach nums[n - 1].
signals: The problem asks for the minimum number of moves, and every move has the same cost. This is a shortest path in an unweighted graph, so think BFS.
Each position reaches a contiguous range of next positions (i + 1 to i + nums[i]). Then each BFS layer is also a contiguous range, so two indices describe it and no queue is necessary.
Moves only go forward along a line. One left-to-right scan visits the BFS layers in order.
n times the maximum jump length is large (here up to 10^7). Relaxing every edge is too slow in Python, so the solution must avoid enumerating individual jumps.
memory_hook: BFS in windows: the next window runs from right + 1 to the farthest reach of this window.
approach: Use BFS by windows. The window [left, right] holds the indices whose minimum jump count is jumps. The next window starts at right + 1. It ends at the farthest i + nums[i] for i in the current window.
rebuild_steps: Set jumps = 0 and the window left = right = 0, because index 0 needs 0 jumps.
Loop while right < n - 1, because the window does not yet cover the last index.
Compute farthest = max(i + nums[i]) for i in left..right.
Move the window: left = right + 1 and right = farthest.
Add 1 to jumps for each new window.
After the loop, return jumps.
key_insight: When each state reaches a contiguous range of next states, every BFS layer is also a contiguous range. You can then run BFS with two boundaries instead of a queue: the end of the current layer and the farthest point of the next layer. The number of times you cross a layer boundary is the minimum number of moves.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code has the same O(n) time and O(1) space. It folds the inner window scan into one flat for loop. It closes a window when i equals cur_end. It needs no inner scan, but you must stop at index n - 2 and update farthest before you check cur_end. Without the reachability guarantee, both forms need a check. In the window form, return -1 when farthest <= right.
ladder: Brute-force recursion: O(max(nums)^n) (exponential) time, O(n) space (too slow)
DP or memoized recursion over all edges: O(n * max(nums)), up to about 10^7 time, O(n) space (too slow)
Backward greedy: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
BFS by window (NeetCode style): O(n) time, O(1) space
Greedy implicit BFS in one loop (optimal, chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Looping through index n - 1 adds an extra jump when cur_end equals n - 1 exactly. Stop at n - 2.
For n = 1 the answer is 0. The loop must not run.
Choosing the index with the largest nums[i] in each window is not the same as choosing the largest i + nums[i]. Compare reach positions, not jump lengths.

title: Permutations
statement: You get an array nums of distinct integers. Return all possible permutations of nums. A permutation is an ordering that uses every element exactly once. You can return the permutations in any order.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
signals: The task says return all orderings or all arrangements. The output has n! items, so enumeration is unavoidable.
The input size is tiny (n <= 6, so n! <= 720). A bound near 10 or less signals exhaustive search.
Every element must appear exactly once in each answer. You must track which elements are already used.
The elements are distinct, so every ordering is unique. If the input has duplicates, you must add sort plus skip pruning.
memory_hook: Pick one from the pool. Recurse on the rest. An empty pool means a finished permutation.
approach: Pick from the pool. Take one item from the pool of remaining items, add it to the path, and recurse on the smaller pool. When the pool is empty, the path is one full permutation.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty result list and a helper build(path, remaining).
Base case: if remaining is empty, append path to result and return.
Loop over every index i of remaining.
Recurse with path + [remaining[i]] and remaining[:i] + remaining[i + 1:].
Call build([], nums) and return result.
key_insight: A permutation is a sequence of n choices where each choice removes one item from the pool. Depth-first search over these choices, with a choose, explore, unchoose step, visits every ordering exactly once.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps one shared path and a used array. It undoes each choice after the recursive call (choose, explore, unchoose). It does not allocate new lists at each call, so its auxiliary space is O(n) instead of O(n^2) along the recursion stack. Both run in O(n * n!) time. The shared-state form is better when the search tree is large and per-call copies cost too much. It is also the usual template for pruning searches such as N-Queens. For Permutations II, the pool form still works: sort nums, then skip remaining[i] when it equals remaining[i - 1].
ladder: Filter all index tuples: O(n * n^n) time, O(n * n!) space
Library call: O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
Remove one, recurse on the rest (NeetCode reference): O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
Iterative insertion: O(n * n!) time, O(n * n!) space
Backtracking with used flags: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary, O(n * n!) for the output space
In-place swap backtracking: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary, O(n * n!) for the output space
Iterative next permutation: O(n * n!) time, O(n) auxiliary for the working copy, O(n * n!) for the output space
pitfalls: If you append path instead of a copy, the result holds the same list object n! times. That list is empty at the end.
If you forget to clear used[i] or to pop the path after the recursive call, later branches see wrong state.
If you start the loop at a start index (as in combinations), you miss orderings. Permutations must loop over all indices at every level.

title: Rotate Image
statement: You get an n x n 2D matrix that represents an image. Rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise. You must rotate the image in-place: modify the input 2D matrix directly. Do not allocate another 2D matrix to do the rotation. The function returns nothing.
signals: The task asks for a geometric transform of a square grid (rotate, flip, mirror, transpose).
Each cell goes to a new position that depends only on its own coordinates. The transform is a fixed permutation of the cells.
The statement says in-place and forbids a second matrix. You need swaps or short cycles instead of a copy.
The input is square. A transpose keeps the same shape, so all swaps stay inside the matrix.
memory_hook: Flip on the diagonal, then flip each row.
approach: Transpose, then reverse each row. Swap each cell with its mirror cell across the main diagonal. Then reverse every row. The two flips together turn the grid 90 degrees clockwise.
rebuild_steps: Write the target map for one cell: (i, j) goes to (j, n-1-i).
Set n = len(matrix).
Transpose: for i in range(n), for j in range(i + 1, n), swap matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i]. Start j at i + 1 so that each pair swaps only once.
Mirror: for row in matrix, call row.reverse().
Return nothing, because the change is in place.
key_insight: A rotation equals the composition of two reflections. Each reflection is a set of disjoint pair swaps, so you can do it in place with no extra buffer.
ladder: Copy into a new matrix: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
