Transpose then reverse each row: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
Flip upside down then transpose: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
Layer-by-layer 4-way cycle: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: If the transpose loop lets j run over all columns, every pair swaps twice and the matrix does not change. Start j at i + 1.
If you change only the step order, or only the mirror axis, you get a counterclockwise rotation. Check the map (i, j) to (j, n-1-i) on one cell.

A one-line rebuild with zip that assigns to the name matrix only rebinds the local name. The caller's matrix does not change. Slice assignment to matrix[:] fixes the binding, but it still allocates a new matrix and breaks the in-place rule.

title: Group Anagrams
statement: You get an array of strings strs. Put the strings that are anagrams of each other into the same group. Two strings are anagrams when one is a rearrangement of the letters of the other, using every letter the same number of times. Return a list of the groups. The order of the groups and the order of strings inside a group do not matter. Every input string appears in exactly one group, and duplicate strings go into the same group. The empty string is a valid input and forms a group with other empty strings. All strings contain only lowercase English letters.
constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
signals: The task asks you to group or cluster items that are equal under some equivalence rule, not under plain equality.
The equivalence ignores one detail of each item, such as the order of letters. This points to a canonical form that removes that detail.
The output order does not matter. You only need the buckets, so a hash map from key to list is enough.
The alphabet is small and fixed (26 lowercase letters). A fixed-size count vector is a cheap, exact fingerprint.
memory_hook: Sort each word, group by the sorted word.
approach: Sorted string as key. Sort the letters of each string to get its key. Put the string into a dict of lists under that key. Anagrams sort to the same string.
rebuild_steps: Import defaultdict from collections.
Make groups = defaultdict(list).
Loop over each string s in strs.
Compute key = "".join(sorted(s)).
Append s to groups[key].
After the loop, return list(groups.values()).
key_insight: When items are equal under a rule that ignores some detail, map each item to a canonical form that removes that detail. Then group by the canonical form in a hash map. One hash lookup per item replaces all pairwise comparisons.
optimal_note: The solution_code uses a 26-letter count tuple as the key. That key costs O(k + 26) per string instead of O(k log k), so it is asymptotically better. In CPython the sorted key is still as fast or faster, because sorted runs in C and the count loop runs in Python. At max size both take about 0.11 s of CPU time. With one string of 10^6 letters, the sorted key also wins (0.17 s against 0.22 s). Use the count key when you must show O(k) work per string. Use the sorted key in all other cases, and also when the alphabet is large or unknown.
ladder: Pairwise comparison with group representatives: O(n^2 * k) time, O(n * k) space (too slow)
Sorted string as key: O(n * k log k) time, O(n * k) space
Letter-count tuple as key (chosen): O(n * (k + 26)), which is O(n * k) for a fixed alphabet time, O(n * (k + 26)), which is O(n * k) for a fixed alphabet space
Prime product as key: O(n * k^2) time, O(n * k) space
pitfalls: A Python list cannot be a dict key. Convert the count array to a tuple.
A set of letters is not a valid key. It loses counts, so aab and abb would merge.
A sum of character codes is not a valid key. Different strings collide, for example bc and ad.

title: Pow(x, n)
statement: Implement pow(x, n). It returns x raised to the power n, that is x^n. x is a real number with -100.0 < x < 100.0. n is an integer from -2^31 to 2^31 - 1, so n can be negative or zero. A negative n means the reciprocal: x^-n = 1 / x^n. Either x is not zero or n > 0, so the input never has x = 0 together with n <= 0. The true answer x^n always lies between -10^4 and 10^4.
constraints: Either x is not zero or n > 0.
signals: A repeat count or exponent can reach 2^31 or more, so one step per repetition is too slow and you need O(log n) steps.
The repeated operation is associative (multiplication, matrix product, function composition), so you can group repetitions into blocks.
The task says compute x^n, apply an operation k times, or find the k-th term of a linear recurrence with a huge k.
The task asks you to build a power function yourself instead of calling the built-in one. The interviewer wants repeated squaring.
memory_hook: Square the half, add one x if odd.
approach: Recursive halving (divide and conquer). Compute the half power x^(n//2) once, square it, and multiply by one more x when n is odd. A negative n becomes a positive n with base 1/x.
rebuild_steps: If n is negative, return myPow(1 / x, -n).
If n is 0, return 1.0.
Compute half = myPow(x, n // 2) one time only.
If n is even, return half * half.
If n is odd, return half * half * x.
key_insight: Do not apply an associative operation n times one by one. Square the base to double the block size, and combine only the blocks that match the set bits of n. This turns n steps into about log2(n) steps.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code is the iterative bit loop. It has the same O(log |n|) time but uses O(1) space instead of about 34 stack frames. Use it when a task forbids recursion or asks for O(1) space. It is also the usual template for modular power and matrix power loops.
ladder: Repeated multiplication: O(|n|) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Recursive halving (divide and conquer): O(log |n|) time, O(log |n|) space
Iterative binary exponentiation (repeated squaring): O(log |n|) time, O(1) space
Built-in power or logarithm identity: O(1) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: A negative n needs the reciprocal. Forgetting it returns x^|n| instead of 1/x^|n|.
Python floor division and right shift round toward negative infinity. Halving -1 gives -1 again, so a loop or a recursion on a negative n never reaches 0.
In Java or C++, -n overflows for n = -2^31 in a 32-bit int. Use a 64-bit type. Python ints have no such limit.

title: N-Queens
statement: Place n queens on an n x n chessboard so that no two queens attack each other. Two queens attack each other when they share a row, a column, or a diagonal (in either direction). Given an integer n, return all distinct solutions. Each solution is a board given as a list of n strings of length n, where 'Q' marks a queen and '.' marks an empty cell. You may return the solutions in any order.
signals: The problem asks for ALL valid configurations, not a count or an optimum. Listing every solution means a full search, usually backtracking.
The input is tiny (here n <= 9). Exponential or factorial search is acceptable.
The answer is a sequence of choices under pairwise conflict rules. A partial assignment can already break a rule, so you can prune early.
The rules force exactly one item per slot (here one queen per row). You can then make one decision per level of recursion.
memory_hook: One queen per row. Block the column, r minus c and r plus c.
approach: Row-by-row backtracking with three sets. Put one queen in each row, skip a column when its column, its r - c diagonal or its r + c diagonal is already used, and undo the marks after the recursive call.
rebuild_steps: Make empty sets cols, diag and anti. Make empty lists queens and res.
Define backtrack(r). If r == n, build one string for each column c in queens: c dots, then Q, then n - c - 1 dots. Append this new board to res and return.
Loop c over range(n). Skip c if c is in cols, r - c is in diag or r + c is in anti.
Add c to cols, r - c to diag and r + c to anti. Append c to queens.
Call backtrack(r + 1). Then pop queens and remove the three keys from the sets.
Call backtrack(0) and return res.
key_insight: Make one decision per level so that one constraint holds by construction (one queen per row). Then turn every remaining conflict line into a hashable key (column c, diagonal r - c, anti-diagonal r + c). This gives an O(1) is-safe check and lets you prune a partial board as soon as it breaks a rule.
ladder: Choose any n cells: O(C(n^2, n) * n^2) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
One queen per row, any column: O(n^n * n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Column permutations, check at the end: O(n! * n^2) time, O(n) space
Row-by-row backtracking with a linear safety scan: O(n! * n^2) loose bound, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
Row-by-row backtracking with column and diagonal sets (optimal, standard): O(n! * n) loose bound, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
Bitmask backtracking: O(n!) search, plus O(S * n^2) to build S boards time, O(n) plus output space
pitfalls: Forgetting to undo all three marks and the queen column (or board cell) after the recursive call. Stale marks block valid cells and lose solutions.
Appending a mutable board to the result instead of a fresh copy. Later changes then overwrite every stored answer.
Mixing up the diagonals. r - c and r + c are different families, and you need both.
solution:
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> List[List[str]]:
        cols = set()
        diag = set()      # r - c is constant on a "\" diagonal
        anti = set()      # r + c is constant on a "/" diagonal
        queens = []       # queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
        res = []

        def backtrack(r: int) -> None:
            if r == n:
                res.append(["." * c + "Q" + "." * (n - c - 1) for c in queens])
                return
            for c in range(n):
                if c in cols or r - c in diag or r + c in anti:
                    continue
                cols.add(c)
                diag.add(r - c)
                anti.add(r + c)
                queens.append(c)
                backtrack(r + 1)
                queens.pop()
                cols.remove(c)
                diag.remove(r - c)
                anti.remove(r + c)

        backtrack(0)
        return res

title: Maximum Subarray
statement: You get an integer array nums. Find the subarray with the largest sum and return that sum. A subarray is a contiguous, non-empty sequence of elements of the array. Elements can be negative, so the answer can be negative. You return only the sum, not the indices.
follow_up: If you have figured out the O(n) solution, try coding another solution using the divide and conquer approach, which is more subtle.
signals: The task asks for the best (max or min) sum over contiguous segments of an array.
Values can be negative, so a variable sliding window has no monotone rule to shrink it.
Only the best value is needed, not the list of all segments, so one rolling state can be enough.
n is up to 10^5, so O(n^2) pair enumeration is too slow and you need O(n) or O(n log n).
memory_hook: A negative running sum only hurts, so drop it and restart.
approach: Kadane's algorithm (extend or restart). Scan once and keep cur, the best sum of a subarray that ends at the current element. If cur is negative, drop it and restart at the current element, then update the best answer.
rebuild_steps: Set best = nums[0] because the subarray must be non-empty.
Set cur = 0 to stand for no previous run.
For each x in nums, set cur = max(cur, 0) + x to extend a positive run or restart at x.
After each step, set best = max(best, cur).
Return best.
key_insight: A segment with a negative sum never helps a segment that extends it to the right. So you drop it and start fresh at the next element. Put another way: the best segment that ends at i either extends the best segment that ends at i-1 or starts at i.
ladder: Brute force over all pairs with inner sum: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Fixed start with running sum: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Prefix sums with minimum prefix so far: O(n) time, O(1) space
Divide and conquer (crossing sum scan): O(n log n) time, O(log n) space
Divide and conquer returning four values: O(n) time, O(log n) space
Kadane's algorithm (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Initializing best to 0 returns 0 for an all-negative array. The subarray must be non-empty, so start best at nums[0] or negative infinity.
If you reset the running sum to 0 before you update best, an all-negative array can record 0. Update best with the sum that includes the current element first.
Iterating over nums[1:] copies the list and uses O(n) extra memory. Iterate over nums directly.

title: Spiral Matrix
statement: You get an m x n matrix. Return all elements of the matrix in spiral order. Spiral order starts at the top-left cell and moves right along the top row. When the next cell is outside the matrix or already visited, it turns clockwise: right, then down, then left, then up. It keeps turning inward until it visits every cell exactly once. The output is a flat list of m * n values.
signals: The problem asks for a fixed visiting order over a grid, not for a computed value. This points to simulation with careful index control.
The order follows the outer ring and then moves inward. This points to four shrinking boundaries, one per side.
The output must contain every cell exactly once, and the grid is small (m, n <= 10). Any correct traversal is O(m * n) and optimal, so the hard part is index correctness, not speed.
The matrix can be non-square, a single row, or a single column. This signals that the last layer can be a single row or column and needs guards.
memory_hook: Walk straight, turn right when blocked.
approach: Direction walk with a turn rule. Walk straight in the current direction and record each cell. When the next cell is outside the grid or already visited, turn clockwise and continue, for exactly rows * cols steps.
rebuild_steps: Write directions as right, down, left, up: (0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0).
Set rows and cols from the matrix. Start at r = c = 0 with direction index d = 0, an empty visited set and an empty result.
Loop rows * cols times: append matrix[r][c] and add (r, c) to visited.
Compute the next cell with directions[d]. If it is out of bounds or visited, set d = (d + 1) % 4 and compute the next cell again with the new direction. One turn is always enough.
Move to the next cell, and return the result after the loop.
key_insight: The unvisited cells always form one rectangle. Each straight side of the spiral consumes one edge of that rectangle. So you only need four bounds that move inward, and you do not need to track visited cells. Use this idea whenever a walk eats a grid from the outside in.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps four shrinking bounds (top, bottom, left, right) instead of a visited set. It uses O(1) extra space instead of O(m * n). It needs two guards so that a single leftover row or column is not read twice. Use it only when a task asks for constant extra space or does not let you mark cells. With m, n <= 10, both run in O(m * n) time and are fast.
ladder: Direction simulation with visited marks: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Rotate and pop: O(m * n * min(m, n)) time, O(m * n) space
Layer peeling with four shrinking boundaries: O(m * n) time, O(1) extra, excluding the output space
pitfalls: Reading the last row or column twice when m != n. A wide matrix leaves one row, and a tall matrix leaves one column. Guard the bottom pass with top <= bottom and the left pass with left <= right.
Mixing inclusive and half-open bounds in the same code. Pick one convention and make every range match it.
Off-by-one errors in the reverse ranges. The stop value of range must be left - 1 or top - 1 to include left or top.
solution:
class Solution:
    def spiralOrder(self, matrix: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        rows, cols = len(matrix), len(matrix[0])
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]  # right, down, left, up
        visited = set()
        result = []
        r, c, d = 0, 0, 0
        for _ in range(rows * cols):
            result.append(matrix[r][c])
            visited.add((r, c))
            nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
            if not (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols) or (nr, nc) in visited:
                d = (d + 1) % 4  # blocked: turn clockwise
                nr, nc = r + directions[d][0], c + directions[d][1]
            r, c = nr, nc
        return result

title: Jump Game
statement: You get an integer array nums. You start at index 0. The value nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. From index i you can move to any index from i + 1 to i + nums[i] that lies inside the array. Return true if you can reach the last index. Otherwise return false. Only reachability matters. The number of jumps does not matter.
signals: Each value gives a maximum step, so every shorter step is also allowed.
The question asks only yes or no for reachability, not a path or a count.
Moves go only forward along a line of positions, so one left-to-right scan can see every move.
n reaches 10^4 and one jump can span the whole array, so expanding each jump target separately costs O(n^2) and is too slow in Python.
memory_hook: Walk forward; if you pass farthest you are stuck, else stretch farthest.
approach: Greedy farthest reach, forward scan. Walk left to right and keep farthest, the right edge of the reachable prefix. If an index lies past farthest, there is a gap, so return false. Otherwise, stretch farthest to i + nums[i] when that is larger.
rebuild_steps: Set farthest = 0, because you stand on index 0.
Loop over i, jump in enumerate(nums).
If i > farthest, nothing reaches i, so return False.
Else set farthest = max(farthest, i + jump).
After the loop, return True, because no gap appeared.
key_insight: When a move allows any step up to a maximum, the reachable positions always form a contiguous prefix. So you track one number, the farthest reachable index, instead of a set of positions.
ladder: Plain recursion (try every jump): O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS (top-down DP): O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Bottom-up DP over good indices: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Greedy farthest reach, forward scan (chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
Greedy goal shift, backward scan (NeetCode): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Check i > farthest before you update farthest. If you update first, an unreachable index with a positive jump extends farthest by mistake. For example, [0,2,0] then returns true instead of false.
Do not return false only because you see a zero. A zero is fatal only when nothing reaches past it. For example, [2,0,0] is true.
A single-element array is always true, because you already stand on the last index.

title: Merge Intervals
statement: You get an array intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. Merge all overlapping intervals. Return an array of the non-overlapping intervals that cover all the intervals in the input. Example 2 shows that two intervals that share only an endpoint, such as [1,4] and [4,5], count as overlapping. Example 3 shows that the input is not necessarily sorted. The source does not state an output order. The standard answer returns the intervals sorted by start.
signals: The input is a collection of [start, end] ranges. The task asks for their union, their overlaps, or a consolidated cover.
The answer depends only on the set of intervals and not on their input order. So you are free to sort them.
The words overlap or merge appear together with intervals, time slots, ranges, or segments.
The input size is about 10^4 or more. A check of every pair is then too slow in Python, so an O(n log n) sort is the budget.
memory_hook: Sort, then extend the last one or append a new one.
approach: Sort by start and sweep. Sort the intervals, then walk them once and either extend the last merged interval or start a new one.
rebuild_steps: Sort the intervals so starts go up.
Make an empty list merged.
For each start, end: if merged is not empty and start <= merged[-1][1], set merged[-1][1] = max(merged[-1][1], end).
Else append a new list [start, end].
Return merged.
key_insight: Sorting by start turns a pairwise overlap relation into a linear scan. After the sort, a new interval can only overlap the group that is still open, so you compare it with one interval and not with all of them.
ladder: Repeated pairwise merge to a fixpoint: O(n^3) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Overlap graph with union-find or DFS: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) with an edge list, O(n) with union-find space (too slow)
Coverage difference array on a doubled coordinate line: O(n + V) time, O(V) space
Sort by start and sweep (optimal, standard): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Event sweep with an active counter: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Using < instead of <= misses touching intervals such as [1,4] and [4,5], which must merge.
Assigning the new end directly instead of taking max shrinks the group for nested input such as [1,10],[2,3].
Forgetting to sort fails on unsorted input such as [[4,7],[1,4]].

title: Insert Interval
statement: You get a list of non-overlapping intervals. Each interval is [start_i, end_i]. The list is sorted in ascending order by start_i. You also get one new interval newInterval = [start, end]. Two intervals overlap if they share at least one point. So [1,2] and [2,3] overlap, but [1,2] and [3,4] do not. Insert newInterval into the list. Merge the intervals that overlap, if necessary. The result must stay sorted by start and must have no overlapping intervals. Return the resulting list. You can build and return a new list. You do not need to change the input in place. The input list can be empty.
constraints: intervals is sorted by starti in ascending order.
signals: The input is a sorted list of disjoint items, and one new item breaks that state.
The task adds one item to a sorted structure and asks you to restore an invariant, such as sorted order with no overlap. This points to one linear pass, not a full re-sort.
The task asks you to merge overlapping intervals. This points to the interval sweep family. Two closed intervals overlap when each one starts at or before the end of the other.
The statement defines overlap as sharing at least one point. So touching endpoints merge, and the choice between strict and non-strict comparisons matters.
memory_hook: Left stays left, right stays right, the middle melts into one.
approach: Three buckets in one loop. An interval that ends before the new start goes to left. An interval that starts after the new end goes to right. Any other interval overlaps, so it melts into the new interval. Return left + [merged] + right.
rebuild_steps: Unpack start, end = newInterval and make two empty lists, left and right.
Loop for s, e in intervals.
If e < start, the interval is fully left: append it to left.
Elif s > end, the interval is fully right: append it to right.
Else it overlaps: set start = min(start, s) and end = max(end, e).
Return left + [[start, end]] + right.
key_insight: When a sorted, disjoint collection receives one new element, the old elements split into three contiguous blocks by their relation to it: entirely before, overlapping, and entirely after. Copy the first block, collapse the middle block into one element, and copy the last block. No sort is necessary.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses the same three-block idea and the same O(n) time. It moves one index through two while loops. It copies the right block with one slice, intervals[i:], so it skips the tests for that block. This changes only a constant factor. Use it when an interviewer asks for the classic three-phase form. Append, sort and merge is also correct and fast enough here, but it costs O(n log n) and ignores the sorted input. If the search must be O(log n), as in Range Module, use bisect on the starts and ends to find the middle block, then splice it.
ladder: Append, sort, merge: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Coverage array on doubled coordinates: O(n + R) where R is the coordinate range time, O(R) space
Three-phase linear scan (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) for the output, O(1) extra space
Binary search for the overlap block: O(log n) search + O(n) to build the result time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Use the correct strictness. Overlap means sharing at least one point, so [1,2] and [2,3] merge. Skip an old interval only when it ends strictly before the new start. Absorb it when it starts at or before the new end.
Integer adjacency is not overlap. [1,2] and [3,4] stay separate.

In phase 2, compare with the grown end. Here the original end gives the same result, because the old intervals are disjoint. But the grown end stays correct when the input can overlap, as in Merge Intervals.

title: Unique Paths
statement: A robot is on an m x n grid. The robot starts at the top-left corner, grid[0][0]. The robot wants to reach the bottom-right corner, grid[m - 1][n - 1]. At each step the robot moves either one cell down or one cell right. No other moves are allowed. Given the integers m and n, return the number of unique paths from the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. The test cases guarantee that the answer is less than or equal to 2 * 10^9.
signals: The question asks for the number of ways, not for the paths themselves. Counting questions point to DP or combinatorics, not to enumeration.
Moves go only down or right. The moves form a DAG on the grid, so each cell depends only on cells above it and to its left.
Many different paths pass through the same cell. Overlapping subproblems mean memoization or a bottom-up table removes repeated work.
The grid has no obstacles or weights. A uniform grid with fixed step types often has a closed-form binomial answer.
memory_hook: Fill the grid with ones, then each cell equals up plus left.
approach: Bottom-up 2-D DP table filled with ones. Each inner cell holds the paths from above plus the paths from the left, and the answer is the bottom-right cell.
rebuild_steps: Make ways = [[1] * n for _ in range(m)]. The first row and the first column stay 1.
Loop r over range(1, m). This skips row 0.
Inside it, loop c over range(1, n). This skips column 0.
Set ways[r][c] = ways[r - 1][c] + ways[r][c - 1]. The first term is the cell above. The second term is the cell to the left.
Return ways[m - 1][n - 1].
key_insight: The number of ways to reach a cell equals the sum of the ways to reach each cell that can step into it. This holds because the last move splits the paths into disjoint groups.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps one row of length n instead of the full table. It updates row[j] += row[j - 1] from left to right, where the old row[j] is the cell above. This cuts space from O(m * n) to O(n) with the same time. The binomial C(m + n - 2, m - 1) gives O(min(m, n)) time and O(1) space. You need these only when a follow-up asks for less memory or the grid is very large. At 100 x 100 the full table uses only 10^4 cells.
ladder: Brute-force recursion: O(2^(m+n)) time, O(m + n) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Bottom-up 2-D DP table: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Bottom-up DP with one rolling row: O(m * n) time, O(n) space
Combinatorics (binomial coefficient): O(min(m, n)) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the base case. The first row and the first column must be 1, not 0.
Updating the single array from right to left. Then row[j - 1] still holds the old row, so the left term is wrong.
Off-by-one in the combinatorial formula. The path has m - 1 downs and n - 1 rights, so the answer is C(m + n - 2, m - 1), not C(m + n, m).

title: Plus One
statement: You get a large integer as an integer array digits. Each digits[i] is the i-th digit of the integer. The digits go from most significant to least significant in left-to-right order. The large integer does not contain any leading 0's. Increment the large integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.
constraints: digits does not contain any leading 0's.
signals: A number is stored as an array, string or linked list of digits, so it can be longer than a machine integer.
The task is an arithmetic operation (add, increment, multiply) on that digit representation.
The digits are ordered most significant first, so the arithmetic must start at the right end.
The added amount is small, such as one. The carry is then at most 1, and it stops at the first digit below the maximum digit.
memory_hook: From the right, each 9 becomes 0 until a digit can take the +1. If all digits are 9, put a 1 in front.
approach: Early-exit carry loop (add 1 by hand). Walk from the right. A 9 becomes 0, and the carry moves left. The first digit below 9 gets plus one, and the function returns. If every digit was 9, put a 1 in front.
rebuild_steps: Loop i from the last index down to 0 with range(len(digits) - 1, -1, -1).
If digits[i] < 9, add 1 to it and return digits at once.
Else set digits[i] = 0, because 9 + 1 = 10 writes 0 and carries 1 to the left.
After the loop, every digit was 9 and is now 0, so return [1] + digits.
Check with 1299 -> 1300 and 99 -> 100.
key_insight: Adding a small constant to a digit array only changes a suffix. The carry moves left through a run of maximum digits (9s) and stops at the first digit that can absorb it. The length grows only when the whole number is made of maximum digits.
ladder: Convert to integer and back: O(n^2) in CPython in general, because decimal string to int conversion and back is quadratic. For n <= 100 the cost is negligible. time, O(n) space
General carry loop (full adder): O(n) time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for a new leading digit space
Early-exit carry loop (optimal): O(n) worst case, O(1) when the last digit is not 9 time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for the all-9s case space
Find last non-9 digit: O(n) time, O(1) extra, O(n) only for the all-9s case space
pitfalls: Forgetting the all-9s case, where the result needs an extra leading 1 (for example [9,9] gives [1,0,0]).
Converting to a fixed-width integer in other languages overflows, because up to 100 digits do not fit in 64 bits.
Iterating left to right instead of right to left, which adds at the wrong end.

title: Climbing Stairs
statement: You climb a staircase. The top is n steps away. Each move climbs either 1 step or 2 steps. Return the number of distinct ways to reach the top. Two ways are different when their sequences of moves are different, so order matters (1+2 and 2+1 are two ways). You must land exactly on step n.
signals: The question asks "how many distinct ways" to reach a target. Counting questions with a choice at each step point to DP.
Each move comes from a small fixed set of options (here 1 or 2). The count for a position is the sum of the counts for the positions that lead into it.
Order of moves matters. This means you count sequences (compositions), not sets, so the outer loop runs over positions.
The plain recursion calls the same subproblem many times. Overlapping subproblems signal memoization or tabulation.
memory_hook: The last move is a 1-step or a 2-step, so add the ways for the two steps below.
approach: Bottom-up DP table. Set ways[0] = 1 and ways[1] = 1. Fill ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2] for i from 2 to n. Return ways[n].
rebuild_steps: Define ways[i] as the number of ways to stand exactly on step i.
Make a list ways of n+1 zeros.
Set ways[0] = 1 for the empty climb. Set ways[1] = 1 for one 1-step. Index 1 exists because n >= 1.
Loop i from 2 to n and set ways[i] = ways[i-1] + ways[i-2].
Return ways[n].
key_insight: Split the count by the last move. The ways to reach a state equal the sum of the ways to reach each state that can move into it. The cases do not overlap, so the sum counts each way exactly once.
optimal_note: The optimal solution keeps only the last two values in prev and curr, so it uses O(1) memory instead of O(n). Both run in O(n) time. Use the rolling form when a problem asks for constant space. To get it, notice that ways[i] reads only ways[i-1] and ways[i-2]. Then replace the table with prev, curr = curr, prev + curr and run the loop n-1 times.
ladder: Brute-force recursion: O(phi^n), about O(1.618^n) time, O(n) recursion stack space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up DP table: O(n) time, O(n) space
Two rolling variables (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) space
Combinatorics: O(n^2) with math.comb, O(n) with incremental binomials time, O(1) space
Matrix exponentiation: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Binet closed form: O(1) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Wrong base case. ways(0) must be 1 (the empty climb), not 0. Otherwise every later value is wrong.
Off-by-one in the loop count. Starting from (ways(0), ways(1)) needs exactly n-1 shifts to reach ways(n).
Updating prev and curr in two separate statements without a temporary loses a value. Use tuple assignment.

title: Edit Distance
statement: You get two strings word1 and word2. Return the minimum number of operations needed to convert word1 into word2. Three operations are permitted on a word, and each costs 1: insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character. Either string can be empty. Both strings contain only lowercase English letters.
constraints: word1 and word2 consist of lowercase English letters.
signals: Two sequences are given and the answer is a minimum cost to transform or align one into the other.
Each allowed operation changes one character at a time: insert, delete, or replace. So you can reason about the last character of each prefix.
Both lengths are small (hundreds to a few thousand), so an O(m*n) table of prefix pairs fits.
Greedy choices fail because a local match or mismatch decision changes what is possible later.
memory_hook: Look at the last chars: same is free diagonal, else 1 plus min of up, left, diagonal.
approach: Bottom-up 2-D table over prefixes. dp[i][j] is the edit cost from word1[:i] to word2[:j]. If the last chars are equal, take the diagonal for free. Else take 1 plus the min of up (delete), left (insert) and diagonal (replace).
rebuild_steps: Make dp of size (m+1) by (n+1). dp[i][j] is the cost to turn word1[:i] into word2[:j].
Fill the edges: dp[i][0] = i (delete all) and dp[0][j] = j (insert all).
Loop i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n.
If word1[i-1] == word2[j-1], copy the diagonal dp[i-1][j-1].
Else set 1 + min(dp[i-1][j] delete, dp[i][j-1] insert, dp[i-1][j-1] replace).
Return dp[m][n].
key_insight: In an optimal edit script, the last character of word1 pairs with the last character of word2 (match or replace), or one of them pairs with nothing (delete or insert). So the answer for two prefixes depends only on three smaller prefix pairs: drop one char from the first, drop one char from the second, or drop one from each. This turns an exponential search over scripts into a table indexed by prefix lengths.
optimal_note: The record solution uses the same recurrence but keeps only two rows, prev and cur. This cuts space from O(m*n) to O(n), or to O(min(m, n)) if you pass the shorter string as word2. Time stays O(m*n). Use it when the strings are too long for the full table, or when the task asks for less space. To get it from the table, note that row i reads only row i-1 and row i. Build a new cur list for each row, set cur[0] = i, and set prev = cur at the end of the row.
ladder: Brute force recursion: O(3^(m+n)) time, O(m+n) space (too slow)
BFS over strings: Exponential, roughly O(26^L * 52L) with L = max(m, n) time, Exponential, roughly O(26^L) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Bottom-up 2-D table: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Bottom-up with two rolling rows (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(n) space
Bit-parallel Myers algorithm: O(m*n/w) time, O(sigma * m / w) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the base row and column. dp[0][j] must be j and dp[i][0] must be i, not 0.
Off-by-one errors between table indices and string indices. dp[i][j] compares word1[i-1] with word2[j-1].
Adding 1 on a match. Equal last characters cost nothing and take the diagonal value.

title: Set Matrix Zeroes
statement: You get an m x n integer matrix. If a cell holds 0, set every cell in its row and every cell in its column to 0. Only zeros that exist in the original matrix trigger this. Zeros that you write do not spread further. You must change the matrix in place. The function returns nothing.
follow_up: A straightforward solution using O(mn) space is probably a bad idea. A simple improvement uses O(m + n) space, but still not the best solution. Could you devise a constant space solution?
signals: The task says to modify a grid in place, and a change at one cell affects a whole row or column.
Writes made during a scan can be confused with original values. This means you must separate the read phase from the write phase.
The follow-up asks for O(1) extra space, and some cells of the input have a final value that you can predict. This points to storing the bookkeeping inside the input.
The needed bookkeeping is one bit per row and one bit per column. A row and a column of the matrix have exactly that shape.
memory_hook: Mark zero rows and zero columns first, then clear.
approach: Two sets, read then write. Pass 1 only reads and puts the index of each row and each column that holds a zero into two sets. Pass 2 only writes and sets a cell to 0 when its row or its column is in a set.
rebuild_steps: Get m and n from len(matrix) and len(matrix[0]).
Make two empty sets: zero_rows and zero_cols.
Pass 1: loop over every cell. If the cell is 0, add i to zero_rows and j to zero_cols.
Do not write anything in pass 1, so new zeros never spread.
Pass 2: loop over every cell again. If i is in zero_rows or j is in zero_cols, set the cell to 0.
Return nothing, because the matrix changes in place.
key_insight: When you need per-row and per-column flags but have no extra space, borrow one row and one column of the input to hold them. This is safe because a borrowed cell is only overwritten with the value it gets at the end anyway. Save the original state of the borrowed row and column first, and restore or apply it last.
optimal_note: The intuitive version uses O(m + n) extra space for the two sets. The record's solution_code reaches O(1) extra space, which the follow-up asks for. It stores zero_cols in row 0 and zero_rows in column 0, because those cells become 0 anyway when they are marked. To build it from the intuitive version, first save two booleans: does row 0 hold a zero, and does column 0 hold a zero. Then run both passes on the inner block only (i and j start at 1). Clear row 0 and column 0 last, from the two booleans. Use it only when constant extra space is required. Time is O(mn) in both versions.
ladder: Copy the matrix: O(mn(m + n)) time, O(mn) space
Collect zero positions: O(mn(m + n)) time, O(mn) space
Row and column flag arrays: O(mn) time, O(m + n) space
First row and first column as markers with two flags: O(mn) time, O(1) space
Markers with one flag (NeetCode style): O(mn) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Zeroing a row and column immediately during the scan. New zeros then spread and can zero the whole matrix.
Forgetting to save whether row 0 and column 0 had zeros before you use them as markers.
Clearing row 0 or column 0 before the inner block. This destroys the markers and wipes columns or rows that should survive.

title: Search a 2D Matrix
statement: You get an m x n integer matrix and an integer target. Each row is sorted in non-decreasing order. The first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row. Return true if target is in the matrix. Otherwise return false. The solution must run in O(log(m * n)) time.
signals: The statement requires O(log(...)) time on sorted data. A log bound on sorted data points to binary search.
Each row is sorted, and each row starts above the end of the previous row. Read row by row, the whole grid is one sorted sequence.
The question is a membership test on sorted data: is the value present or not.
A 2D container with a total order across all cells suggests that you can treat it as 1D through an index mapping.
memory_hook: The grid is one sorted list cut into rows, so binary search the flat index and divmod by cols.
approach: Single binary search on the virtual flat array. Read the grid row by row as one sorted list of length rows * cols, and run the standard binary search on flat indices with divmod(mid, cols) to find the cell.
rebuild_steps: Get rows and cols from the matrix. Set lo = 0 and hi = rows * cols - 1.
Loop while lo <= hi. Set mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
Convert mid to a cell with r, c = divmod(mid, cols). Read val = matrix[r][c].
Return True if val equals target.
If val is smaller than target, set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise, set hi = mid - 1.
After the loop, return False.
key_insight: When a multi-dimensional structure is totally ordered in its natural traversal order, it is a sorted 1D array in disguise. Binary search the flat index and convert the index to coordinates on demand with divmod.
ladder: Brute force scan: O(m * n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Binary search each row: O(m log n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Staircase search from the top-right corner: O(m + n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Two binary searches: row, then column: O(log m + log n) = O(log(m * n)) time, O(1) space
Single binary search on the virtual flat array (optimal, chosen): O(log(m * n)) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Dividing by the number of rows instead of the number of columns gives wrong coordinates on non-square matrices.
Setting hi = m * n instead of m * n - 1 with a closed interval reads past the end of the matrix.
Flattening the matrix into a new list costs O(m * n) time and breaks the required complexity, although it still gives correct answers.

title: Minimum Window Substring
statement: You get two strings s and t with lengths m and n. Return the shortest contiguous non-empty substring of s that contains every character of t, including duplicates. A character that appears k times in t must appear at least k times in the window. The window can contain extra characters that are not in t. Characters are case-sensitive. If no such substring exists, return the empty string. The test cases guarantee that the answer is unique.
constraints: s and t consist of uppercase and lowercase English letters.
follow_up: Could you find an algorithm that runs in O(m + n) time?
signals: The answer is a contiguous substring or subarray, and the task asks for the shortest one that satisfies a condition.
The condition is monotone in the window: if a window satisfies it, every larger window that contains it also satisfies it.
The condition is about multiset coverage: the window must contain required items with required counts, and extra items are allowed.
The input length is up to 10^5, so O(m^2) substrings are too many and you need a linear or near-linear scan.
memory_hook: Grow right until have equals required, then shrink left while it holds.
approach: Expand-then-shrink sliding window with a have/required counter. Grow the window to the right until every character of t has its count, then shrink from the left while the window stays valid and record the shortest one.
rebuild_steps: If len(t) > len(s), return the empty string.
Set need = Counter(t) and window = Counter(). Set have = 0 and required = len(need).
Set best_len = float("inf"), best_start = 0 and left = 0.
For each right, c in enumerate(s), add 1 to window[c]. If c is in need and window[c] == need[c], add 1 to have.
While have == required, record the window. If right - left + 1 < best_len, set best_len to that length and best_start to left.
Still in the while loop, set out = s[left] and subtract 1 from window[out]. If out is in need and window[out] < need[out], subtract 1 from have. Then add 1 to left.
After the scan, return the empty string if best_len is still infinity. Otherwise return s[best_start:best_start + best_len].
key_insight: For a shortest window that must satisfy a monotone coverage condition, the best left end never moves backward as the right end moves forward. So expand right until the window is valid, then shrink left while it stays valid. Track validity with a counter of satisfied requirements so that each step costs O(1).
ladder: Brute force over all substrings: O(m^2 * (m + |Sigma|)) time, O(|Sigma|) space (too slow)
Fix left end, extend right end incrementally: O(m^2) time, O(|Sigma|) space (too slow)
Binary search on window length plus fixed sliding window: O(m log m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
Variable sliding window with satisfied-distinct counter (optimal): O(m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
Single missing-count variant: O(m + n) time, O(|Sigma|) space
Filtered sliding window: O(m + n) time, O(m) space
pitfalls: Duplicates in t: a character must appear at least as many times as in t, not only once.
Increase have only when window[c] becomes equal to need[c], not on every add. Otherwise surplus copies count twice.
Decrease have only when window[c] drops below need[c]. Removing a surplus copy keeps the window valid.

title: Subsets
statement: You get an integer array nums. All elements of nums are unique. Return all possible subsets of nums (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets. The empty subset is part of the answer. You can return the subsets in any order.
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique.
signals: The task says return all possible subsets, combinations or selections. You must list every answer, so exponential output is expected.
n is very small (about 10 to 20). This allows 2^n enumeration.
Each element is either in or out of an answer. This is one binary decision per element.
The order inside the answer does not matter. Fix the element order to avoid counting the same set twice.
memory_hook: Each number doubles the list. Keep the old subsets and add each one plus the number.
approach: Iterative cascade (doubling). Start with only the empty subset. For each number, keep every subset you have and add a copy of each subset with the number appended.
rebuild_steps: Set res = [[]], because the empty subset is always an answer.
Loop over each number x in nums.
In the loop, write res += [subset + [x] for subset in res]. Python builds the full new list first, so the comprehension reads only the old subsets.
Do not use res.extend with a generator or append inside a loop over res. Then the loop also sees the new subsets and does not stop.
After the loop, return res. It holds 2^n subsets.
key_insight: A subset is a sequence of independent include or exclude decisions, one for each element, made in a fixed order. Enumerate all decision sequences and you get every subset exactly once. The fixed order is what prevents duplicates.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses backtracking with take or skip and one shared path. It has the same O(n * 2^n) time, so you do not need it for speed here. Learn it as the template for related problems. Subsets II, Combinations, Combination Sum and Permutations all use the same append, recurse and pop pattern with pruning. The cascade builds every subset and cannot prune, so it is a weaker template for those problems.
ladder: Ordered generation plus dedupe (naive): O(n! * n log n) time, O(n * 2^n) space (too slow)
Iterative cascade: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) for the output, O(1) extra space
Bitmask enumeration: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) for the output, O(1) extra space
Backtracking with include or exclude (chosen): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, O(n * 2^n) for the output space
Backtracking with a start index (for-loop template): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, O(n * 2^n) for the output space
pitfalls: Appending subset instead of subset.copy() stores the same list many times. At the end every entry is empty.
Forgetting the pop after the take branch leaks nums[i] into the skip branch.
Mixing the two templates causes errors. In the include or exclude template, record only at i == n. In the start-index template, record at every node.

title: Word Search
statement: You get an m x n grid of characters board and a string word. Return true if word exists in the grid, else return false. The word must be built from the letters of sequentially adjacent cells. Adjacent cells are horizontal or vertical neighbors only. Diagonal cells are not adjacent. One path may not use the same cell more than once. Board and word contain only lowercase and uppercase English letters. A letter matches only the identical character, so 'a' does not match 'A'.
follow_up: Could you use search pruning to make your solution faster with a larger board?
signals: The task asks if a sequence can be traced through a grid or graph by moving between neighbors.
A rule forbids reuse of a cell inside one path. The state then depends on the whole path, not only on the current cell.
The limits are tiny (here at most 36 cells and at most 15 letters). An exponential search with pruning is acceptable.
The answer is a yes/no existence question. The search can stop at the first success.
memory_hook: Check the cell, mark it, try four neighbors, unmark it. Speed-up: fill can-finish cells from the back first.
approach: Backtracking DFS with a can-finish guard table. First fill can[i], the cells that could spell word[i:] if a path could reuse cells. Then run the usual mark, recurse, unmark DFS with a used set, and step only on cells in can[i].
rebuild_steps: List all cells. Write neighbors(r, c) that returns the 4 moves. Set last = len(word) - 1.
Make can as one empty set per letter of word.
For i from last down to 0, add a cell to can[i] if its letter is word[i] and (i == last or a neighbor is in can[i + 1]).
Make an empty set used for the cells on the current path.
Write dfs(r, c, i). Return False if (r, c) is not in can[i] or is in used. Return True if i == last.
Add (r, c) to used. Set found = any(dfs(nr, nc, i + 1)) over the 4 neighbors. Remove (r, c) from used. Return found.
Return any(dfs(r, c, 0)) over all cells.
key_insight: Grow the path one matched letter at a time and drop a branch as soon as the next letter does not match. Handle the no-reuse rule by marking a cell on the way down and unmarking it on the way back. Then one shared grid always shows exactly the current path. For speed, solve the easy version that allows reuse with a small DP table. A cell that fails the easy version also fails the real one, so the search skips it.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses the same table and DFS. It adds two O(m*n + L) prunes before the search: a letter count check and a reversal that starts from the rarer end of the word. It also marks used cells in place with '#' and starts the DFS only from cells in ok[0]. These make easy rejections instant (for example a word that needs more copies of a letter than the board has) and save a small constant factor. They do not change the worst case found. Rows BBBBBB and five rows of AAAAAA with word 'A'*13 + 'BA' make about 1.2 million dfs calls in both versions (about 0.64 s CPU intuitive, 0.58 s CPU record). The reversal does help on some boards. AAAAAB/AAAAAA/BAAAAA/AAAAAA/AAAAAA/AABAAB with word 'A'*12 + 'BAB' makes about 0.9 million calls (about 0.5 s) without it and 60 calls with it. Add them when you want the fastest constant factor or when the board can be much larger than 6x6.
ladder: Enumerate ordered cell sequences: O((m*n)!/(m*n-L)! * L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
Enumerate all simple walks, then compare: O(m*n*3^L*L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
Plain backtracking DFS (visited set or in-place mark): O(m*n*3^L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
Backtracking DFS with count and reversal prunes (NeetCode reference): O(m*n*3^L) time, O(L) space (too slow)
Count and reversal prunes plus an adjacent letter pair check: O(m*n*3^L) time, O(m*n + L) space (too slow)
Count and reversal prunes plus a reachability table (chosen): O(m*n*L + m*n*3^L) time, O(m*n*L) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to unmark the cell after the recursive calls corrupts the board for later branches and later start cells.
Returning true before you restore the cell leaves the caller's board changed. Compute the result, restore the cell, then return.
Memoizing dfs(r, c, i) is wrong, because the answer depends on which cells the current path already uses.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
statement: You get an array of integers heights. Each value is the height of one bar in a histogram. Each bar has width 1, and the bars stand next to each other in array order. Return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram. The rectangle covers a contiguous run of bars. Its height cannot exceed the shortest bar in that run. Heights can be 0.
signals: The score of a contiguous range is the minimum (or maximum) element of the range times the range length.
Each element can be the limiting value, and its reach ends at the nearest smaller element on each side.
A brute force needs the first element to the left or right that is smaller than the current one, for every index.
The input is a row of bars or buildings, and a shorter item stops a taller item's span from going further.
memory_hook: Each bar is the shortest: stretch it to the nearest shorter bar on both sides.
approach: Nearest shorter bar on each side, found with one monotonic stack helper called twice. Treat each bar as the shortest bar of its rectangle. Find the closest strictly shorter bar on its left and on its right. The area is the bar height times the gap between those two bars.
rebuild_steps: Set n = len(heights).
Define nearest_smaller(order, default). Make result = [default] * n and an empty stack of indices.
For each i in order, pop while heights[stack[-1]] >= heights[i]. The pop leaves only strictly shorter bars.
If the stack is not empty, set result[i] = stack[-1]. Push i. After the loop, return result.
Call left = nearest_smaller(range(n), -1). The default -1 means no shorter bar on the left.
Call right = nearest_smaller(range(n - 1, -1, -1), n). The default n means no shorter bar on the right.
Return the max of heights[i] * (right[i] - left[i] - 1) over all i.
key_insight: Enumerate the limiting element instead of the range. If a bar is the shortest bar of the rectangle, the rectangle is as wide as the gap between the nearest strictly shorter bars on its left and right. A monotonic stack finds all those nearest-smaller boundaries in one linear pass, because the moment a bar is popped is the moment its right boundary appears.
optimal_note: The record solution_code does the same work in one pass. It keeps (start, height) pairs, and a popped bar gets its area at the moment the shorter bar arrives. The new bar inherits the start of the last popped bar, and a final loop flushes the bars that reach the end. It saves the two helper arrays and one pass. Both versions are O(n) time and O(n) space. Use it when you need a single pass or shorter code. The two-pass version is easier to rebuild and to adapt to counting problems such as Sum of Subarray Minimums.
ladder: Brute force over all ranges: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Expand from each bar: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Divide and conquer on the minimum: O(n log n) average, O(n^2) worst case with a linear minimum search time, O(n) recursion depth in the worst case space (too slow)
Two passes for nearest smaller on each side: O(n) time, O(n) space
One-pass monotonic stack with start index (chosen): O(n) time, O(n) space
One-pass monotonic stack with sentinels: O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to process bars that remain on the stack after the loop. They extend to the end of the array and often hold the answer, for example in an increasing array.
Using i - index_of_popped_bar as width without the start-index inheritance. A bar that popped taller bars can extend further left than its own index.
Off-by-one in the sentinel version: the width is i - stack[-1] - 1 after the pop, or i when the stack is empty.

title: Subsets II
statement: You get an integer array nums. The array can contain duplicate values. Return all possible subsets of nums (the power set). The result must not contain duplicate subsets. Two subsets are duplicates when they contain the same values with the same counts, no matter which indices the values came from. The empty subset is part of the answer. You can return the subsets in any order.
signals: The task asks for all subsets, all combinations or the power set. This means you must enumerate, so use backtracking.
The input length is very small (n <= 10 or n <= 20). An exponential output of 2^n items is acceptable.
The input may contain duplicates, but the output must not contain duplicate groups. This means you must deduplicate by value, not by index.
Order inside a group does not matter. Sort the input so that equal values sit next to each other and each group has one canonical order.
memory_hook: Count each value. Every old subset takes 0 to count copies of it.
approach: Iterative cascade over distinct values. It is the Subsets I cascade with counts. Count each value. Start with only the empty subset. For each value with count c, replace the list with every old subset plus 0, 1, ..., c copies of the value.
rebuild_steps: Start with only the empty subset: res = [[]].
Count each value with Counter(nums). Sort the (value, count) pairs. The sort is not needed for correctness, but each subset then comes out in sorted order.
Loop over each value and its count.
Build a new list. For each old subset and each k from 0 to count, add subset + [value] * k.
Assign the new list to res. Do not extend res in place, because k = 0 already keeps every old subset.
After the loop, return res.
key_insight: Duplicates come from equal values at different indices. Sort the input so that equal values are adjacent. Then, at one decision point, try each distinct value only once. Equal values give identical subtrees, so the first branch already covers them.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code sorts nums and uses start-index backtracking with the skip rule j > start and nums[j] == nums[j - 1]. It has the same O(n * 2^n) time, so you do not need it for speed here. Learn it as the template for Combination Sum II and Permutations II. In Combination Sum II, the search must stop when the sum exceeds the target, and the cascade cannot prune. In Permutations II, the order of the values matters, so counts alone do not describe an answer. The skip rule tries each value only once at one level of the search.
ladder: Brute force: all index subsets plus a set of sorted tuples: O(n * 2^n * log n) time, O(n * 2^n) space
Sort, then backtracking with a for-loop and skip of equal siblings (chosen): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra for the recursion and the path, plus the output space
Sort, then include or exclude with a jump over the equal block (NeetCode style): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
Counter of distinct values, choose a count for each: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
Iterative build with the size of the previous step: O(n * 2^n) time, O(1) extra plus the output space
Bitmask with a canonical-choice filter: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra plus the output space
pitfalls: Forgetting to sort. Without the sort, equal values are not adjacent and the skip check misses duplicates.
Using j > 0 instead of j > start in the skip check. This wrongly blocks subsets like [2,2], because it also skips a copy at the start of a deeper level.
Appending path instead of path[:]. Every entry then points to the same list, which ends empty.

title: Decode Ways
statement: A message of letters A-Z is encoded with the mapping "1" -> 'A', "2" -> 'B', ..., "26" -> 'Z'. Some codes are contained in other codes, for example "2" and "5" versus "25", so one string can have many decodings. You get a string s that contains only digits. Count the number of ways to split s into consecutive pieces so that each piece is a valid code. A valid code is a string from "1" to "26" with no leading zero, so "06" is not valid and "0" alone is not valid. For example, "11106" decodes as "AAJF" with the grouping (1, 1, 10, 6) or as "KJF" with the grouping (11, 10, 6). The grouping (1, 11, 06) is invalid. Some strings cannot be decoded. Return the number of ways to decode s. If s cannot be decoded in any valid way, return 0. The test cases guarantee that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zero(s).
signals: The task asks for the number of ways, not the list of ways. A count of ways usually points to DP, not backtracking.
The count can grow exponentially with the input length. The problem only promises that it fits in 32 bits. So you cannot list the ways one by one.
You cut a sequence into consecutive pieces, and each piece must pass a local validity test.
Each piece has a small maximum length (here 1 or 2 characters). The transition then looks back only a constant number of steps.
memory_hook: Climbing Stairs with guards: one step if the digit is not 0, two steps if the pair is 10 to 26.
approach: Bottom-up DP array over prefix length. dp[i] counts the decodings of s[:i]. Each decoding ends with a one-digit piece or a two-digit piece, so dp[i] adds dp[i-1] when the last digit is valid and dp[i-2] when the last two digits are valid.
rebuild_steps: Let n = len(s). Make dp = [0] * (n + 1). dp[i] counts the ways to decode s[:i].
Set dp[0] = 1, because the empty prefix has one way.
Loop i from 1 to n.
If s[i-1] is not '0', add dp[i-1] to dp[i]. The last piece is one digit.
If i >= 2 and 10 <= int(s[i-2:i]) <= 26, add dp[i-2] to dp[i]. The last piece is two digits.
After the loop, return dp[n].
key_insight: Classify each decoding by the length of its last piece. That length is 1 or 2, so there are exactly two disjoint cases. The count for a prefix is the sum of the counts for the two shorter prefixes, and each term is used only when its last piece is valid. The count for a prefix does not depend on the characters after it. This gives a Fibonacci-like recurrence with validity guards.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses the same recurrence. It keeps only the last two values (prev2, prev1) instead of the full array, like iterative Fibonacci. This drops the space from O(n) to O(1). The time stays O(n). You need it only when a task asks for constant space. To get it, replace dp[i-1] with prev1 and dp[i-2] with prev2. Then shift them with prev2, prev1 = prev1, cur.
ladder: Brute force over all cut positions: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Plain recursion (take 1 or 2 digits): O(phi^n), about O(1.62^n), worst case (Fibonacci growth on strings like "111...1") time, O(n) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up DP array: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up DP with two rolling variables: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: A leading '0' makes the answer 0. A guard on the single-digit case handles this.
A '0' after a digit other than '1' or '2', for example in "30", "40" or "00", makes the answer 0 for the whole string. The '0' cannot stand alone and cannot pair with the previous digit.
A two-digit piece with a leading zero, like "05", is not valid. The check 10 <= value <= 26 rejects it. The check value <= 26 alone does not.
solution:
class Solution:
    def numDecodings(self, s: str) -> int:
        n = len(s)
        dp = [0] * (n + 1)  # dp[i] = number of ways to decode s[:i]
        dp[0] = 1           # the empty prefix has one way
        for i in range(1, n + 1):
            if s[i - 1] != "0":                       # last piece: one digit
                dp[i] += dp[i - 1]
            if i >= 2 and 10 <= int(s[i - 2:i]) <= 26:  # last piece: two digits
                dp[i] += dp[i - 2]
        return dp[n]

title: Interleaving String
statement: Given strings s1, s2 and s3, find whether s3 is formed by an interleaving of s1 and s2. Return true or false. An interleaving of two strings s and t divides s into n non-empty substrings and t into m non-empty substrings. So s = a1 + a2 + ... + an, t = b1 + b2 + ... + bm, and |n - m| <= 1. The interleaving is a1 + b1 + a2 + b2 + a3 + b3 + ... or b1 + a1 + b2 + a2 + b3 + a3 + .... Here x + y is the concatenation of strings x and y. The source names the pieces s1, s2, ... and t1, t2, .... This record names them a and b, so they do not clash with the inputs s1 and s2. The definition is equal to a simpler rule. s3 uses each character of s1 and of s2 exactly once, and it keeps the relative order of the characters of each string. Any such merge splits into maximal runs that alternate between the two strings, so the run counts differ by at most 1. Thus len(s3) must equal len(s1) + len(s2). Any of the three strings can be empty.
constraints: s1, s2, and s3 consist of lowercase English letters.
follow_up: Could you solve it using only O(s2.length) additional memory space?
signals: Two or more sequences are consumed in order to build or match a target sequence. The natural state is the tuple of prefix lengths, here (i, j).
Each step can take the next item from one of two sources, and both sources can match the same item. A greedy choice can fail, so you must track every reachable state.
One index follows from the others. Here the target position is i + j. Such an index adds no dimension to the state.
The question is yes or no (can we form it, can we reach it). This points to a boolean reachability DP or a memoized DFS.
memory_hook: Take from s1 or s2 if it matches s3[i + j]; cache (i, j).
approach: Memoized DFS on (i, j). can(i, j) asks if s1[i:] and s2[j:] can form s3[i + j:]. Try to take the next character from s1. Then try to take it from s2. Cache each (i, j), so the code solves each pair only once.
rebuild_steps: Return false if len(s1) + len(s2) != len(s3).
Define can(i, j) with lru_cache. It asks: can s1[i:] and s2[j:] form s3[i + j:]?
Base case: if i == len(s1) and j == len(s2), return true.
Set k = i + j. This is the next character of s3 to match.
If i < len(s1) and s1[i] == s3[k] and can(i + 1, j), return true.
If j < len(s2) and s2[j] == s3[k] and can(i, j + 1), return true.
Otherwise return false.
Return can(0, 0).
key_insight: The position in the target is determined by how much of each source you used (k = i + j). So the state is only the pair of prefix lengths. Many different choice sequences reach the same pair, so the exponential choice tree collapses to (m + 1) * (n + 1) states.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code is a rolling 1-D bottom-up DP. It uses the same state, flipped to prefixes: dp[j] means s1[:i] and s2[:j] form s3[:i + j]. It uses O(n) memory instead of the O(m * n) cache plus the recursion stack. You need it for the follow-up that asks for O(s2.length) extra memory. You also need a loop form when the strings are long enough to exceed the recursion limit. Both solutions run in O(m * n) time.
ladder: Plain recursion (try both sources): O(2^(m+n)) time, O(m+n) space (too slow)
Enumerate positions of s1 in s3: O(C(m+n, m) * (m+n)) time, O(m+n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on (i, j): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Bottom-up 2-D DP table: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Rolling 1-D DP (optimal, answers follow-up): O(m*n) time, O(n) space
BFS or DFS on the grid graph: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Missing length check. If len(s3) < m + n, the code indexes past the end of s3. If len(s3) > m + n, dp[m][n] can be true while s3 has extra characters.
Greedy two pointers fail when both next characters match s3[k]. Example: s1 = "ab", s2 = "ac", s3 = "acab" is true, but a greedy that prefers s1 returns false.
Off-by-one with prefix lengths. The prefix form compares s1[i - 1], s2[j - 1] and s3[i + j - 1], not s1[i] or s3[i + j].

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return true if the tree is a valid binary search tree (BST), else return false. A valid BST obeys three rules. The left subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly less than the node's key. The right subtree of a node contains only nodes with keys strictly greater than the node's key. Both the left and right subtrees must also be binary search trees.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
signals: The task asks you to check an ordering property of the whole tree, not to compute a value.
The rule compares every node of a subtree with an ancestor, so a check of each parent against its children is not enough.
The input is said to be a BST, so two views apply: each node owns an open value interval, and the inorder sequence is sorted.
The definition uses strict inequalities, so every comparison must be strict, and any duplicate key makes the answer false.
memory_hook: Every node lives in a window: going left lowers the ceiling, going right raises the floor.
approach: Top-down DFS with an open value window, on an explicit stack. Each node must fit strictly inside the window (low, high) that its ancestors set, and each child gets the window narrowed at its parent's value.
rebuild_steps: Push (root, -inf, inf) onto a stack.
Pop (node, low, high) while the stack is not empty, and skip a None node.
Return False if not (low < node.val < high).
Push (node.left, low, node.val), because the parent value is the new ceiling.
Push (node.right, node.val, high), because the parent value is the new floor.
Return True when the stack is empty.
key_insight: A node in a BST must fit inside an open interval set by all its ancestors, not only by its parent. The interval is fully described by the nearest ancestor bound on each side, so you pass two numbers down and narrow them at each step. Equivalently, a BST is exactly a binary tree whose inorder sequence is strictly increasing.
ladder: Brute force by definition: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up min/max per subtree: O(n) time, O(h) space
Inorder traversal must be strictly increasing: O(n) time, O(h) space
Top-down DFS with value bounds (optimal, chosen): O(n) time, O(h) for the call stack or the explicit stack; h is n for a skewed tree space
Morris inorder traversal: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Comparing a node only with its direct children misses deeper violations, for example [5,4,6,null,null,3,7].
Using <= or >= accepts duplicates. The definition is strict, so [2,2] and [2,null,2] are false.
Using sentinel bounds such as -2^31 or 2^31-1 breaks on trees that contain those exact values. Use float('inf') or None.

title: Same Tree
statement: You get the roots p and q of two binary trees. Either root can be null. Return true if the two trees are the same, else return false. Two trees are the same when they have identical structure and each pair of corresponding nodes has the same value. A null child in one tree must match a null child at the same position in the other tree.
constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in the range [0, 100].
signals: The input is two trees and the question asks if they match position by position.
Equality of a recursive structure follows from equality of the roots and equality of the matching substructures.
Structure matters, not only the multiset or sequence of values, so a plain traversal of values is not enough.
The answer is a yes or no that can fail early at the first mismatch.
memory_hook: Both null is true, one null or different values is false, else check left pair and right pair.
approach: Recursive paired DFS. Walk both trees in lockstep: two nulls match, one null or different values fail, else the left pair and the right pair must both match.
rebuild_steps: If p and q are both null, return True.
If only one is null, or p.val differs from q.val, return False.
Recurse on the pair (p.left, q.left).
Recurse on the pair (p.right, q.right).
Return the two results joined with and.
key_insight: Two recursive structures are equal exactly when their roots are equal and each pair of matching children is equal. So compare the trees in lockstep, one node pair at a time, and treat null as a real value that must match null.
ladder: Serialize both trees and compare: O(m + n) time, O(m + n) space
Recursive paired DFS: O(min(m, n)) time, O(min(h_p, h_q)), worst case O(min(m, n)) for a skewed tree space
Iterative paired BFS or DFS: O(min(m, n)) time, O(min(m, n)) space
pitfalls: Do not compare value traversals without null markers. In example 2 the preorder of values is 1, 2 for both trees, but the shapes differ.
Handle the null cases before you read a node value. Otherwise the code fails with an attribute error on None.
Test the node for null, never its value. A node with value 0 is still a node.

title: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return the values of its nodes in level order. Group the values by level: one list for each depth, from the root level down to the deepest level. Inside each level, list the values from left to right. If the tree is empty, return an empty list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 2000].
signals: The output groups items by distance from a start point (level, depth, layer, wave, ring).
The words 'level by level' ask for breadth-first order. The words 'left to right' alone do not, because inorder also goes left to right.
The result is a list of lists where each inner list is one layer.
Any question about 'each level' (its average, its maximum, its rightmost node, its width) uses the same layered traversal.
memory_hook: Take the whole level, save its values, swap in its children.
approach: BFS with a current-level list (frontier swap). Keep a list that holds one whole level. Record its values, then replace it with the list of its children, left child before right child.
rebuild_steps: If the root is empty, return an empty list.
Set level to a list that holds only the root. Set res to an empty list.
While level is not empty, append the values of all nodes in level to res as one list.
Set next_level to an empty list. For each node in level, add its left child, then its right child, if the child exists.
Set level to next_level. After the loop, return res.
key_insight: A BFS queue holds the frontier. At the start of each round it contains exactly one complete level. If you snapshot its size before you pop, you can process one whole layer at a time.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses one deque and snapshots len(q) to pop exactly one level. It has the same O(n) time and O(w) space. It does not build a new list of nodes for each level, but it still builds a new list of values for each level. The deque form is the common template for graph and grid BFS that pops one node at a time and stores a distance with each node. For level-grouped tree output, both forms are equally valid.
ladder: Depth-by-depth re-scan: O(n*h), O(n^2) for a skewed tree time, O(h) recursion; h can be 2000 for a skewed tree, so raise the recursion limit or use an explicit stack space

DFS with depth index: O(n) time, O(h) recursion plus O(n) output; h can be 2000 for a skewed tree, which is above the CPython default recursion limit of 1000, so raise the limit or use an explicit stack that pushes the right child before the left child space
BFS with level-size snapshot (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(w) for the queue, where w is the maximum width (up to about n/2), plus O(n) output space
BFS with two lists (current and next level): O(n) time, O(w) space
pitfalls: Return [] for an empty tree. Do not return [[]] and do not push None into the queue.
Capture the level size before the inner loop. range(len(q)) evaluates once, but a while loop that re-reads len(q) mixes levels.
Push the left child before the right child, or the order inside each level breaks.

title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return its maximum depth. The maximum depth is the number of nodes on the longest path from the root node down to the farthest leaf node. Depth counts nodes, not edges. An empty tree (root is null) has depth 0. A tree with only a root has depth 1.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].
signals: The answer for a tree is a single number that you can build from the same number for the left and right subtrees.
The question asks for a longest, deepest, tallest or maximum value over all root-to-leaf paths.
The tree has no ordering rule such as a BST rule, so you cannot skip a branch. Plan one full traversal that visits each node once.
The words depth, height or level point to recursion on height or to a level-by-level BFS.
memory_hook: Depth is 1 plus the deeper child; for a very deep tree, count the BFS levels instead.
approach: BFS level count with a list per level. Keep the nodes of the current level in a list. Replace the list with the children of its nodes. Count one level for each replacement. Stop when the list is empty.
rebuild_steps: Set depth to 0 and level to [root], or to [] when root is None.
Loop while level is not empty.
Add 1 to depth at the start of each loop.
Build next_level from the non-null left and right children of every node in level.
Set level to next_level.
After the loop, return depth.
key_insight: A tree property that is defined over paths below a node often equals a simple combination of the same property on the two child subtrees. Here height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), with height(null) = 0.
optimal_note: The record solution is the short recursive form 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)), with 0 for a null node. Both solutions run in O(n) time. The recursion uses O(h) stack space, and the level list uses O(w) space, where w is the widest level. The recursive form is shorter. It is the base shape for bottom-up tree problems such as balanced tree, diameter and maximum path sum. Its recursion depth grows with the tree height, which reaches 10^4 here. This is above the default CPython limit of 1000, so it needs sys.setrecursionlimit or a judge that raises the limit. Use it when the tree height is safe or when you must combine child results bottom-up.
ladder: Brute force: depth of every node by walking to the root: O(n * h), O(n^2) for a skewed tree time, O(n) space
Recursive DFS, bottom-up height: O(n) time, O(h), O(n) for a skewed tree space
Iterative DFS with (node, depth) pairs: O(n) time, O(h), O(n) for a skewed tree space
BFS level-order count: O(n) time, O(w), where w is the maximum width of a level space
pitfalls: Depth counts nodes, not edges. A single node has depth 1, not 0.
Return 0 for an empty tree. Do not dereference root before the null check.

A skewed tree with 10^4 nodes makes the recursion 10^4 calls deep. The default CPython limit is 1000, so plain recursion raises RecursionError in a local run. The LeetCode judge raises the limit, so the recursive solution passes there. Use BFS or an explicit stack when you cannot control the limit.

title: Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal
statement: You get two integer arrays, preorder and inorder. preorder is the preorder traversal of a binary tree. inorder is the inorder traversal of the same tree. Construct the binary tree and return its root. All values are unique. Each value of inorder also appears in preorder. Both arrays are guaranteed to be valid traversals of one tree, so exactly one tree matches them.
constraints: preorder and inorder consist of unique values.
signals: The input is two traversal orders of the same tree and the task is to rebuild the tree.
One traversal tells you which node is the root. In preorder the root is first. In postorder the root is last.
The other traversal tells you which nodes go left and which go right of that root. Inorder splits at the root.
Values are unique. So a hash map gives the position of any value in O(1).
memory_hook: Preorder names the root. Inorder splits at the root. Slice both lists and push each side as a job.
