approach: Slice split with a job stack. The first preorder value is the root, and its inorder position splits the other values into a left part and a right part. Each job is a node with the preorder and inorder lists of its subtree.
rebuild_steps: Make root from preorder[0] and push the job (root, preorder, inorder) on a stack.
While the stack is not empty, pop a job (node, pre, ino). Set mid = ino.index(node.val). mid is the size of the left subtree.
The left lists are pre[1:mid+1] and ino[:mid]. The right lists are pre[mid+1:] and ino[mid+1:].
For each side with a non-empty preorder list, make the child from the first value of that list. Link the child to node and push its job.
After the loop, return root.
key_insight: One traversal identifies the root, and the inorder traversal partitions the remaining nodes around that root. Every subtree is a contiguous block in every traversal, so you can describe a subtree by index bounds and recurse. Precompute value-to-index with a hash map so each split costs O(1).
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses the same split rule in O(n) time. It removes the two costs of the slice version. A hash map from value to inorder index replaces ino.index. Inorder bounds (lo, hi) replace the copied lists. One shared preorder pointer gives the next root. This works only if you build the left subtree before the right subtree. Use it when the task asks for O(n) time or when n is much larger than 3000. It recurses to depth n. In plain CPython, a 3000-node chain needs sys.setrecursionlimit. To upgrade from the intuitive version, keep the hook and make two changes. Look up mid in a dict. Then recurse on inorder bounds with a shared preorder pointer.
ladder: Brute force over all tree shapes: O(Catalan(n) * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Recursion with list slicing and linear search: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
Hash map of inorder indices plus preorder pointer (optimal, chosen): O(n) time, O(n) space
Recursion with index arithmetic (preorder start, inorder start, size): O(n) time, O(n) space
Iterative stack: O(n) time, O(n) space
Recursion with a stop value (no hash map): O(n) time, O(h) space
pitfalls: Building the right subtree before the left subtree breaks the shared preorder pointer.
Off-by-one errors in the preorder block sizes. With copied sublists, the left block is the mid values after the root. With index bounds, the left size is mid - lo, not mid.
A linear search for the root in inorder at each call makes the solution O(n^2). Use a hash map.
solution:
class Solution:
    def buildTree(self, preorder: List[int], inorder: List[int]) -> Optional[TreeNode]:
        # Job = (node, preorder of its subtree, inorder of its subtree).
        # The node is already made from the first preorder value.
        root = TreeNode(preorder[0])
        stack = [(root, preorder, inorder)]
        while stack:
            node, pre, ino = stack.pop()
            mid = ino.index(node.val)  # values left of the root = size of the left subtree
            left_pre, left_ino = pre[1:mid + 1], ino[:mid]
            right_pre, right_ino = pre[mid + 1:], ino[mid + 1:]
            if left_pre:
                node.left = TreeNode(left_pre[0])
                stack.append((node.left, left_pre, left_ino))
            if right_pre:
                node.right = TreeNode(right_pre[0])
                stack.append((node.right, right_pre, right_ino))
        return root

title: Balanced Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return true if the tree is height-balanced, else return false. A tree is height-balanced when, at every node, the heights of the left subtree and the right subtree differ by at most one. The rule applies to every node, not only to the root. An empty tree is height-balanced. Node values do not affect the answer.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 5000].
signals: The condition must hold at every node, and each node's check needs a number computed from its subtrees, such as height, size or sum.
A first idea calls a helper on every node, and that helper traverses the whole subtree again. This repeats work and signals that the helper and the check can merge into one pass.
The output is one yes or no for the whole tree, but the local check needs numeric data from the children. The recursion must return more than the final answer.
The tree can be skewed, so its height can reach n. A full subtree scan at every node then costs up to O(n^2), and the recursion can go n calls deep.
memory_hook: List parents first, walk backwards, compare child heights.
approach: Reverse a parent-first list and keep a height dictionary. Use a stack to list the nodes so that each parent comes before its children. Walk the list backwards. Both children of a node then have a height before you reach the node. At each node, compare the two child heights. Return false when they differ by more than one. Otherwise store 1 + the larger height.
rebuild_steps: Make order = []. Start stack with root, or with nothing when root is None.
Pop a node, append it to order, and push its non-None children. Repeat until the stack is empty.
Make height = {None: 0}. A missing child then has height 0.
Loop over reversed(order). Both children of each node already have a height.
Read left = height[node.left] and right = height[node.right]. Return False if abs(left - right) > 1.
Store height[node] = 1 + max(left, right).
After the loop, return True. An empty tree gives an empty order, so it also returns True.
key_insight: When a rule at every node depends on a value that its subtrees produce, compute that value bottom-up once and test the rule in the same call. Return the extra status with the value, as a pair or as an impossible sentinel value.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code is a recursive postorder. It returns the height, or -1 when a subtree is unbalanced. It also runs in O(n) time. It stops at the first failure and skips the rest of the tree. The intuitive version always lists all nodes first. The recursive version uses O(h) extra space instead of an O(n) list and dictionary, and it needs no hashing. Use it when you must write the recursive form or save memory. Test each child result for -1 before you compare heights. In plain CPython, raise the recursion limit for a 5000-node chain.
ladder: Top-down height recomputation (brute force): O(n^2) upper bound, O(n log n) on a balanced tree time, O(h), O(n) worst case space
Bottom-up postorder returning a (balanced, height) pair: O(n) time, O(h), O(n) worst case space
Bottom-up postorder with -1 sentinel and early exit (chosen): O(n) time, O(h), O(n) worst case space
Iterative postorder with an explicit stack: O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Checking only the root. Two equal-length chains under the root pass at the root but fail at the nodes below.
Not propagating the -1 sentinel. If left is -1 and right is 0, abs(-1 - 0) is 1, so the check passes and the failure disappears. Test each child result for -1 before you use it.
Mixing height conventions. If an empty tree has height -1 (edge count), then -1 cannot be the failure sentinel. Use -2, None or a tuple instead.
solution:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, val=0, left=None, right=None):
#         self.val = val
#         self.left = left
#         self.right = right
class Solution:
    def isBalanced(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> bool:
        # 1. List the nodes so that each parent comes before its children.
        order = []
        stack = [root] if root else []
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            order.append(node)
            if node.left:
                stack.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                stack.append(node.right)

        # 2. Walk the list backwards: children are done before parents.
        height = {None: 0}
        for node in reversed(order):
            left = height[node.left]
            right = height[node.right]
            if abs(left - right) > 1:
                return False
            height[node] = 1 + max(left, right)
        return True

title: Distinct Subsequences
statement: Given two strings s and t, return the number of distinct subsequences of s that equal t. A subsequence keeps the relative order of the characters and may delete any number of characters. Two subsequences are different when they use different sets of indices in s, even if they spell the same string. Letters are case sensitive. The test cases guarantee that the answer fits in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: s and t consist of English letters.
signals: The question asks for the number of ways, not one witness. Counting all choices points to DP that adds disjoint cases, not to backtracking.
Two sequences appear, and one must fit inside the other in order. This points to a DP state over a pair of prefixes (i, j).
The word subsequence means you may skip characters of the long string but must keep order. Skip gives one transition and match gives another.
Both lengths are up to 1000. An m x n table has about 1e6 cells, which fits the time budget. Exponential enumeration does not.
memory_hook: Ways equal skip plus use: dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j], plus dp[i-1][j-1] on a match.
approach: Bottom-up 2D table over prefixes (skip or use the last character of s). dp[i][j] counts the ways to form t[:j] from s[:i]: you always add the ways that skip s[i-1], and you also add the ways that use s[i-1] when it equals t[j-1].
rebuild_steps: Define dp[i][j] as the number of ways to form t[:j] from s[:i], with an (m+1) x (n+1) table of zeros.
Set dp[i][0] = 1 for every i, because an empty t has exactly one way: choose nothing.
Loop i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n.
Skip case: set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j].
Use case: if s[i-1] == t[j-1], add dp[i-1][j-1].
Return dp[m][n].
key_insight: Split the ways to form t[:j] from s[:i] by the fate of the last character of s: skip it or use it as the last character of t[:j]. These two groups do not overlap and together cover every way, so the count is their sum. Each group is a smaller prefix-pair problem.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps only one row of length n+1 and updates j from right to left, so space drops from O(m*n) to O(n). The right-to-left order keeps dp[j-1] at its old value, as in 0/1 knapsack. Time stays O(m*n). Use it when memory is tight or an interviewer asks for O(n) space. The constraints do not require it.
ladder: Enumerate index combinations: O(C(m, n) * n), up to O(2^m * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Plain take-or-skip recursion: O(2^m) time, O(m) recursion depth space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on (i, j): O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Bottom-up 2D table: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
1D rolling array, j from right to left (chosen): O(m * n) time, O(n) space
1D array with precomputed positions in t: O(m + n + number of matching (i, j) pairs), worst O(m * n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: In the 2D table, set dp[i][0] = 1 for every i, not only dp[0][0]. Without it, a character of s after index 0 can never start a match of t[0]. For example s = 'ba', t = 'a' gives 0 instead of 1.
In the 1D version a left-to-right inner loop reads an already updated dp[j-1]. Then one character of s matches two characters of t. For example s = 'a', t = 'aa' gives 1 instead of 0.
On a match you must add both cases, skip and use. Taking only dp[i-1][j-1] loses all ways that skip s[i-1].

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock
statement: You get an array prices. prices[i] is the price of one stock on day i. You may do at most one transaction: buy one stock on a single day, then sell it on a different, later day. You must buy before you sell. Return the maximum profit you can get from this transaction. If no transaction gives a profit, return 0.
signals: The task asks for the maximum of a[j] - a[i] (or another pair score) with the order constraint i < j.
The length goes up to 10^5, so a check of all O(n^2) pairs is too slow and the target is one O(n) pass.
The answer depends on the best partner on one side only. For a fixed right end, only one summary of the prefix matters (here, the minimum).
The rule 'return 0 if no profit' means the empty choice is allowed. Start the answer at 0.
memory_hook: Remember the cheapest day, sell today.
approach: Running minimum in one pass. Treat each day as the sell day. Buy at the lowest price seen so far. The answer is the largest value of price - min_price.
rebuild_steps: Set min_price = prices[0] and best = 0. A best of 0 means no trade.
Loop over each price. Treat it as the sell day.
Update min_price = min(min_price, price). Now min_price is the lowest price from the first day to today, so the buy day is never after the sell day.
Update best = max(best, price - min_price). If today is the new minimum, this profit is 0 and changes nothing.
Return best after the loop.
key_insight: For a pair problem with the order i < j, fix the right element and ask what the best left partner is. If that partner is an extreme value of the prefix, one running variable replaces the inner loop.
ladder: Brute force over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Suffix maximum array: O(n) time, O(n) space
Running prefix minimum (one pass): O(n) time, O(1) space
Two pointers / sliding window (NeetCode video): O(n) time, O(1) space
Kadane on daily differences: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Do not return a negative value. Start the answer at 0, because not trading is allowed.
Do not use the global minimum and global maximum. The minimum can come after the maximum, as in [2,4,1] where the answer is 2, not 0 or 3.
Do not sell before you buy. The buy price must come from an index at or before the sell index.

title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
statement: A path in a binary tree is a sequence of nodes where each pair of adjacent nodes in the sequence has an edge that connects them. A node can appear in the sequence at most once. The path does not need to pass through the root. The path sum of a path is the sum of the node values in the path. Given the root of a binary tree, return the maximum path sum of any non-empty path.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 3 * 10^4].
signals: The task asks for a best path in a tree that can start and end at any node, not only at the root or a leaf.
The path can bend at a node and use two child branches. A shape with one turning point suggests that you enumerate the turning point.
The best value at a node depends on results from both subtrees, which points to a post-order (bottom-up) DFS.
Values can be negative, so a part of the path can make the total worse and you must be able to drop it.
memory_hook: List parents first, then walk back. At each node, cut negative sides to 0, record left plus me plus right, and store me plus the better side.
approach: Parents-first list, then a backward loop with a gain map. Collect the nodes with a stack so each parent comes before its children. Then walk the list backwards and apply the apex rule at each node. Clamp each child gain at 0, record the path that bends at the node, and store the best one-sided chain.
rebuild_steps: Set stack = [root] and order = []. Pop a node, append it to order, and push its children that are not None. Repeat until the stack is empty. Now every parent comes before its children.
Set gain = {None: 0} and best = root.val. The None entry gives a missing child a gain of 0.
Loop over reversed(order), so both children of a node already have a gain.
Set left and right to the child gains, clamped at 0 with max(..., 0).
Update best with node.val + left + right, the path that bends at this node.
Store gain[node] = node.val + max(left, right), because only one side can go up to the parent.
After the loop, return best.
key_insight: A tree path has one highest node. At that node, the path is a left chain plus the node plus a right chain. So the DFS returns a different value than it records: it returns the best one-sided chain to the parent, and it records the best two-sided path in a global answer.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code is the recursive form of the same O(n) idea. It is shorter and reads like the definition of gain, but it uses a nonlocal variable and its depth equals the tree height. A skewed tree with 3 * 10^4 nodes raises RecursionError at the default CPython limit of 1000, so it needs sys.setrecursionlimit to run locally. Use the recursive form when the judge raises the limit or when the tree is balanced; use the backward loop when the depth can be large.
ladder: All pairs of endpoints: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Try each node as apex, recompute chains: O(n^2) worst case, O(n log n) when balanced time, O(h) space (too slow)
Post-order DFS with gain return and global best: O(n) time, O(h) recursion stack, O(n) for a skewed tree space
Iterative post-order with a gain map: O(n) time, O(n) space
DFS that returns a pair: O(n) time, O(h) space
pitfalls: Returning node.val + left + right to the parent is wrong. A path cannot branch, so only one side can go up.
Initializing best to 0 is wrong when all values are negative. The answer must be a non-empty path, so start from root.val or negative infinity.
Clamping the node's own value at 0 is wrong. The node is always on its own chain; only child gains are optional.
solution:
class Solution:
    def maxPathSum(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        # 1. List the nodes so that every parent comes before its children.
        order = []
        stack = [root]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            order.append(node)
            if node.left:
                stack.append(node.left)
            if node.right:
                stack.append(node.right)

        # 2. Walk the list backwards, so both children finish before the parent.
        gain = {None: 0}  # gain[node] = best downward chain that starts at node
        best = root.val   # a single node is a valid path
        for node in reversed(order):
            left = max(gain[node.left], 0)    # drop a negative branch
            right = max(gain[node.right], 0)
            best = max(best, node.val + left + right)  # path that bends here
            gain[node] = node.val + max(left, right)   # only one side goes up
        return best

title: Valid Palindrome
statement: A phrase is a palindrome if it reads the same forward and backward after two changes. First, convert all uppercase letters to lowercase. Second, remove all non-alphanumeric characters. Alphanumeric characters are letters and digits. Given a string s, return true if s is a palindrome under this rule, else return false. A string that becomes empty after filtering is a palindrome.
constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters.
signals: The task asks if a sequence reads the same forward and backward. This means you compare position k with position n-1-k.
The task says to ignore some characters or to normalize case. This means you skip or transform items on the fly instead of building a clean copy.
The answer is a yes or no about symmetry of the whole sequence. Two pointers that move from both ends toward the middle give this check in one pass.

The input can be long (here up to 2 * 10^5), so quadratic work is too slow and one linear pass is the target. When the task wants O(1) extra space, walk the original input with pointers instead of building a cleaned copy.
memory_hook: Clean it, flip it, compare.
approach: Clean, then compare with the reverse. Keep only the letters and digits in lowercase, then check that this list equals its own reverse.
rebuild_steps: Clean: build a list named cleaned that holds ch.lower() for each ch in s where ch.isalnum() is true.
Flip: get the reverse of the list with the slice cleaned[::-1].
Compare: return cleaned == cleaned[::-1].
Check the edge: a string with no letters or digits gives an empty list, and an empty list equals its reverse, so the result is true.
key_insight: A symmetry check needs only pairwise comparisons from the two ends. You can filter and normalize characters during the walk, so you never need to build a cleaned copy.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses two pointers that move inward from both ends. They skip characters that are not letters or digits and compare lowercase pairs. It uses O(1) extra space instead of an O(n) cleaned copy, and it stops at the first mismatch. Use it when a task asks for constant extra space, or as the template for Valid Palindrome II, where you branch on the first mismatch. Both solutions are O(n) time and both fit the limits.
ladder: Filter and reverse: O(n) time, O(n) space
Filter by repeated string concatenation: O(n^2) worst case, O(n) typical in CPython time, O(n) space
Filter into a list, then two pointers: O(n) time, O(n) space
Two pointers converging with skips (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Digits count as alphanumeric. "0P" is false, not true, because '0' and 'p' differ.
A string with no alphanumeric characters, such as " " or ".,", is a palindrome. Return true, not false.
If you skip invalid characters with inner while loops, each inner loop must also check i < j. Without that check, a string of only punctuation, such as "!!", moves the index out of range.

title: Word Ladder
statement: You get two words, beginWord and endWord, and a dictionary wordList. A transformation sequence is beginWord -> s1 -> s2 -> ... -> sk. Every adjacent pair of words in the sequence differs by exactly one letter. Every si for 1 <= i <= k is in wordList. beginWord does not need to be in wordList. The last word sk equals endWord. Return the number of words in the shortest transformation sequence, counting beginWord. Return 0 if no such sequence exists. All words have the same length and contain only lowercase English letters. beginWord is different from endWord, and all words in wordList are unique.
signals: The question asks for the shortest sequence or the minimum number of steps from a start state to a target state.
Each step makes one small local change to a state, such as one letter, one digit or one swap.
Every step costs the same, so the implicit graph is unweighted and BFS gives the minimum.
The legal states come from a given list or set, so a hash set tells you if a state is legal.
memory_hook: BFS of (word, length) pairs: change one letter, keep the word only if it is still in the unvisited set.
approach: Use BFS with (word, length) pairs and one unvisited set. Start from beginWord with length 1. Change one letter at a time. Enqueue each new word that is still in the unvisited set, with length + 1.
rebuild_steps: Import deque from collections and ascii_lowercase from string.
Make unvisited = set(wordList) and discard beginWord from it.
Put (beginWord, 1) in a deque. The 1 counts beginWord itself.
While the queue is not empty, pop (word, length) from the left. If word == endWord, return length.
For each position i and each letter c, build nxt = word[:i] + c + word[i + 1:].
If nxt is in unvisited, remove it and append (nxt, length + 1).
When the queue is empty, return 0.
key_insight: Treat each state as a node and each allowed one-step edit as an unweighted edge. The minimum number of edits is the BFS distance. Generate neighbors from the small edit space (positions times letters) and check them in a hash set. Do not compare every pair of states.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses the same algorithm with the same O(26 * N * L^2) time. It processes the queue level by level with one length counter. It slices the prefix and the suffix once per position, not once per letter. It also returns 0 at once when endWord is not in wordList, so it skips a search that cannot succeed. On a full scan of 5000 words of length 10, it used about 0.25 s of CPU time and the intuitive code used about 0.46 s. You do not need this speed at these constraints. The level-by-level form is useful when you must act on a whole level at once, as in Word Ladder II. Bidirectional BFS is the next step when the graph is much larger.
ladder: Backtracking DFS over all ladders: O(N!) in the worst case time, O(N) space (too slow)
Explicit graph by pairwise comparison, then BFS: O(N^2 * L) time, O(N + E), E <= 25 * L * N space (too slow)
BFS with letter substitution (chosen): O(26 * N * L^2) time, O(N * L) space
BFS with wildcard pattern buckets: O(N * L * (L + 26)) time, O(N * L^2) space
Bidirectional BFS: O(26 * N * L^2) time, O(N * L) space
pitfalls: The answer counts words, not edges. Start the counter at 1 for beginWord.
Return 0 at once if endWord is not in wordList.
beginWord can also be in wordList. Remove it from the unvisited set so it is not enqueued again.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
statement: You get an unsorted array of integers nums. Return the length of the longest sequence of consecutive integer values (x, x+1, x+2, ...) whose values all appear in nums. The values do not need to be adjacent in the array, and their order in the array does not matter. Duplicate values count only once in a sequence. An empty array gives 0. Your algorithm must run in O(n) time.
signals: The answer depends on the order of values, not on positions in the array. Sorting is the first idea.
The statement demands O(n) time on a problem that sorting solves in O(n log n). You must replace the sort with hash lookups.
The question asks about neighbors in value space (x-1 and x+1), not neighbors in index space. A hash set answers 'is this neighbor present?' in O(1) on average.
The values span about 2*10^9. A counting array indexed by value does not fit, but a hash set does.
memory_hook: Only start counting where x-1 is missing.
approach: Hash set, count only from run starts. Put the values in a set. A value starts a run when its predecessor is missing. From each start, count up while the next value is in the set.
rebuild_steps: Make values = set(nums) and set longest = 0.
Loop over the set, not over nums, so a repeated start walks once.
If start - 1 is in values, skip it, because it is not a run start.
Set length = 1 and add 1 while start + length is in values.
Keep longest = max(longest, length) and return longest.
key_insight: Do the work only at the start of each group. A value starts a run exactly when its predecessor is absent. Each run is then measured once, and the total work is linear.
ladder: Brute force scan: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Hash set, walk from every value: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Sort and scan: O(n log n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Hash set, walk only from run starts: O(n) average, because each set lookup is O(1) on average time, O(n) space
Hash map of run lengths at boundaries: O(n) average time, O(n) space
Union-find on values: O(n alpha(n)) average, because the value-to-node map is a hash map time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Iterating over nums instead of the set can give O(n^2) time when one run start appears many times. An example is 50000 copies of 1 followed by 1..50000.
Forgetting the start check makes the algorithm O(n^2) on one long run.
An empty array must return 0. Initialize longest to 0, not 1.

title: Surrounded Regions
statement: You get an m x n matrix board. Each cell holds the letter 'X' or 'O'. A cell connects to its horizontal and vertical neighbors only, not to diagonal neighbors. A region is a maximal group of connected 'O' cells. A region is surrounded if none of its 'O' cells is on the edge of the board; such a region is completely enclosed by 'X' cells. Capture every surrounded region: replace all its 'O' cells with 'X'. Modify the board in place. Do not return anything. 'O' regions that touch the edge stay unchanged.
signals: The grid holds two cell types, and the task changes whole 4-connected groups of one type.
A group's fate depends on whether it touches the border. This is a reachability question.
The rule says 'surrounded', 'enclosed' or 'cannot escape'. The complement, 'can reach the edge', is easier to test from the edge.
Up to 40,000 cells means one search per cell, O((m*n)^2), is too slow. Aim for one pass that visits each cell a constant number of times.
memory_hook: Flood from the border, O becomes T; then O to X, T to O.
approach: Flood from the border, then decode. Push every border cell onto a stack. Pop a cell. If it is an 'O' on the board, mark it 'T' (safe) and push its 4 neighbors. When the stack is empty, sweep the board once: each remaining 'O' becomes 'X', and each 'T' becomes 'O' again.
rebuild_steps: Get rows and cols. Put every border cell (r in (0, rows-1) or c in (0, cols-1)) on a stack.
Pop a cell. If it is on the board and is 'O', change it to 'T'.
After you mark it, push its 4 neighbors. Do not check them yet.
Repeat until the stack is empty.
Sweep the board: 'O' becomes 'X' (captured), 'T' becomes 'O' (safe).
key_insight: Do not test each region for being enclosed. Test the opposite, reachability from the boundary, with one flood fill that starts at all boundary cells. Everything the flood does not reach is enclosed.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same reverse flood from the border, with O(m*n) time and space. The record's solution_code checks each neighbor before it pushes it and uses a BFS deque. So each cell enters the queue at most once. The intuitive version checks a cell when it pops it, so a cell can be pushed up to 4 times. This costs a constant factor only. Check before push when memory is tight, or when you need exact BFS distances with mark-on-push, for example in Walls and Gates.
ladder: Per-cell search (brute force): O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
Per-region search from the interior: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Reverse flood fill from the border (BFS or DFS): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Union-Find with a virtual border node: O(m*n * alpha(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Checking 'O' cells from the interior and deciding too early: a region is safe if any one of its cells touches the edge.
Treating diagonal neighbors as connected; only up, down, left and right count.

Recursive DFS can reach a depth near m*n (40,000) on a 200x200 board, for example an all-'O' board or a long snake path. This exceeds CPython's default recursion limit of 1000. Use iterative BFS or an explicit stack, or raise the limit.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
statement: You get a string s. Split s into contiguous, non-empty substrings so that every substring is a palindrome. A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Return all possible palindrome partitions of s. Each partition is a list of the substrings in their original left-to-right order. The statement does not specify an order for the partitions in the output.
constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
signals: The task says return all possible ways, so the output itself can be exponential and you must enumerate.
The input limit is tiny (n <= 16). A limit near 15 to 20 allows an O(n * 2^n) search.
The task splits a sequence into contiguous pieces where each piece must pass a local test. Each partition is a chain of choices for where the next piece ends.
The same substring test (is s[i..j] a palindrome) repeats across branches, so a precomputed O(n^2) table pays off.
memory_hook: Cut a palindrome off the front, recurse on the rest.
approach: Use backtracking that cuts a palindrome off the front of the string. Try every first piece s[start:end]. Keep the piece only if it equals its reverse. Then recurse on the rest of the string.
rebuild_steps: Make result and path lists, and a function backtrack(start).
If start equals len(s), append a copy path[:] to result and return.
Loop end from start + 1 to len(s) inclusive and take piece = s[start:end].
If piece equals piece[::-1], append it to path, call backtrack(end), then pop it.
Call backtrack(0) and return result.
key_insight: A partition of a sequence is a chain of decisions about where the next piece ends. Recurse on the remaining suffix and follow only the choices whose piece passes the test. When the same piece test repeats across branches, precompute it in a table.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code adds a pal[i][j] table that it fills by interval DP before the search. Each palindrome check is then one lookup instead of an O(n) reversal. This changes the bound from O(n^2 * 2^n) to O(n * 2^n). At n = 16 both run in well under 0.1 s, so the table is optional here. You need the table when the same substring test repeats a lot on longer strings, or in variants such as minimum cuts (LeetCode 132) where you use it inside a DP.
ladder: Brute force over cut masks: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n) extra, excluding output space
Backtracking with two-pointer palindrome check (NeetCode): O(n^2 * 2^n) upper bound time, O(n) extra, excluding output space
Backtracking with precomputed palindrome table (optimal): O(n * 2^n) time, O(n^2) for the table plus O(n) recursion, excluding output space
Memoized DP over suffixes: O(n * 2^n) time, O(n * 2^n) for the memo space
pitfalls: Appending part instead of a copy. Later pops then empty every stored answer.
Building the 2D table by repeating one row object with list multiplication. All rows then alias one list, so the table is wrong.
Filling the table in the wrong order. pal[i+1][j-1] must exist before pal[i][j], so i must go from n-1 down to 0.
solution:
class Solution:
    def partition(self, s: str) -> List[List[str]]:
        result = []
        path = []  # palindrome pieces chosen so far

        def backtrack(start: int) -> None:
            if start == len(s):  # whole string is cut into palindromes
                result.append(path[:])
                return
            for end in range(start + 1, len(s) + 1):
                piece = s[start:end]
                if piece == piece[::-1]:  # keep only palindrome pieces
                    path.append(piece)
                    backtrack(end)
                    path.pop()

        backtrack(0)
        return result

title: Clone Graph
statement: You get a reference to one node of a connected undirected graph. Each node has an integer val and a list neighbors of Node references. Return a deep copy (clone) of the graph. The copy has one new node for each original node, with the same val. The neighbor lists of the new nodes refer only to new nodes and copy the original structure. Return the copy of the given node as the reference to the cloned graph. In the test format, each node's val equals its 1-indexed position, and the graph is given as an adjacency list. The adjacency list is a collection of unordered lists. Each list gives the set of neighbors of one node. The given node is always the node with val = 1. The graph can be empty. Then the input is null and you return null. Edges are undirected, so if node a lists node b, node b also lists node a. There are no repeated edges and no self-loops, and every node is reachable from the given node.
constraints: The number of nodes in the graph is in the range [0, 100].
Node.val is unique for each node.
There are no repeated edges and no self-loops in the graph.
signals: The task says deep copy or clone of a structure made of nodes and references.
Nodes can be reached by more than one path, so the copy must share nodes the same way the original does.
The structure can contain cycles. In an undirected graph each edge lets a traversal go from a to b and back to a, so a plain recursive copy never stops.
The answer must be a reference into the new structure, and no new node may point to an old node.
memory_hook: Copy a tree, but check the map first and register the copy before you recurse.
approach: Use DFS with a map from each original node to its copy. dfs(cur) returns the copy of cur. If the map has cur, return its copy. Else make the copy and store it in the map at once. Then append dfs(nei) for each neighbor and return the copy.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty dict old_to_new from original node to copy.
Write dfs(cur). If cur is in old_to_new, return old_to_new[cur].
Else create copy = Node(cur.val). Set old_to_new[cur] = copy before any recursion.
For each nei in cur.neighbors, append dfs(nei) to copy.neighbors.
After the loop, return copy.
Return dfs(node) if node is not None. Else return None.
key_insight: When you copy or transform a structure that has shared references or cycles, keep a map from each original object to its result. Check the map before you create anything. The map is both the visited set that stops cycles and the table that translates old references into new ones.
ladder: Plain recursive copy without a visited map: unbounded (does not terminate on a cycle) time, unbounded (does not terminate on a cycle) space (too slow)
Two passes with linear search (no hash map): O(V * (V + E)) time, O(V) space
Two passes indexed by value: O(V + E) time, O(V) space
DFS with an old-to-new hash map (optimal, standard): O(V + E) time, O(V) extra for the map and the call stack, plus O(V + E) for the output graph space
BFS with an old-to-new hash map: O(V + E) time, O(V) extra for the map and the queue, plus O(V + E) for the output graph space
pitfalls: Empty graph: the input is None. Return None. Do not read None.val.
Store the copy in the map before you recurse into the neighbors. If you store it after, the first cycle causes infinite recursion.
Append the copies of the neighbors, not the original neighbors. Appending originals gives a shallow copy that points back into the old graph.

title: Gas Station
statement: There are n gas stations along a circular route. The amount of gas at station i is gas[i]. You have a car with an unlimited gas tank. It costs cost[i] of gas to travel from station i to its next station (i + 1). You begin the journey with an empty tank at one of the gas stations. Given two integer arrays gas and cost, return the index of the starting gas station if you can travel around the circuit once in the clockwise direction. Otherwise, return -1. If a solution exists, it is guaranteed to be unique.
constraints: The input is generated such that the answer is unique.
signals: The route is circular and the task asks for a start index from which a full lap is possible.
Each step has a gain and a loss, so you can merge them into one net change per step.
Success means a running balance never drops below zero, which is a prefix-sum condition.
n is up to 10^5, so simulating a lap from every start (O(n^2)) is too slow and a single pass is expected.
memory_hook: Not enough total gas means -1; out of gas means start after here.
approach: Greedy reset with a total check. If the total gas is less than the total cost, return -1. Otherwise, drive once from left to right with a tank. When the tank goes below zero, move the start to the next station and empty the tank. After the loop, return the start.
rebuild_steps: If sum(gas) < sum(cost), return -1.
Set start = 0 and tank = 0.
For each station i, add gas[i] - cost[i] to tank.
If tank < 0, set start = i + 1 and set tank = 0.
After the loop, return start.
key_insight: If a running balance that starts at i first fails at j, then no start between i and j can succeed, because each of those starts only drops a non-negative prefix. So you can jump the candidate past j. A total balance of zero or more then guarantees that the last surviving candidate completes the circle.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same as solution_code. Only the loop form differs: solution_code walks enumerate(zip(gas, cost)) and this version uses range(len(gas)) with indexes.
ladder: Brute force simulation from every start: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Doubled array window: O(n) time, O(1) space
Minimum prefix sum: O(n) time, O(1) space
Greedy reset with total check (chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
Two pointers growing a circular window (NeetCode style): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Reset only when the tank is strictly below zero. Resetting at tank == 0 can skip the real answer and even return n (for example gas = [2,0], cost = [0,2] gives 2 instead of 0).
Do not skip the total check. Without it, gas = [2,3,4], cost = [3,4,3] returns 2 instead of -1.
Reset the tank to zero, not to the current station's net change, because the new start is the next station.

title: Single Number
statement: You get a non-empty array of integers nums. Every element appears exactly twice, except one element that appears exactly once. Return that single element. The solution must run in linear time and use only constant extra space.
constraints: Each element in the array appears twice except for one element which appears only once.
signals: Every value appears an even number of times, except one value that appears an odd number of times.
The task asks for linear time and constant extra space, so a hash map, a set or a sort is not allowed.
Values come in matched groups, and the answer is the one value without a match.
The order of the elements does not matter. Only the parity of each value count matters.
memory_hook: Pairs cancel under XOR, so XOR everything.
approach: XOR fold. Start at 0 and XOR every number into one accumulator. Each pair cancels to 0, so only the single number stays.
rebuild_steps: Recall the two XOR rules: x ^ x == 0 and x ^ 0 == x.
Set result = 0, because 0 is the XOR identity.
Loop over nums and do result ^= num.
Order does not matter, so every pair cancels to 0.
Return result. It is the number without a pair.
key_insight: Use an operation that is order-independent and where each value is its own inverse. XOR cancels every value that appears an even number of times. So the XOR of all elements equals the XOR of the values that appear an odd number of times.
ladder: Nested loop count: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort and scan pairs: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the sort buffer in Python space (too slow)
Hash map or hash set: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Math with set sum: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
XOR fold (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Start the accumulator at 0. 0 is the identity for XOR, and any other start value changes the result.
A hash map or set solution passes on LeetCode, but it breaks the constant space rule that the problem states.
XOR works only when the other values appear an even number of times. For three repeats (LeetCode 137), plain XOR fails.

title: Copy List with Random Pointer
statement: You get the head of a singly linked list of length n. Each node has an integer val, a next pointer, and an extra random pointer. The random pointer points to any node in the list or is null. Build a deep copy of the list. The copy must contain exactly n brand new nodes. Each new node has the same val as its original node. The next and random pointers of each new node must point to new nodes in the copy, so that the copy has the same structure as the original. If original X.random points to Y, then copy x.random points to copy y. No pointer in the copy may point to a node of the original list. Return the head of the copied list. Input and output use a list of [val, random_index] pairs, where random_index is the 0-based index of the random target or null. Your code receives only the head node.
constraints: Node.random is null or is pointing to some node in the linked list.
signals: The task asks for a deep copy or clone of a structure whose nodes point to arbitrary other nodes.
A pointer can point forward, backward, to itself, or to null, so the target copy may not exist yet when you need it.
Node values can repeat, so you cannot identify a node by its value. You must identify it by object identity.
The output must not share any node with the input, which means you need a one-to-one correspondence from old nodes to new nodes.
memory_hook: Make every copy first, then link copies through the old-to-new map.
approach: Two-pass hash map (old node -> new node). Pass 1 makes a copy of every node and stores old -> new in a dict. Pass 2 sets each copy's next and random by looking up the old pointers in that dict.
rebuild_steps: Create old_to_new = {None: None}, so a null pointer maps to null.
Walk the list with cur from head. For each cur, set old_to_new[cur] = Node(cur.val). Then move cur = cur.next.
Walk the list again with cur from head. Get copy = old_to_new[cur].
Set copy.next = old_to_new[cur.next] and copy.random = old_to_new[cur.random]. Then move cur = cur.next.
Return old_to_new[head]. For an empty list, this returns None.
key_insight: To copy pointers that can point anywhere, first build a correspondence from each original node to its copy, then translate every pointer through that correspondence. Create all nodes before you connect any edges, so every target already exists.
ladder: Index arrays with linear search (brute force): O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Two-pass hash map (old node -> new node): O(n) time, O(n) space
Recursive DFS with memo (graph clone): O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Interleave copies in place: O(n) time, O(1) extra (output excluded) space
pitfalls: Do not key the map by val. Values repeat, as in example 3. Key by the node object.
Do not set random in the same pass that creates the nodes, unless you create missing targets on demand. A random target ahead of cur has no copy yet.
Handle null next and null random. Seeding the map with None -> None removes these checks.
solution:
"""
# Definition for a Node.
class Node:
    def __init__(self, x: int, next: 'Node' = None, random: 'Node' = None):
        self.val = int(x)
        self.next = next
        self.random = random
"""


class Solution:
    def copyRandomList(self, head: "Optional[Node]") -> "Optional[Node]":
        old_to_new = {None: None}

        # Pass 1: make a copy of every node (no links yet).
        cur = head
        while cur:
            old_to_new[cur] = Node(cur.val)
            cur = cur.next

        # Pass 2: link each copy through the map.
        cur = head
        while cur:
            copy = old_to_new[cur]
            copy.next = old_to_new[cur.next]
            copy.random = old_to_new[cur.random]
            cur = cur.next

        return old_to_new[head]

title: Word Break
statement: You get a string s and a list of strings wordDict. Return true if you can split all of s into a sequence of one or more dictionary words, placed one after another with no gaps and no overlap. Return false otherwise. You can use the same dictionary word many times. All dictionary words are unique. All strings use only lowercase English letters.
constraints: s and wordDict[i] consist of only lowercase English letters.
signals: The question asks if a sequence can be split into pieces that each come from an allowed set. This is a segmentation problem.
The answer is yes or no, not the list of splits. You only need to know if one valid way exists, so you do not enumerate splits.
Pieces can repeat without limit. So the state needs no record of which pieces you used. The current position alone is enough, as in Coin Change.
The sequence length is small, in the hundreds. A loop over positions with a short inner loop is cheap, but the number of ways to cut is exponential.
memory_hook: Cut off a first word, ask if the rest can split, and cache by start index.
approach: Use a memoized DFS on the start index. can_split(start) tries every first piece s[start:end] that is in the word set. Then it asks if the rest s[end:] also splits. The cache makes each start index run only once.
rebuild_steps: Import cache from functools. Put wordDict in a set called words.
Write the nested function can_split(start) with @cache. It returns True when s[start:] splits into words.
Base case: if start == len(s), return True.
Loop end over range(start + 1, len(s) + 1), so end can reach len(s). If s[start:end] in words and can_split(end), return True.
After the loop, return False. Return can_split(0) as the answer.
key_insight: Whether the rest of a string can be split depends only on where the rest starts, not on how you got there. So the exponential set of split paths collapses to n + 1 boolean states. Each state depends only on earlier states that are at most one piece length back.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code is a bottom-up DP over prefixes instead of suffixes. dp[i] is True when s[:i] splits, and it looks back at most max_len characters. It needs no recursion, and its slice work is O(n * L^2) instead of O(n^3). You need it when s is long, for example thousands of characters. Then the recursion depth passes the default limit of 1000, and the O(n^3) slice work gets slow. At n = 300 both forms are fast. You can add the max_len bound to the DFS loop for the same slice work, but the recursion depth stays.
ladder: Plain recursion (backtracking): O(2^n) worst case, for example s = 'aaa...ab' with words 'a', 'aa', 'aaa' time, O(n) recursion depth space (too slow)

Memoized DFS on start index (top-down DP): O(n * L^2 + total characters in wordDict), where L is the longest word length. Each slice and each hash costs O(L). time, O(n + total characters in wordDict) space
Bottom-up DP over prefixes with a hash set: O(n * L^2 + total characters in wordDict) with the length bound. O(n^3) slice work without it. time, O(n + total characters in wordDict) space
Bottom-up DP that loops over words (NeetCode style): O(n * m * L), where m is the number of words (about 6e6 character steps at the limits) time, O(n) space
DP with a trie walk: O(n * L + total characters in wordDict) time, O(total characters in wordDict + n) space
BFS over start indices: O(n * L^2 + total characters in wordDict) time, O(n + total characters in wordDict) space
pitfalls: Do not use greedy longest match or shortest match. 'cars' with 'car', 'ca', 'rs' needs 'ca' + 'rs', and a greedy 'car' fails.
Plain recursion without a cache times out on inputs like 'aaa...ab' with words 'a', 'aa', 'aaa'.
Forgetting the base case dp[0] = True makes every answer False.

title: Linked List Cycle
statement: You get head, the head of a singly linked list. Find out if the list has a cycle. The list has a cycle if some node can be reached again by following the next pointer repeatedly. Internally, pos is the index of the node that the tail's next pointer connects to. pos is -1 when there is no cycle. pos is not passed as a parameter, so you see only head. Return true if the list has a cycle. Otherwise, return false.
constraints: The number of the nodes in the list is in the range [0, 10^4].
pos is -1 or a valid index in the linked-list.
follow_up: Can you solve it using O(1) (i.e. constant) memory?
signals: Each element has at most one successor, and the question asks if a walk can repeat or loop forever.
A visited set solves it at once, but the problem asks for O(1) extra memory.
A sequence comes from applying the same deterministic step again and again to a finite set of states. Such a sequence must stop or enter a loop.
Access is forward only, with no index and no known length, and you need a position fact such as a loop, a loop entry or the middle.
memory_hook: Hare runs two, tortoise runs one. If they meet, it loops. If the hare falls off the end, it does not.
approach: Use Floyd tortoise and hare. Start slow and fast at head. In each step, slow moves 1 node and fast moves 2 nodes. If slow and fast reach the same node, the list has a cycle. If fast reaches the end, the list has no cycle.
rebuild_steps: Put slow and fast on head.
Loop while fast and fast.next exist, so fast can take two steps.
Move slow one node and fast two nodes.
If slow is fast (the same node object), return True.
When the loop ends, fast reached the end, so return False.
key_insight: Two walkers that move through the same cycle at speeds that differ by exactly 1 must meet. The gap between them shrinks by 1 each step, so it cannot skip over 0. A meeting proves a cycle with O(1) memory, and the faster walker reaching the end proves there is none.
ladder: Quadratic rescan with no extra memory: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Hash set of visited nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space
Step limit from the constraint: O(L), where L = 10^4 is the size bound time, O(1) space
Destructive marking: O(n) time, O(1) space
Floyd tortoise and hare (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) space
Brent's algorithm: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Check that fast and the node after fast exist before you move fast two nodes. Otherwise you read next from None and get an AttributeError.
Compare nodes by identity, not by value. Equal values do not mean the same node.
Compare after you move the pointers. Both start at head, so a check before the first move returns true at once.
solution:
# Definition for singly-linked list.
# class ListNode:
#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.next = None

class Solution:
    def hasCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
        slow = fast = head
        while fast and fast.next:          # fast can still take 2 steps
            slow = slow.next               # tortoise: 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next          # hare: 2 steps
            if slow is fast:               # same node object -> loop
                return True
        return False                       # hare hit the end -> no loop

title: Reorder List
statement: You get the head of a singly linked list L0 -> L1 -> ... -> Ln-1 -> Ln. Reorder the list into the form L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... The result takes nodes alternately from the front and from the back, starting with the front. You must not change the values in the nodes. You may only change the nodes themselves, that is, their next links. Modify the list in place and return nothing. The head node stays the head.
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is in the range [1, 5 * 10^4].
signals: The output alternates between the front and the back of a sequence: first, last, second, second-to-last, and so on.
In a list of n nodes with 0-based indices, node i pairs with its mirror node n-1-i.
The input is a singly linked list, so you can only move forward, but the task needs access from both ends.
The task forbids changes to node values and asks for an in-place change. This points to pointer rewiring. An O(1) extra space answer is possible and is the expected one.
memory_hook: Put the nodes in an array, take front then back, chain them, end with None.
approach: Array of nodes, then relink in order. Copy the node references into an array, list them in the order front, back, front, back with two indices that move inward, and then chain the nodes in that order.
rebuild_steps: Walk the list and append each node to an array called nodes.
Make an empty array called order. Set left to 0 and right to len(nodes) - 1.
While left <= right, append nodes[left] to order. Append nodes[right] to order only if left < right. Then add 1 to left and subtract 1 from right.
For each adjacent pair a, b in order, set a.next = b.
Set the next link of the last node in order to None.
key_insight: The target order reads the list from both ends at the same time. A singly linked list only reads forward. Reverse the back half in place, so its last node becomes a head you can read forward. The problem then becomes an alternating merge of two forward lists.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses O(1) extra space instead of O(n). It finds the end of the front half with slow and fast pointers, cuts the list, reverses the back half in place, and weaves the two halves. Both solutions run in O(n) time. The statement asks only for in-place rewiring of the nodes, and the array solution does that. Use the optimal form when O(1) extra space is required. It is also the shared pattern for palindrome linked list and maximum twin sum.
ladder: Repeated tail removal: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Recursion with a front pointer: O(n) time, O(n) call stack space (too slow)
Array of nodes with converging pointers: O(n) time, O(n) space
Stack of nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space
Find middle, reverse second half, merge alternately: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: If you do not cut the list after the first half, the old link from the last front node stays. The result then has a cycle.

The front half must not be shorter than the back half. The left middle (front gets ceil(n/2) nodes) works. The right middle for even n also works, because the extra front node is already in its final place. A split that gives the back half more nodes makes the merge read the next link of None and crash.
Save both next pointers before you rewire. If you overwrite the next link of first before you save it, you lose the rest of the front half.
solution:
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        """
        Do not return anything, modify head in-place instead.
        """
        # 1. Copy the node references into an array.
        nodes = []
        node = head
        while node:
            nodes.append(node)
            node = node.next

        # 2. Build the target order: front, back, front, back, ...
        order = []
        left, right = 0, len(nodes) - 1
        while left <= right:
            order.append(nodes[left])
            if left < right:
                order.append(nodes[right])
            left += 1
            right -= 1

        # 3. Chain the nodes in that order and end the list.
        for a, b in zip(order, order[1:]):
            a.next = b
        order[-1].next = None

title: LRU Cache
statement: Design a data structure that follows the rules of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache. Implement the class LRUCache. LRUCache(capacity) creates the cache with a positive capacity. get(key) returns the value of key if key exists, else it returns -1. put(key, value) updates the value of key if key exists, else it adds the key-value pair to the cache. If the number of keys becomes larger than capacity after a put, the cache evicts the least recently used key. A successful get and every put count as a use of that key. get and put must each run in O(1) average time.
constraints: At most 2 * 10^5 calls will be made to get and put.
signals: The problem asks you to design a class, and each operation must run in O(1) time.
Words like cache, capacity, evict and recently used appear in the statement.
You must find an item by key and also keep the items in an order that changes on every access.
An accessed item must move from any position in the order to one end.
memory_hook: Ordered dict: move to end on use, pop the front on overflow.
approach: Use collections.OrderedDict as the cache. The dict keeps keys from oldest to newest, so on every use you move the key to the end, and on overflow you pop the first key.
rebuild_steps: In __init__, store the capacity and create an empty OrderedDict. Its front is the oldest key and its end is the newest key.
In get, return -1 if the key is not in the dict.
Else call move_to_end(key), because a get is a use, and return the value.
In put, assign cache[key] = value and call move_to_end(key), because a put is a use.
If len(cache) is larger than capacity, call popitem(last=False) to drop the oldest key.
key_insight: When you need O(1) lookup by key and O(1) reordering or removal from the middle of a sequence, store the items in a doubly linked list and keep a hash map from key to node. The map finds the node, and the prev and next pointers let you unlink it without a search.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code builds the same structure by hand: a dict from key to node plus a doubly linked list with left and right sentinels. The big-O is the same. In CPython, OrderedDict is about 1.5 to 2 times faster, because its linked list is written in C. You need the hand-built version when an interviewer forbids OrderedDict, asks you to show the linked list, or uses a language without an ordered map. Hook for it: map finds the node, list keeps the order, remove then insert at the right, evict left.next. Remember to store the key in each node so eviction can delete the map entry. Do not replace OrderedDict with a plain dict and next(iter(d)), because eviction is not O(1) in CPython.
ladder: Hash map plus timestamps: O(1) get, O(capacity) put when it evicts time, O(capacity) space (too slow)
Hash map plus ordered Python list of keys: O(capacity) per operation time, O(capacity) space (too slow)
Hash map plus doubly linked list with sentinels: O(1) per operation time, O(capacity) space
collections.OrderedDict: O(1) per operation time, O(capacity) space
Plain dict insertion order: O(1) average for get and for put without eviction, O(capacity) amortized per eviction in CPython time, O(capacity) space
pitfalls: Forgetting that get also counts as a use. A successful get must move the node to the MRU end.
Forgetting that put on an existing key counts as a use. Update the value, move the node to the MRU end, and do not evict.

Evicting first when the cache is full and only then handling the put. If the key already exists, this evicts a key for no reason. Handle the existing key first, or insert first and evict only when the size is larger than capacity.

title: Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation
statement: You get an array of strings tokens. The array is an arithmetic expression in Reverse Polish Notation (postfix): each operator comes after its two operands. Evaluate the expression and return its integer value. The valid operators are '+', '-', '*' and '/'. Each operand is an integer or another expression. Division between two integers truncates toward zero. No division by zero occurs. The input is always a valid RPN expression. The answer and all intermediate results fit in a 32-bit signed integer.
constraints: tokens[i] is either an operator: "+", "-", "*", or "/", or an integer in the range [-200, 200].
signals: The input is a postfix or prefix token stream. Each operator comes after (or before) the values it acts on.
Each operator uses the most recent values that no operator has used yet. Newest first is last in, first out, so a stack fits.
The result of one step is an input to a later step. You must keep partial results until an operator needs them.
Some tokens close a unit of work and consume items that came before them. A token that reduces earlier pending items points to a stack.
memory_hook: Push numbers. An operator pops b, then a, and pushes a op b. Divide with int(a / b).
approach: Operand stack, one pass. Push each number. On an operator, pop the right operand, then the left operand, and push the result.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty list called stack and loop over the tokens.
Compare the whole token with the set of four operators, so that '-11' stays a number.
For an operator, pop b first (right operand), then pop a (left operand).
Push a + b, a - b or a * b, and push int(a / b) for division so that it truncates toward zero.
For a number, push int(tok).
After the loop, return stack[0], the single value left.
key_insight: In postfix order, every operator acts on the most recent pending results. A stack of pending values gives exactly this last-in, first-out access. One left-to-right pass evaluates the expression with no precedence or bracket logic.
ladder: Repeated collapse of the first num-num-op triple: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Recursive descent from the end (expression tree): O(n) time, O(n) recursion depth space
Operand stack, single pass (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
In-place stack inside the tokens array: O(n) time, O(1) extra space
pitfalls: Popping operands in the wrong order. The top of the stack is the right operand, so a - b and a / b need b = pop() first, then a = pop().
Using // for division. -7 // 2 is -4, but the problem needs -3.
Detecting operators with tok[0] or a substring test. Negative numbers like '-11' start with '-'. Compare the whole token against the set of operators.

title: Maximum Product Subarray
statement: You get an integer array nums. Find a non-empty contiguous subarray that has the largest product. Return that product. The product of a single-element subarray is the value of that element. The values can be negative, zero or positive. The test cases guarantee that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer, and the product of any subarray of nums fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: The product of any subarray of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.
signals: The problem asks for the best value of an aggregate over a contiguous, non-empty subarray. This points to a 'best ending at index i' scan (Kadane style).
The aggregate is a product and the values can be negative. A negative factor reverses the order of candidates, so the largest can become the smallest and the reverse.
Zeros can occur. A zero sets every running product to 0 and acts as a barrier between independent segments.
n is up to 2 * 10^4. O(n^2) is about 2 * 10^8 steps and is too slow in CPython, so you need one linear pass.
memory_hook: Kadane, but carry the biggest and the smallest, because a negative swaps them.
approach: Max and min product ending here (Kadane with two states). Carry the biggest and the smallest product of a subarray that ends at the current value, because a negative value turns the smallest into the biggest.
rebuild_steps: Set best = nums[0] and big = small = 1, the empty product.
Loop over each x in nums.
Build the three candidates: x alone, big * x and small * x.
Set big, small = max(candidates), min(candidates) in one assignment, so both use the old values.
Update best = max(best, big) inside the loop.
Return best after the loop.
key_insight: When the step that extends a partial result can reverse order, such as a multiplication by a negative number, the best result at the next step can come from the worst result at this step. Carry both the maximum and the minimum ending here. A monotone step maps extremes to extremes, so these two values are sufficient.
ladder: Brute force over all subarrays: O(n^3) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Brute force with running product: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Max and min product ending here (Kadane variant): O(n) time, O(1) space
Prefix and suffix product scan: O(n) time, O(1) space
Split by zeros and count negatives: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: You update cur_max first and then compute cur_min with the new cur_max. Use simultaneous assignment or a temporary variable.
You track only the maximum. This fails on [-2, 3, -4], where the answer 24 needs the minimum -6.
You start res at 0. This fails on [-2], where the answer is -2.

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
statement: An array of length n is sorted in ascending order and then rotated between 1 and n times. For example, nums = [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] becomes [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] after 4 rotations. It becomes [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] again after 7 rotations. Rotating [a[0], a[1], a[2], ..., a[n-1]] one time gives [a[n-1], a[0], a[1], a[2], ..., a[n-2]]. You get the sorted rotated array nums of unique elements. Return the minimum element of this array. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(log n) time.
constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
signals: The input is a sorted array that was rotated or shifted. A rotated sorted array is two sorted runs, so binary search still applies.
The statement demands O(log n) time on an array. This rules out a scan and points to binary search.
The elements are unique. Then one comparison with an end value always tells which half to keep. With duplicates, a tie can block that decision.
You look for a boundary or turning point, not a given target value. Search for the first index where a yes/no property becomes true.
memory_hook: Low run means at most the last value; find the first one.
approach: First-true binary search against the last element. The test nums[i] <= nums[-1] is false on the high run and true on the low run, so the minimum is the first index where the test is true.
rebuild_steps: Save last = nums[-1]. The low run holds every value <= last.
Set lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. The last index is always in the low run.
Loop while lo < hi and take the lower midpoint mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
If nums[mid] <= last, set hi = mid, because mid can be the answer.
Else set lo = mid + 1, because mid is in the high run.
Return nums[lo] when lo == hi.
key_insight: A rotated sorted array splits into two sorted runs. Every value in the first run is greater than the last element, and every value in the second run is not. So the comparison nums[i] <= nums[-1] is a monotone false-then-true predicate, and the minimum is the first true index. Binary search finds that boundary.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code compares nums[mid] with nums[hi] instead of the fixed nums[-1]. It has the same O(log n) time and O(1) space and gives the same result on unique values. It adds nothing you need for this problem. The nums[hi] form is the one that extends to problem 154 with duplicates, where a tie nums[mid] == nums[hi] lets you do hi -= 1.
ladder: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Find the drop by scanning: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Binary search, compare mid with right end: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Binary search with running minimum (NeetCode style): O(log n) time, O(1) space
Binary search with a fixed last-element pivot: O(log n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Comparing nums[mid] with nums[lo] instead of nums[hi]. An unrotated array such as [1,2,3] then moves right and returns 3 unless you add a special check.
Setting hi = mid - 1 in the else branch drops mid, which can be the minimum. Use hi = mid, or track a running minimum as NeetCode does.
Using while lo <= hi with hi = mid causes an infinite loop when lo == hi.

title: Min Stack
statement: Design a stack class MinStack that supports push, pop, top and retrieval of the minimum element. MinStack() creates an empty stack. push(val) puts the integer val on top of the stack. pop() removes the top element. top() returns the top element. getMin() returns the smallest element that is currently in the stack. Each method must run in O(1) time. pop, top and getMin are always called on a non-empty stack. Values are 32-bit signed integers, and there are at most 3 * 10^4 calls in total.
constraints: Methods pop, top and getMin operations will always be called on non-empty stacks.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to push, pop, top, and getMin.
signals: The task is to design a container that answers an aggregate query, such as min or max, in O(1) next to its normal operations.
Removals happen only at one end in LIFO order. So every earlier state of the container comes back exactly after a pop.
The aggregate is easy to update when an element is added. It is impossible to undo by arithmetic when an element leaves, because min and max have no inverse.
The statement demands O(1) per operation. This rules out a scan, and it also rules out a heap or a sorted structure.
memory_hook: Push the pair (value, min so far). Pop removes both.
approach: Use one stack of (value, min so far) pairs. Each pair stores a value and the minimum of that value and all values below it. top reads the value in the last pair. getMin reads the minimum in the last pair.
rebuild_steps: In __init__, set self.stack to an empty list. Each entry is a (value, min_so_far) pair.
In push, set min_so_far to min(val, self.stack[-1][1]) when the stack has entries. Else set min_so_far to val.
In push, append the pair (val, min_so_far) to self.stack.
In pop, call self.stack.pop() once. The pair below already holds the old minimum.
In top, return self.stack[-1][0].
In getMin, return self.stack[-1][1].
key_insight: When removals follow LIFO order, every earlier state returns exactly. So store a snapshot of the aggregate with each push, and undo becomes a pop of that snapshot. This works even for aggregates like min and max that you cannot reverse by arithmetic.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses the same prefix-minimum idea. It has the same O(1) time per operation and O(n) space. It only splits each pair into two parallel lists, stack and min_stack. So pop must remove from both lists. The split adds nothing that this problem needs.
ladder: Brute force scan: O(1) push/pop/top, O(n) getMin time, O(n) space (too slow)
Single cached minimum with rescan on pop: O(1) push/top/getMin, O(n) worst-case pop time, O(n) space (too slow)
Heap or sorted container with lazy deletion: O(log n) amortized per operation time, O(n) space (too slow)
Parallel prefix-minimum stack (optimal, standard): O(1) per operation time, O(n) space
Lean minimum stack (store only new minima): O(1) per operation time, O(n) worst case space
Difference encoding with one minimum variable: O(1) per operation time, O(1) extra beyond the stored elements space
pitfalls: One cached minimum variable fails after a pop removes the current minimum.
If you forget to pop the minimum stack together with the value stack, the two stacks lose their alignment.
The first push needs a special case when the minimum stack is empty. Use an emptiness check or a float('inf') sentinel at the bottom.

title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
statement: You get a 1-indexed array of integers numbers that is already sorted in non-decreasing order. Find two numbers that add up to a specific target number. Let these two numbers be numbers[index1] and numbers[index2], where 1 <= index1 < index2 <= numbers.length. Return the indices index1 and index2, each incremented by one (so 1-based), as an integer array [index1, index2] of length 2. The tests are generated such that there is exactly one solution. You may not use the same element twice. Your solution must use only constant extra space.
constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
signals: The input array is sorted, and the task asks for a pair whose sum meets a target (equal to it, closest to it, or below it).
The problem demands O(1) extra space, so a hash map of seen values is not allowed. The sorted order must do the work of the hash map.
The pair sum never decreases when either index moves toward larger values. So one comparison can rule out a whole row or a whole column of the pair table.
A sum that is too small tells you to raise the smaller value. A sum that is too large tells you to lower the larger value. One clear move per comparison points to converging pointers.
memory_hook: Sorted pair sum: start at both ends. Too small, move left up. Too big, move right down.
approach: Use two pointers from both ends. Start left at the smallest value and right at the largest value. If the sum is too small, move left up. If the sum is too large, move right down. Stop when the sum equals target.
rebuild_steps: Put one pointer at each end: left = 0 and right = len(numbers) - 1.
Loop while left < right, so the two pointers never use the same element.
Compute total = numbers[left] + numbers[right].
If total == target, return [left + 1, right + 1] (1-based).
If total < target, do left += 1. Otherwise do right -= 1.
After the loop, return []. The one-solution guarantee means this line never runs.
key_insight: In a sorted range, the pair (smallest, largest) tells you which element to discard. If their sum is too small, the smallest element is useless, because no partner is larger than the current largest. If their sum is too large, the largest element is useless by the same argument. So each comparison shrinks the search range by one, and the search becomes linear.
ladder: Brute force over all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Hash map of complements (original Two Sum): O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Binary search for each complement: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
Two pointers converging from both ends (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Returning 0-based indices. The problem wants 1-based indices, so add 1 to both.

Use left < right, not left <= right. With left <= right, the loop can pair an element with itself when no valid pair exists. The one-solution guarantee hides this bug here, but it breaks variants without that guarantee.
Using a hash map breaks the constant-space requirement, even though it passes the tests.

title: Reverse Bits
statement: Reverse the bits of a given 32-bit signed integer n. Treat n as a fixed-width 32-bit value, including its leading zeros. Bit i of n moves to bit 31 - i of the result. Return the integer that the reversed bit pattern represents. The constraints keep n in the range 0 to 2^31 - 2 and require n to be even. So bit 0 and bit 31 of n are both 0. The result is then also an even value from 0 to 2^31 - 2, and no sign bit is involved. The leading zeros count: a value with few significant bits becomes a large value after the reversal.
follow_up: If this function is called many times, how would you optimize it?
signals: The problem states a fixed bit width, such as 32 bits. Leading zeros then count as real digits.
The output is a rearrangement of the bit positions of the input, not an arithmetic result.
The problem asks for a positional transform of the binary form of an integer, such as reverse, rotate, or swap of bits.
A follow-up asks about many calls on small fixed-width values. This points to a precomputed table over small chunks, such as bytes.
memory_hook: Peel the low bit off n, push it onto res, 32 times.
approach: Use peel and push for exactly 32 steps. Read the lowest bit of n and push it onto the low end of res. Then drop that bit from n. The first bit that you read ends at the top.
rebuild_steps: Set res to 0.
Loop exactly 32 times, not while n is above zero.
Shift res left by 1, then OR in n & 1 to push the lowest bit of n.
Shift n right by 1 to peel that bit off.
Return res.
key_insight: You can read the bits of a number from its low end and write them into a new number with a left shift and an OR. This reverses the order. It is the same loop that reverses decimal digits with a remainder by 10 and a multiply by 10. With a fixed width, run the loop for every position, because leading zeros become trailing zeros.
ladder: String reversal: O(32) = O(1) time, O(32) = O(1) space
Bit-by-bit shift and append (standard): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
Bit-by-bit with explicit target position (NeetCode): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
Byte lookup table (follow-up): O(1) per call after O(256) setup time, O(256) space
Divide-and-conquer mask swaps: O(log w) for width w, so 5 steps for 32 bits = O(1) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Looping while n is above zero instead of exactly 32 times. This drops the leading zeros of n, so the result is shifted wrong. For example, n = 2 returns 1 instead of 2^30.
Converting with bin and no zero padding. The string then has fewer than 32 digits and the reversal is wrong. Pad to exactly 32 digits.
Shifting res after the OR instead of before it. The answer is then twice the correct value. Shift first, then OR, inside the loop.

title: Number of 1 Bits
statement: You get a positive integer n. Return the number of set bits (bits equal to 1) in the binary representation of n. This count is also called the Hamming weight. The input is always positive and fits in a signed 32-bit integer.
follow_up: If this function is called many times, how would you optimize it?
signals: The statement asks about the bits of an integer (set bits, binary representation, Hamming weight). This points to bitwise operators, not arithmetic on decimal digits.
The input fits in a fixed width of 32 bits. Any loop over bit positions is bounded by a constant, so brute force over bits is already fast.
The task is to count or visit only the 1 bits. An operation that jumps from one set bit to the next beats a scan over every position.
A follow-up says the function is called many times. This signals precomputation: a lookup table over small chunks, or a cache.
memory_hook: Read the last bit, then shift it away.
approach: Check every bit with shift and mask. Add the last bit (n & 1) to a counter, then shift n right by one to drop that bit, and repeat until n is 0.
rebuild_steps: Start count at 0.
Loop while n > 0.
Add n & 1 to count, because n & 1 is the last bit.
Shift n right by one with n >>= 1 to drop the last bit.
When the loop ends, n is 0. Return count.
