key_insight: Subtracting 1 from a number flips its lowest set bit and every bit below it. So x & (x - 1) deletes exactly the lowest set bit. Use this operation to step from one set bit to the next and skip all zero bits.
optimal_note: The optimal solution uses n &= n - 1 to clear the lowest set bit in each step. It loops once per 1 bit instead of once per bit position, so it skips all the 0 bits. For 32-bit input this saves at most 30 cheap steps (for example n = 2^30 has 31 bit positions but only 1 set bit), so you need it only to show the trick or when most bits are 0 in very wide numbers. For the follow-up with many calls, use a 256-entry byte lookup table or n.bit_count(). Both loops need a mask n &= 0xFFFFFFFF first if the input can be negative.
ladder: Binary string count: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
Check every bit with shift and mask: O(log n), at most 31 steps time, O(1) space
Brian Kernighan: clear the lowest set bit: O(k), k = number of set bits time, O(1) space
Lookup table over bytes (follow-up): O(1) per call after O(256) setup time, O(256) space
Parallel bit count (SWAR, divide and conquer): O(1) time, O(1) space
Built-in popcount: O(log n), effectively O(1) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Negative input in Python never reaches 0 with n &= n - 1, because Python ints are unbounded and negatives have infinite leading 1 bits. If input can be a signed 32-bit value, mask first with n &= 0xFFFFFFFF.
In Java or C, an arithmetic right shift on a negative number copies the sign bit, so a shift-until-zero loop never ends. Use the unsigned shift >>> in Java or loop exactly 32 times.

In C and Java, == binds tighter than &, so n & 1 == 0 parses as n & (1 == 0). In C it always gives 0. In Java it does not compile. Add parentheses. In Python, & binds tighter than ==, but parentheses still make the intent clear.

title: House Robber
statement: You get an integer array nums. nums[i] is the amount of money in house i. The houses stand in a line on a street. You can rob any set of houses, but you must not rob two adjacent houses on the same night, because adjacent houses have connected security systems that call the police. Return the maximum total amount of money you can rob without alerting the police. Robbing no house is allowed, so the answer is at least 0.
signals: The task asks for a maximum or minimum total over a sequence of items.
Each item has a binary choice: take it or skip it.
A local rule links neighbors: taking one item forbids taking the next one (or the next k items).
Greedy choices fail on small counterexamples, such as [2,1,1,2] where taking every other item is not optimal.
memory_hook: Skip it and keep the last best, or rob it and add its money to the best two back.
approach: Growing best list (bottom-up DP without index math). Start with best = [0, 0] for no houses. For each house, append max(skip it: best[-1], rob it: best[-2] + money), and return best[-1].
rebuild_steps: Start best = [0, 0] so two earlier answers always exist.
Loop over each money value in nums.
Set skip = best[-1] because leaving the house keeps the best so far.
Set take = best[-2] + money because robbing it forces the previous house to stay empty.
Append max(skip, take) to best.
After the loop, return best[-1].
key_insight: Decide about the last item only. Either you skip it and inherit the best answer of the shorter prefix, or you take it and inherit the best answer of the prefix that excludes its forbidden neighbor. The best answer of a prefix is all you need, not which items it used.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps only the last two entries of the best list in two variables (prev2, prev1). This gives O(1) extra space instead of O(n). The time is O(n) in both. With n <= 100 the list costs nothing. Use the two-variable form only when the task asks for constant extra space. To convert, replace best[-2] and best[-1] with prev2 and prev1, and update both in one tuple assignment.
ladder: Brute force over subsets: O(2^n * n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Plain recursion (rob or skip): O(phi^n), about O(1.618^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized recursion (top-down DP): O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up DP table: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up DP with two variables (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
Two-state machine (rob / skip): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Greedy fails. Taking all even or all odd indices misses [2,1,1,2] where the answer 4 skips two houses in a row.
Do not pick the largest house first. In [3,4,3] the largest house gives 4, but 3 + 3 = 6.
dp[i] means the best of the first i houses, not the best ending exactly at house i. If you define it as ending at i, the answer is the max over all i, not dp[n-1].

title: Binary Tree Right Side View
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Imagine that you stand on the right side of the tree. Return the values of the nodes that you can see, ordered from top to bottom. At each depth you see exactly one node: the rightmost node at that depth. That node can be in the left subtree when the right subtree is shorter. The tree can be empty; then return an empty list.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
signals: The answer has one value per depth of a tree. Think of a level-order traversal or a DFS that carries the depth.
The word 'view' (right, left, top, bottom) means you pick one extreme node per level or per column.
The output is ordered top to bottom. BFS produces levels in that order for free.
A node is visible only if no other node at the same depth is further right. This is a per-level comparison, not a path property.
memory_hook: Level-order BFS; the last node of each level is the one you see.
approach: BFS by level, take the last node of each level. Process the queue one level at a time. Before you drain a level, the last node in the queue is the rightmost node of that depth, so you record its value.
rebuild_steps: If the root is None, return an empty list.
Make an empty result list. Put the root in a deque.
While the queue is not empty, append the value of queue[-1] to the result. The queue holds exactly one level, left to right, so queue[-1] is the node you see.
Loop range(len(queue)) times. The range reads the level size once, before you push any child.
In each pass, pop a node from the left. Push its left child, then its right child, if they exist.
Return the result list.
key_insight: A side view is a per-level extreme. Group the nodes by depth with level-order BFS, then pick the first or last node of each level. In DFS form, visit the preferred side first, and the first node that reaches a new depth is the answer for that depth.
ladder: Brute force: one depth-limited search per depth: O(n*h), O(n^2) for a chain time, O(h) space
Full level-order lists, then take the last of each: O(n) time, O(n) space
BFS by level, record the last node (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(w), w = maximum level width, O(n) worst case space
BFS that enqueues null children (NeetCode version): O(n) time, O(w) space
DFS right-first with depth check: O(n) time, O(h), O(n) for a skewed tree space
pitfalls: Do not follow only right pointers. A deeper left subtree contributes visible nodes, as in example 2 and in the tree [1,2].
Return an empty list for an empty tree. Do not read the root value before the None check.
Read the queue size once before the inner loop. The queue grows while you push children.

title: Number of Islands
statement: You get an m x n 2D grid named grid. Each cell holds the character '1' (land) or '0' (water). Land cells connect only when they are adjacent horizontally or vertically. Diagonal neighbors do not connect. An island is a maximal group of connected land cells, surrounded by water. All four edges of the grid are surrounded by water. Return the number of islands.
signals: A 2D grid where each cell links to its 4 (or 8) neighbors is an implicit graph. Each cell is a node. Each adjacency is an edge.
The question asks how many separate groups, regions, or blobs exist. That is a count of connected components.
A phrase such as 'connected horizontally or vertically' defines the edge set. It tells you which neighbor offsets to use.
The grid has at most 300 x 300 = 90,000 cells. One pass that touches each cell a constant number of times fits easily. Repeated full passes do not.
memory_hook: Count each new land cell, then sink its whole island.
approach: Scan and sink with a stack-based DFS. Scan every cell, and each time you find a '1', add one island and sink its whole island to '0' with a stack that pushes all four neighbors and checks each cell only when it pops.
rebuild_steps: Set rows and cols to the grid height and width.
Define sink(r, c). Start a stack that holds (r, c).
Pop from the stack until it is empty.
After each pop, skip the cell if it is out of bounds or not '1'.
Otherwise, set the cell to '0' and push its four neighbors.
Set islands to 0. Loop over every row r and every column c.
If grid[r][c] is '1', add one to islands and call sink(r, c).
Return islands.
key_insight: A grid region count is a connected-component count on an implicit graph. Scan all cells, and each time you meet an unvisited node, count it and flood-fill its whole component so you never count it again.
optimal_note: The optimal code uses BFS with a deque and sinks each cell when it enters the queue. So each cell enters the queue at most once. The stack version can push the same cell up to four times. It also pushes water cells and off-grid positions, and the check after the pop discards them. Both are O(m*n) in time and space, and both fit easily. The BFS form matters when you need distances or levels, such as shortest path or rotting oranges, because BFS visits cells in order of distance.
ladder: Label propagation (brute force): O((m*n)^2) worst case time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
Recursive DFS flood fill: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) recursion depth space
Iterative BFS flood fill (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) worst case for the queue space
Union-find: O(m*n * alpha(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Cells hold the strings '1' and '0', not integers. A comparison with the integer 1 never matches.
Mark a cell visited when you enqueue it, not when you dequeue it. Otherwise the same cell can enter the queue many times. The count stays correct, but the work grows.
Recursive DFS can raise RecursionError in Python. On an all-land 300 x 300 grid, the depth reaches 90,000. The default limit is 1000. Use an explicit stack or queue, or raise the limit.

title: Happy Number
statement: You get a positive integer n. Repeatedly replace the number with the sum of the squares of its decimal digits. The process either reaches 1 and stays there, or it loops forever in a cycle that does not contain 1. A number is happy if the process ends in 1. Return true if n is happy and false if not.
signals: The statement applies a fixed function to a value again and again: x -> f(x). This sequence is a walk in a functional graph, where each node has exactly one outgoing edge.
The statement says the process ends at a target or loops endlessly. Any deterministic process on a finite state set must eventually repeat a state, so the question is cycle detection.
The step function shrinks large inputs fast (a d-digit number maps to at most 81d). This shows the reachable state set is small and finite, so the walk must cycle.
The target value (1) is a fixed point: f(1) = 1. Reaching it means the walk enters a cycle of length 1, so the answer is a test of which cycle you enter.
memory_hook: Walk until you hit 1 or a repeat. A seen set catches the repeat.
approach: Hash set of seen values. Walk the sequence and remember every value. Stop when the value is 1 (happy) or when a value repeats (a loop without 1).
rebuild_steps: Make an empty set called seen.
Loop while n is not 1 and n is not in seen.
Inside the loop, add n to seen.
Replace n with the sum of int(d) ** 2 for each digit d in str(n).
After the loop, return n == 1.
key_insight: Repeatedly applying a function to a value on a finite state set always ends in a cycle. So reframe the question as cycle detection on an implicit linked list: the target is reached exactly when the cycle you enter is the fixed point.
optimal_note: The record solution uses Floyd fast/slow pointers instead of a set. Floyd uses O(1) extra memory. The set uses O(log n) memory, and here it never holds more than 20 values. Use Floyd when the problem asks for constant extra space, or when you must show the linked-list cycle pattern. Both run in about 10 to 15 microseconds of CPU time per call near the maximum n.
ladder: Simulation with a step cap: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Hash set of seen values: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
Floyd fast/slow pointers: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Known-cycle check: O(log n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Looping until the value is 1 with no cycle check never ends for unhappy numbers.
Checking only whether n itself reappears misses cycles that do not include the starting value (for example 2 enters the cycle at 4 and never returns to 2).
Starting slow and fast at the same value with a while slow != fast loop exits at once. Start fast one step ahead, or use a do-while style loop.

title: Reverse Linked List
statement: You get the head of a singly linked list. Reverse the list and return the head of the reversed list. The list can be empty; then return an empty list (None).
constraints: The number of nodes in the list is the range [0, 5000].
follow_up: A linked list can be reversed either iteratively or recursively. Could you implement both?
signals: The task asks you to change the order or direction of the links in a singly linked list, not to compute a value.
Each node knows only its successor, so you cannot walk backward. You must flip each next pointer while you still hold a reference to the rest of the list.
The output must contain the same nodes in a new order, and you need O(1) extra space. This points to in-place pointer rewiring.

A list problem needs access from the tail end, for example to compare both ends or to add digits from the least significant end. Reversing the list, or one part of it, in place gives this access in O(1) space.
memory_hook: Save next, flip the arrow, step both, return prev.
approach: Iterative prev/curr reversal. Walk the list once and flip each next pointer to point back at the previous node, saving the forward link first.
rebuild_steps: Set prev = None and curr = head.
Loop while curr is not None.
Save nxt = curr.next before you change anything.
Flip the arrow: curr.next = prev.
Step both pointers: prev = curr, then curr = nxt.
After the loop, return prev, because curr is None and prev is the old tail.
key_insight: To reverse a singly linked list, you do not move nodes. You flip each next pointer to point backward. Save the forward link before you overwrite it, because it is the only way to reach the rest of the list.
ladder: Copy values to array and rewrite: O(n) time, O(n) space
Stack of nodes: O(n) time, O(n) space
Recursive reversal: O(n) time, O(n) call stack space
Head insertion with a dummy node: O(n) time, O(1) space
Iterative three-pointer reversal (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Overwriting curr.next before you save it. You lose the rest of the list.
Returning curr or head instead of prev. At the end curr is None and head is now the tail.
Forgetting that the old head must point to None. Starting prev at None handles this. In the recursive form, set head.next = None, or you create a two-node cycle.

title: Course Schedule
statement: There are a total of numCourses courses that you must take. They are labeled from 0 to numCourses - 1. You get an array prerequisites. Each entry prerequisites[i] = [ai, bi] means that you must take course bi first if you want to take course ai. For example, the pair [0, 1] means that to take course 0 you must first take course 1. Return true if you can finish all courses. Otherwise, return false.
signals: The input gives pairwise rules of the form 'do B before A' over a set of labeled items. Each rule is a directed edge.
The question asks if all items can be completed, or if a valid order exists. That is a feasibility question about a dependency graph.
The input is a node count plus an edge list, not an adjacency structure. This points to a graph problem where you build an adjacency list first.
Node and edge counts are in the thousands. This rules out trying all orders. A linear O(V + E) traversal fits easily.
memory_hook: Take what is ready, free its dependents, check that you took everything.
approach: Kahn's algorithm: take the courses that are ready. Count the unmet prerequisites of each course. Take any course with zero unmet prerequisites. Each taken course frees the courses that depend on it. You can finish all courses if and only if you take all of them.
rebuild_steps: Make graph as one empty list per course and indegree as one zero per course.
For each pair [course, pre], append course to graph[pre] and add 1 to indegree[course].
Put every course with indegree 0 into a deque. Set taken to 0.
While the queue is not empty, pop a course from the left and add 1 to taken.
For each dependent of that course, subtract 1 from its indegree. Push the dependent when its indegree becomes 0.
After the loop, return taken == numCourses.
key_insight: A set of 'X before Y' rules can be satisfied if and only if the directed rule graph has no cycle. Kahn's algorithm checks this constructively. In an acyclic graph, some node always has zero unmet requirements, so it can go next. If the process stalls before it covers every node, the remaining nodes lie on a cycle or depend on one.
ladder: Brute force: try every order: O(n! * (n + m)) time, O(n) space (too slow)
DFS cycle check without memoization: Exponential in the worst case time, O(n + m) space (too slow)
Repeated full scans (naive peeling): O(n * (n + m)) time, O(n + m) space (too slow)
DFS with three colors (white, gray, black): O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
Kahn's algorithm (BFS topological sort): O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
pitfalls: Edge direction: [a, b] means b before a, so the edge is b -> a. Reversing every edge keeps the cycle answer the same here, but it gives a reversed order in Course Schedule II.
Disconnected graph: seed the queue with every indegree-0 course, or start DFS from every course. Checking only course 0 misses cycles in other components.
A self-loop [x, x] is a cycle. Kahn handles it because x never reaches indegree 0.

title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
statement: A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree data structure that stores and retrieves keys in a set of strings efficiently. Applications include autocomplete and spell checkers. Implement the Trie class. Trie() initializes the trie object. insert(word) inserts the string word into the trie. search(word) returns true if the string word is in the trie (that is, it was inserted before), and false otherwise. startsWith(prefix) returns true if a previously inserted string word has the prefix prefix, and false otherwise. A word counts as a prefix of itself. Inserts and queries arrive mixed in any order, and each query must reflect all inserts made before it. All strings are non-empty and use only lowercase English letters.
constraints: word and prefix consist only of lowercase English letters.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls in total will be made to insert, search, and startsWith.
signals: The task stores many strings and asks whether some stored string starts with a given prefix.
Queries come online and mix with inserts, so a one-time precomputation does not work.
The alphabet is small and fixed, so each step down a tree has a bounded number of choices.
The task asks two questions about one string: is it a whole stored key, and is it the start of some stored key. One walk answers both when the last node carries an end-of-key flag.
memory_hook: One node per prefix: walk the letters, flag the word end.
approach: Trie with dict children and an end flag. Each node maps a letter to a child node and has an is_end flag. One helper walks a string down from the root, and search and startsWith differ only in the final check.
rebuild_steps: Write TrieNode with children = {} and is_end = False. Trie holds one root TrieNode.
insert: start at the root. For each letter, create the child if it is missing, then move to it. Set is_end to True on the last node.
_walk: start at the root. For each letter, move to the child with children.get. Return None when the child is missing. Otherwise, return the last node.
search: return True only when _walk gives a node and that node has is_end set to True.
startsWith: return True when _walk gives any node.
key_insight: When many queries ask about prefixes of stored strings, store the strings as paths in a tree that shares common beginnings. Each node then stands for exactly one prefix, so a prefix query is a walk of length L. An end-of-word flag on the node separates 'is a prefix' from 'is a whole stored word'.
ladder: List of words with linear scan: O(1) insert, O(n * L) per query, n = stored words time, O(T), T = total inserted characters space (too slow)
Hash set of words plus hash set of all prefixes: O(L^2) insert, O(L) per query time, O(sum of L^2) space (too slow)
Sorted unique list plus binary search: O(n + L log n) insert (list shift), O(L log n) per query time, O(T) space
Trie with a fixed 26-slot child array: O(L) per query; O(26 * L) worst-case insert, because each new node allocates 26 slots time, O(26 * T) pointers space
Trie with a dict of children (chosen): O(L) per call time, O(T) nodes space
pitfalls: Forgetting the end flag. After inserting only 'apple', search('app') must return False even though the path exists.
Returning True from search when the walk finishes, instead of returning node.is_end.
A word is a prefix of itself, so startsWith(word) must return True for a stored word.

title: Course Schedule II
statement: There are a total of numCourses courses that you must take. They are labeled 0 to numCourses - 1. You get an array prerequisites where prerequisites[i] = [ai, bi]. This pair means that you must take course bi first if you want to take course ai. For example, the pair [0, 1] means that you must take course 1 before course 0. Return an ordering of courses that lets you finish all courses. If many valid orders exist, return any of them. If you cannot finish all courses, return an empty array.
signals: The input is a list of pairs that say "X must happen before Y". These pairs are directed edges of a dependency graph.
The task asks for an order that respects every dependency. This order is a topological order.
The task says to return an empty result when no order exists. No order exists exactly when the dependency graph has a directed cycle.

The task accepts any valid order. You do not need a special order, so a plain BFS or DFS topological sort is enough. A required order, such as the lexicographically smallest one, needs a min-heap instead of a queue.
memory_hook: Count unmet prerequisites. Take any course at zero. A short order means a cycle.
approach: Kahn's algorithm (peel off free courses). Keep a count of unmet prerequisites for each course, and repeatedly take a course whose count is 0. If some courses never become free, a cycle blocks them, so return an empty list.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty adjacency list and an indegree of 0 for each course.
For each pair [course, pre], append course to graph[pre] and add 1 to indegree[course].
Put every course with indegree 0 into a deque. Start an empty order list.
While the deque is not empty, pop a course from the left and append it to order.
For each dependent of that course, subtract 1 from its indegree. Push the dependent when its indegree reaches 0.
Return order if len(order) == numCourses. Otherwise, return [].
key_insight: A node with no unmet dependencies can always go next. Removing it can only free more nodes. So you peel off indegree-0 nodes layer by layer. If you cannot peel off every node, the leftover nodes contain a cycle.
ladder: Brute force over permutations: O(V! * (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space (too slow)
Repeated scan for a free course: O(V * (V + E)) time, O(V + E) space (too slow)
Kahn's algorithm (BFS on indegrees): O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
DFS postorder with three colors: O(V + E) time, O(V + E) space
pitfalls: Edge direction: [a, b] means b comes before a. For Kahn's algorithm, the edge goes b -> a and indegree[a] increases. If you reverse the edges, the output lists dependents first, so the order is backward.
Forgetting the final count check. Courses on a cycle never reach indegree 0, so the order is just shorter. You must return [] in that case, not the partial order.
Forgetting isolated courses. Courses that appear in no pair still need to be in the order. Seed the queue by scanning all numCourses indegrees, not only the courses that appear in edges.
solution:
from collections import deque
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def findOrder(self, numCourses: int, prerequisites: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        # Edge b -> a means "take b before a".
        graph = [[] for _ in range(numCourses)]
        indegree = [0] * numCourses
        for course, pre in prerequisites:
            graph[pre].append(course)
            indegree[course] += 1

        # Start with every course that has no prerequisites.
        queue = deque(c for c in range(numCourses) if indegree[c] == 0)
        order = []
        while queue:
            course = queue.popleft()
            order.append(course)
            for nxt in graph[course]:
                indegree[nxt] -= 1
                if indegree[nxt] == 0:
                    queue.append(nxt)

        # A cycle leaves some courses with indegree > 0 forever.
        return order if len(order) == numCourses else []

title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
statement: Design a class WordDictionary that stores words and tells whether a query matches a stored word. WordDictionary() creates an empty structure. addWord(word) stores word so that later searches can match it. search(word) returns true if any stored word matches word. Otherwise it returns false. A query can contain dots. Each dot matches any one letter. Every other character must equal the letter at the same position. A match covers the whole stored word, so the lengths must be equal. A stored word that only starts with the query does not match. Added words contain only lowercase English letters. Queries contain lowercase letters and dots. Each word has length 1 to 25. A query has at most 2 dots. There are at most 10^4 calls in total, and adds and searches can interleave.
constraints: word in addWord consists of lowercase English letters.
word in search consist of '.' or lowercase English letters.
There will be at most 2 dots in word for search queries.
signals: The task asks you to design a structure that stores many strings and answers match or prefix queries about them. A trie is the default candidate.
A query contains a wildcard that matches any single character. One query then stands for many strings, so plain hashing of the query does not work directly.
The alphabet is small (26 lowercase letters) and strings are short (length 25 or less). Trie nodes stay cheap and the depth stays small.
The statement bounds the number of wildcards per query (here at most 2). The bound caps the branching to alphabet^k paths and makes branching search or explicit enumeration affordable.
memory_hook: Mask one letter on add, fill one dot on search.
approach: One-dot pattern set. Store each word and each copy of it with one letter replaced by a dot in one set. A query with at most one dot is one lookup, and a query with more dots fills its first dot with each letter and searches again.
rebuild_steps: Keep one set named patterns.
addWord(word): add word, then for each index i add word[:i] + '.' + word[i + 1:].
search(word): if word.count('.') <= 1, return word in patterns.
Else let i = word.index('.'), the first dot.
Return any(self.search(word[:i] + letter + word[i + 1:]) for letter in 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz').
key_insight: Index the stored strings in a trie so that one walk compares a query against all strings at once. A fixed character follows one edge, and a wildcard follows every edge at that depth. The search cost then depends on the number of wildcards and the trie shape, not directly on the number of stored strings.
optimal_note: The record solution_code is a trie with DFS on dots. It is the standard answer when the question asks for a trie. The same walk solves Word Search II, prefix queries and autocomplete. With many dots, a trie search never visits more than all trie nodes. Its worst case is slow in CPython: a crafted input with all 676 two-letter prefixes takes about 24 s of CPU time for 9324 searches. Use the trie when a trie is required, when you also need prefix queries, or when the dot limit is large. In CPython the trie does not save memory here. Each node is an object with its own dict. For 10^4 random words of length 25, the trie used 58 MiB and the pattern set used 24 MiB. The pattern set search cost grows as 26^(k-1) lookups for k dots, so it suits only a small dot limit.
ladder: List of words with linear scan: addWord O(L); search O(N * L) time, O(N * L) space (too slow)
Buckets by length with linear scan: addWord O(L); search O(N * L) worst case time, O(N * L) space (too slow)
Precompute all wildcard patterns: addWord O(L^3) for up to 2 dots; search O(L) time, O(N * L^3) space (too slow)
Hash set with dot expansion: addWord O(L); search O(26^k * L), k <= 2 time, O(N * L) space

Trie with DFS on dots (optimal, standard): addWord O(L); search O(L) without dots, O(26^k * L) with k dots (at most about 1.7e4 node steps here), and never more than the trie size; about 1.5e8 node steps over all calls on a crafted worst case time, O(total characters inserted) nodes; recursion depth k + 1, because the code recurses only at dots space
Trie with BFS frontier: addWord O(L); search O(26^k * L) time, O(total characters) plus O(26^k) frontier space
One-dot pattern sets (fast worst case, depends on k <= 2): addWord O(L^2); search O(L) for 0 or 1 dots, O(26 * L) for 2 dots time, O(N * L^2) space
pitfalls: Returning true when the path exists but the end node is not a word end. For example, "ab" must not match when only "abc" is stored.
Treating '.' as zero or more characters. It matches exactly one letter, so the query and the stored word must have the same length.
Returning the result of the first child for a dot. You must try every child and return true if any branch succeeds.

title: Word Search II
statement: You get an m x n board of lowercase letters and a list of unique lowercase words. Return every word that appears on the board. A word appears if you can spell it along a sequence of cells where each next cell is horizontally or vertically adjacent to the current cell. Diagonal moves are not allowed. A single cell may not be used more than once within one word. Different words may use the same cells. Each found word appears once in the result. LeetCode accepts the result in any order.
constraints: board[i][j] is a lowercase English letter.
signals: Many query strings are matched against one shared search space. A separate search per query repeats the work for shared prefixes.
The answer strings grow one step at a time along a path in a grid or graph. The search can stop as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any query.
The number of queries is large (here up to 3 * 10^4), so one full search per query is too slow.
Each query is short (here at most 10 letters) and the grid is small, so a depth-limited DFS from every cell is affordable when it is pruned.
memory_hook: Word Search I, but walk a trie instead of one word, and cut empty leaves on the way back.
approach: Trie plus the Word Search I grid DFS. Put all words in a trie. Run the usual grid DFS from every cell. Each step into a cell also steps one trie edge. The DFS returns at once when the cell letter is not a child of the current trie node. On the way back, the DFS deletes a trie node that has no children left.
rebuild_steps: Build a trie. Each node has a children dict and a word field. Store the full word at its end node.
Set rows and cols, and make an empty found list.
Define dfs(r, c, parent). Return if the cell is off the board or its letter is not in parent.children.
Set node = parent.children[letter]. If node.word is set, append it to found and set it to None.
Mark the cell '#'. Call dfs on the 4 neighbors with node. Then restore the letter.
If node has no children left, delete it from parent.children.
Call dfs(r, c, root) from every cell. Return found.
key_insight: When many patterns are searched in the same space, merge the patterns into a trie and run one search that advances in the trie as it extends the path. A missing trie child proves that no pattern can continue, so the search stops at once. Shared prefixes are then explored only once for all patterns.
optimal_note: The algorithm and the complexity are the same: a trie, a backtracking DFS, and leaf pruning. Only the code form changes. The record's solution_code checks bounds and the trie child before each call, so it makes fewer function calls that return at once. In CPython this gives no clear gain here: both took about 0.85 s to 0.95 s CPU time on the all-'a' worst cases. Its prune test also checks node.word is None, but that check is always true after the visit, because the DFS clears the word on entry. Keep the leaf prune in both forms: without it, the all-'a' board with words 'a' to 'aaaaaaaaaa' took about 2 s CPU time in the guard-at-top form (1.97 s and 2.03 s in two runs).
ladder: Word Search I once per word: O(W * m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)) where W is the number of words and L is the maximum word length time, O(L) recursion depth space (too slow)
Enumerate all board paths and look them up in a word set: O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1) * L) time, O(S) for the set, where S is the total number of letters in words space
Prefix hash set with pruned DFS: O(S * L + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1) * L) time, O(S * L) for the stored prefixes space

Trie plus backtracking DFS with leaf pruning (optimal, standard): O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)); at most 1883664 DFS calls on a 12x12 board with L = 10, and pruning makes real runs much smaller time, O(S) for the trie plus O(L) recursion depth space
Trie with input heuristics: O(S + m * n * 4 * 3^(L-1)) time, O(S + L) space
pitfalls: A word can be reachable along several paths. Clear the word at its node, or use a set, so it is reported once.
Do not return after the first found word at a node. Longer words can extend it, for example 'cat' and 'cats'.
Always restore the cell after the recursive calls. Otherwise later searches see a corrupted board, and the caller's board changes.

title: House Robber II
statement: You are a professional robber who plans to rob houses along a street. Each house has an amount of money in it. The houses are arranged in a circle, so the first house is the neighbor of the last house. Adjacent houses have a connected security system. The system automatically contacts the police if two adjacent houses are broken into on the same night. The integer array nums gives the amount of money in each house. Return the maximum amount of money you can rob tonight without alerting the police.
signals: You pick a subset of items in a sequence, and two neighboring items cannot both be picked. This points to the take-or-skip linear DP.
The goal is a best total over valid selections, not the list of selections. This points to DP, not backtracking.
The items form a circle, so the first item and the last item are neighbors. A wrap-around constraint usually means you cut the circle into one or more straight lines.
The problem is a known linear problem plus one extra constraint between the two ends. Reuse the linear solver and remove the extra constraint by case analysis.
memory_hook: Drop the first or drop the last, rob each row, take the max.
approach: Drop one end and reuse House Robber I. The first house and the last house are neighbors. So every valid plan leaves at least one of them unrobbed. Run House Robber I on nums[1:] and on nums[:-1]. Return the larger result. One house has no neighbor, so return nums[0] in that case.
rebuild_steps: If there is one house, return nums[0].
Inside rob, write the helper rob_row(houses). Set two_back and one_back to 0. two_back is the best total two houses back. one_back is the best total up to the previous house.
For each money value, set two_back, one_back = one_back, max(one_back, two_back + money).
Return one_back from rob_row.
Return max(rob_row(nums[1:]), rob_row(nums[:-1])).
key_insight: A circle is a line plus one extra edge between the two ends. Remove that edge by case analysis: either the first item is unused or the last item is unused. Each case is the linear problem you already know, so the answer is the better of two linear runs.
optimal_note: The optimal code uses the same algorithm. It passes index bounds (lo, hi) instead of slices, so it makes no list copies and uses O(1) extra space. The slices cost O(n) extra memory. This does not matter for n <= 100. Use index bounds only when you must avoid copies of a very large array.
ladder: Brute force over all subsets: O(n * 2^n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Plain recursion with a first-house flag: O(1.618^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on state (index, first_robbed): O(n) time, O(n) space
Two linear DP tables (drop first, drop last): O(n) time, O(n) space
Two linear passes with two rolling variables (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
Case split on house 0 (equivalent alternative): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: With n == 1 both rows are empty and the split returns 0. Return nums[0] in that case.
Do not run the linear solver once on the whole array. Its best plan can rob both the first and the last house. For [2,3,2] it returns 4, but the answer is 3.
Do not exclude both ends in one run. That loses every plan that robs exactly one end. For [5,1,1,5] it returns 1, but the answer is 6.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
statement: You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the kth largest element in the array. The rank counts duplicates: it is the kth element in sorted (descending) order, not the kth distinct value. The problem asks if you can solve it without sorting.
follow_up: Can you solve it without sorting?
signals: The question asks for one value at a given rank (kth largest, kth smallest, median), not for the whole order.
The text asks you to avoid a full sort. A full O(n log n) order then does more work than needed.
k can be much smaller than n. A structure of size k can summarize everything that matters.
Values lie in a small fixed range (here 2*10^4 + 1 values). A count array over the value range is then possible.
memory_hook: Top k in a min-heap: push, trim to k, return the root.
approach: Min-heap of size k, push then trim. Push every value into a min-heap. When the heap holds more than k values, pop the smallest. At the end, the root is the kth largest.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq. Make an empty list top_k to use as a min-heap.
For each x in nums, heappush x into top_k.
If len(top_k) > k, heappop to drop the smallest value.
After the loop, top_k holds the k largest values.
Return top_k[0], the smallest of them, which is the kth largest.
key_insight: To find the kth largest, you only need to remember the k largest values. Keep them in a min-heap so the weakest of them sits at the root. The root is the threshold a new value must beat, and at the end the root is the answer.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses the same size-k min-heap. It adds a gate: it pushes only while the heap has fewer than k values, and after that it calls heapreplace only when x > heap[0]. A value that cannot enter then costs O(1) instead of a push and a pop. Big-O stays O(n log k) time and O(k) space. Use the gate when you want fewer heap operations on long streams. Use quickselect when you need O(n) average time, and counting when the value range is small.
ladder: Sort: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Repeated max removal: O(n*k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Heapify all then pop: O(n + (n-k) log n) time, O(1) extra if done in place on nums space
Min-heap of size k (chosen): O(n log k) time, O(k) space

Quickselect with three-way partition: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case time, O(n) average for the list version, O(n^2) worst case because each level keeps its lists alive. O(1) extra for an iterative in-place version. space
Counting over the value range: O(n + R) where R = max - min + 1 <= 20001 time, O(R) space
pitfalls: Using a max-heap of size k is wrong. To keep the k largest you must evict the smallest, so use a min-heap.
Treating duplicates as one value. The rank counts every copy, so do not use a set.
Returning nums[k-1] after an ascending sort. The kth largest is at index n-k ascending, or index k-1 descending.

title: Contains Duplicate
statement: You get an integer array nums. Return true if any value appears at least twice in the array. Return false if every element is distinct. Only the yes or no answer matters. You do not return the duplicate value or its indices.
signals: The question asks if any value repeats, or if all values are distinct.
For each element, the answer depends on whether an equal value appeared earlier. You need fast lookup of what you already saw.
n goes up to 10^5. An O(n^2) pair check is too slow, so you need O(n) or O(n log n).

Values go up to 10^9 in absolute value. A fixed-size counting array is not practical, so a hash set is the right container. If values are small and bounded, a boolean array indexed by value also works.
memory_hook: Ask the set if you saw it, then add it.
approach: Seen-before hash set. Walk the array once. Keep a set of the values that you already saw. If the current value is already in the set, you found a duplicate.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty set called seen.
Loop over each value x in nums.
If x is in seen, return True.
Otherwise add x to seen.
After the loop, return False.
key_insight: Replace the inner loop of a pair search with a lookup structure. For each element, ask the hash set if you saw this value before. The set remembers the whole prefix, so one pass is enough.
ladder: Brute force all pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort and compare neighbors: O(n log n) time, O(n). A sorted copy needs O(n) memory. An in-place sort avoids the copy, but Timsort can still use up to n/2 scratch slots. space
Hash set with early exit: O(n) average, because each set lookup and insert is O(1) on average time, O(n) space
Set size comparison: O(n) average time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Do not add the value before you check it. Every element then finds itself, and you return true wrongly.
Do not use a list for seen. The in operator on a list is O(n), so the total becomes O(n^2).
An in-place sort changes the caller's array. Sort a copy if the input must stay unchanged.

title: Invert Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Invert the tree and return its root. To invert a tree, swap the left child and the right child of every node. The result is the mirror image of the original tree. The tree can be empty. In that case, return null (None).
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 100].
signals: The task applies the same local change at every node of a tree.
The result for a subtree comes only from the results for its two child subtrees, so the problem is self-similar.
The answer is the input tree with a new shape, so you can change the child pointers in place and return the original root.
The node values do not matter. Only the links between nodes change.
memory_hook: Swap the two children, then invert each child.
approach: Recursive preorder swap. At each node, swap the left and right child pointers. Then call the function on each child. An empty node returns None.
rebuild_steps: If root is None, return None.
Swap the children in one line: root.left, root.right = root.right, root.left.
Call invertTree on root.left.
Call invertTree on root.right.
Return root.
key_insight: A whole-tree transformation that applies the same local rule at every node is one traversal. Apply the local rule at each node (here, swap the two children) and trust recursion to handle the subtrees.
optimal_note: The record solution_code is the same algorithm in postorder form. It puts the two recursive calls inside the swap line, so it saves two lines. It adds no speed or memory gain: both are O(n) time and O(h) stack space. It depends on Python evaluating the full right side before it assigns, which is easy to get wrong from memory. For trees deeper than about 1000 levels, use the iterative stack or queue version instead of either recursive form.
ladder: Build a new mirrored copy: O(n) time, O(n) for the new nodes, plus O(h) for the call stack space
Recursive DFS, swap in place (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(h) for the call stack, where h is the tree height. This is O(n) for a skewed tree and O(log n) for a balanced tree. space
Iterative BFS or DFS with a queue or stack: O(n) time, O(w) for BFS, where w is the maximum width. O(h) for DFS. Both are O(n) in the worst case. space
pitfalls: Do not set the new left child and then the new right child in two separate statements. The second statement then reads the left pointer that you already overwrote. Use one simultaneous assignment, or save one child in a temporary variable first.
Handle the empty tree. The input can have 0 nodes, so return None for a None root.
Return the root. The function must return the tree, not only change it.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a BST
statement: You get the root of a binary search tree and an integer k. Return the kth smallest value among all node values in the tree. The count k is 1-indexed, so k = 1 means the minimum value. The tree has n nodes and 1 <= k <= n, so the answer always exists.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is n.
follow_up: If the BST is modified often (i.e., we can do insert and delete operations) and you need to find the kth smallest frequently, how would you optimize?
signals: The input is a binary search tree and the question asks about rank or order (kth smallest, kth largest, successor, sorted position). An in-order traversal gives the values in sorted order.
The question asks for the kth item in sorted order. You can stop the sorted stream after k items and skip the rest.
The tree can be a chain of up to 10^4 nodes. Recursion at that depth fails in CPython with the default limit of 1000, so plan an explicit-stack traversal.
The follow-up mentions frequent inserts, deletes and rank queries. This points to augmenting each node with extra data such as subtree size.
memory_hook: Push the left spine; pop, count, push the right child's left spine.
approach: Iterative in-order with a push_left helper (BST iterator template). Push the left spine of the root. Then pop a node and decrement k. If k is 0, return the node value. Else push the left spine of its right child and repeat.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty stack and a helper push_left(node) that appends node and moves to node.left until node is None.
Call push_left(root). Now the top of the stack is the smallest value.
Loop forever: pop a node and decrement k.
If k is 0, return node.val.
Else call push_left(node.right) so the next smallest value is on top.
key_insight: An in-order traversal of a BST produces the values in sorted order. So treat the BST as a sorted list that you read lazily, and stop after k items.
ladder: Collect all values and sort: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Max-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k + H) space
Recursive in-order into a full list: O(n) time, O(n) space
Iterative in-order with early stop (optimal, standard): O(H + k) time, O(H) space
Morris in-order traversal: O(n) time, O(1) space
Order-statistic tree (follow-up): O(H) per query and per update, O(log n) when balanced time, O(n) for the size fields space
pitfalls: k is 1-indexed. Decrement k before the check, or compare a visit counter with k, not k - 1.
A recursive DFS on a skewed tree of 10^4 nodes exceeds the default CPython recursion limit of 1000.

The outer loop condition must be 'stack or curr'. With only 'stack', the loop does not start. With only 'curr', the loop stops when a popped node has no right child, but the stack still holds unvisited nodes.

title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary search tree (BST) and two nodes p and q of that tree. Return the lowest common ancestor (LCA) node of p and q. The LCA is the lowest node in the tree that has both p and q as descendants. A node counts as a descendant of itself. So if p is an ancestor of q, the answer is p. All node values are unique, p and q are different nodes, and both exist in the tree. Return the node itself, not its value.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [2, 10^5].
signals: The input is a binary search tree. One comparison with node.val tells you which subtree holds a target value.
The question asks where two targets in an ordered structure meet or split, such as an ancestor, a fork, or a shared prefix of search paths.
The problem guarantees that both targets exist. So the first split node is the answer, and you do not need a separate check that the targets are present.
The tree can have up to 10^5 nodes and can be a skewed chain. Deep recursion can then pass the default CPython recursion limit, so prefer an iterative walk.
memory_hook: Both smaller go left, both bigger go right, else this node is the split.
approach: BST split-point walk. Start at the root and move one pointer down: go left when both values are smaller, go right when both are larger, and stop at the first node where they are not on the same side.
rebuild_steps: Set node = root.
Loop while node is not None.
If p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val, both targets are in the left subtree. Set node = node.left. Use strict <, so the walk does not move past a target.
Elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val, both targets are in the right subtree. Set node = node.right. Use strict > for the same reason.
Else return node. The targets split here, or one target is this node.
After the loop, return None. This line does not run when p and q exist in the tree.
key_insight: In a BST, the LCA of two values is the first node on the path from the root whose value lies between them, inclusive. Above that node both targets go the same way. At that node their search paths diverge or end. So the problem reduces to one guided descent, like a binary search for the split point.
ladder: Root paths and compare: O(h) with BST search, O(n) with general DFS time, O(h) space
Parent map and ancestor set: O(n) time, O(n) space
General binary tree LCA (post-order DFS): O(n) time, O(h) space
BST split-point recursion: O(h) time, O(h) space
BST split-point iteration (optimal): O(h), O(n) worst case for a skewed tree, O(log n) for a balanced tree time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Using the general binary tree LCA works, but it wastes the BST order and costs O(n) instead of O(h).
Forgetting that a node is its own descendant. When p.val == node.val, return node. The else branch covers this case.
Using <= or >= in the move conditions moves past a target and loses the answer. Use strict < and > to move.

title: Product of Array Except Self
statement: Given an integer array nums, return an array answer such that answer[i] is equal to the product of all the elements of nums except nums[i]. The product of any prefix or suffix of nums is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and without using the division operation.
constraints: The input is generated such that answer[i] is guaranteed to fit in a 32-bit integer.
follow_up: Can you solve the problem in O(1) extra space complexity? (The output array does not count as extra space for space complexity analysis.)
signals: The answer for each index is an aggregate of all other elements, so it excludes exactly one position.
The phrase 'except self' or 'all others' means that the value splits into a part before i and a part after i.
The statement forbids the inverse operation (division). Thus you cannot compute the total and remove one element.
The statement guarantees that every prefix and suffix product fits. This hints that prefix and suffix products are the intended building blocks.
memory_hook: Answer = left product times right product. In each pass, use the running product, then multiply in nums[i].
approach: Left pass, right pass. Walk left to right and write the product of everything to the left of i into answer[i]. Then walk right to left and multiply in the product of everything to the right of i.
rebuild_steps: Set n = len(nums) and make answer = [1] * n.
Set prefix = 1. For i from left to right: answer[i] = prefix, then prefix *= nums[i].
Set suffix = 1. For i from right to left: answer[i] *= suffix, then suffix *= nums[i].
Return answer.
Check: in each pass, use the running product before you multiply nums[i] into it.
key_insight: An aggregate over all elements except one position equals the aggregate of everything before it combined with the aggregate of everything after it. Prefix and suffix accumulations give both sides in linear time, and they need no inverse operation.
ladder: Brute force: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Total product with division and zero counting: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Prefix and suffix product arrays: O(n) time, O(n) space
Prefix in output, running suffix scalar: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: An off-by-one error makes answer[i] include nums[i]. Write or multiply into answer[i] before you multiply nums[i] into the running product.
The prefix and suffix start at 1, the identity of multiplication. Do not start them at 0 or at nums[0].
Division fails with zeros. With one zero, every position except the zero gets 0. With two or more zeros, every answer is 0.
solution:
class Solution:
    def productExceptSelf(self, nums: List[int]) -> List[int]:
        n = len(nums)
        answer = [1] * n
        # Pass 1: answer[i] = product of nums[0..i-1]
        prefix = 1
        for i in range(n):
            answer[i] = prefix
            prefix *= nums[i]
        # Pass 2: multiply in product of nums[i+1..n-1]
        suffix = 1
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            answer[i] *= suffix
            suffix *= nums[i]
        return answer

title: Sliding Window Maximum
statement: You get an integer array nums and an integer k. A window of size k starts at the left end of the array. The window moves right by one position at a time until it reaches the right end. You can only see the k numbers inside the window. Return a list that holds the maximum of each window, in order from left to right. The result has n - k + 1 values, where n is the length of nums.
signals: The problem asks for the max or min of every contiguous window of fixed size k.
The window slides by one, so each step adds one element and removes one element.
n reaches 10^5 and k is free. When k is near n/2, rescanning every window costs about 2.5 * 10^9 steps. So you need about O(1) amortized work per window.
A running max cannot be undone when the current max leaves the window, so a plain variable is not enough.
memory_hook: Kick out the old from the front, kick out the weak from the back, and the front is the max.
approach: Monotonic deque (kick out old and weak). Keep a deque of candidate indices. Their values go down from front to back. Drop the front index when it leaves the window. Drop back indices whose values are not bigger than the new value. Read the max at the front.
rebuild_steps: Make an empty deque of indices and an empty result list.
Loop over i, x with enumerate(nums).
Old: if the front index is <= i - k, popleft it.
Weak: while the value at the back index is <= x, pop it.
Append i to the back of the deque.
When i >= k - 1, append nums[front index] to the result.
After the loop, return the result.
key_insight: An older element that is not larger than a newer element is dominated: it leaves the window first and never wins. Delete dominated candidates as soon as they appear. The survivors form a monotonic sequence, so the best candidate is always at one end.
optimal_note: The intuitive solution is the optimal solution. It runs in O(n) time because each index enters and leaves the deque at most once. It uses O(k) extra space.
ladder: Brute force rescan: O(n*k) time, O(1) extra (O(n-k+1) for output) space (too slow)
Max-heap with lazy deletion: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Sorted container (multiset) of window values: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
Block prefix/suffix maximum: O(n) time, O(n) space
Monotonic decreasing deque (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(k) space
pitfalls: Store indices, not values. You need the index to know when the front leaves the window.
The front expires when its index is i - k or less. An off-by-one error here keeps a stale max or drops a valid one.
Start output only when i >= k - 1. The first k - 1 steps build the first window.

title: Valid Anagram
statement: You get two strings s and t. Return true if t is an anagram of s, and false otherwise. An anagram uses all the characters of the original string exactly once, in any order. So each character must occur the same number of times in both strings. The constraints allow s and t to have different lengths. Both strings contain only lowercase English letters.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase English letters.
follow_up: What if the inputs contain Unicode characters? How would you adapt your solution to such a case?
signals: The question asks if two collections are the same when order does not matter. Compare them as multisets (value plus count).
The words anagram, permutation of, rearrange, or same characters point to a frequency count.
A small fixed alphabet (26 lowercase letters) allows a fixed-size count array instead of a hash map.
Input length up to 5 * 10^4 rules out trying orderings and also rules out O(n^2) work (about 2.5 * 10^9 steps). Aim for O(n) or O(n log n).
memory_hook: Count both, compare counts.
approach: Count both and compare. Build a Counter for s and a Counter for t, then return whether the two count tables are equal.
rebuild_steps: Import Counter from collections.
Count the characters of s with Counter(s).
Count the characters of t with Counter(t).
Return True only if the two Counters are equal.
key_insight: Two sequences are equal up to reordering exactly when their frequency counts are equal. Replace the order-dependent object with an order-free signature (counts or sorted form) and compare the signatures.
optimal_note: The record solution uses one Counter, a length check, and an early exit when a count goes below zero. It has the same O(n) time and O(k) space. It keeps one table instead of two and stops at the first extra character. Use it when a task asks for one table or an early exit, or as the base for one-sided checks such as Ransom Note. In CPython the two-Counter version is faster in practice (about 0.007 s against 0.02 s of CPU time at n = 5 * 10^4) because Counter counts in C.
ladder: Try all permutations: O(n! * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Repeated search and remove: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Sort and compare: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Two hash maps: O(n) time, O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters (at most 26 here) space
One counter with early exit (chosen): O(n) time, O(k), where k is the number of distinct characters (at most 26 here) space
Fixed array of 26: O(n) time, O(1) (26 slots) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the length check. With one counter and early exit on negatives, unequal lengths like s = "ab", t = "a" wrongly return true.
Comparing letter sets with set(s) == set(t). This ignores counts and fails on "aab" vs "abb".
Comparing plain dicts after decrementing to zero. A key with value 0 makes the dicts unequal. Counter equality ignores zeros only on Python 3.10 and later.

title: Meeting Rooms
statement: You get an array of meeting times named intervals, where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. A person can attend all meetings if no two meeting intervals overlap. A meeting that ends at time t and a meeting that starts at time t do not overlap. Return true if the person can attend all meetings. Otherwise, return false. The array can be empty. Each interval has start_i < end_i. The input is not guaranteed to be sorted.
signals: The input is a list of [start, end] pairs and the question asks whether any two of them conflict.
The answer is a yes or no about pairwise overlap. A check of all pairs is O(n^2), so look for an order in which only neighbors can conflict.
The input order has no meaning, so you can sort it freely.
The statement defines what happens at a shared endpoint. This tells you to choose strict or non-strict comparison with care.
memory_hook: Sort by start. No meeting may start before the previous one ends.
approach: Sort by start, compare neighbors. Sort the meetings by start time, then check that each meeting starts no earlier than the previous meeting ends.
rebuild_steps: Sort intervals by start time with intervals.sort(key=lambda iv: iv[0]).
Loop i from 1 to len(intervals) - 1, so each step looks at one adjacent pair.
Read prev_end from intervals[i - 1][1] and cur_start from intervals[i][0].
If cur_start < prev_end, return False. Use strict less-than, because touching meetings are fine.
After the loop, return True. An empty or single-meeting list skips the loop and also returns True.
key_insight: After you sort intervals by start, an overlap anywhere implies an overlap between some adjacent pair. So you only need to compare each interval with its direct predecessor, not with all earlier intervals.
ladder: Brute force: check every pair: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Timeline marking: O(n + M), where M is the largest end (M <= 10^6) time, O(M) space
Sort by start, compare neighbors: O(n log n) time, O(n) auxiliary for Python's Timsort in the worst case. The scan itself uses O(1) extra space. space
Sweep over separately sorted starts and ends: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Using <= instead of < in the overlap test. Meetings that touch at time t do not overlap, so [1,5] and [5,10] must return true.
Forgetting to sort. The input can arrive unsorted, as Example 2 shows.
Checking only some neighbors after sorting, or comparing start with start. The test must compare the current start with the previous end.

title: Meeting Rooms II
statement: You get an array intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i] is the time of one meeting. Return the minimum number of conference rooms that the meetings need. One room holds one meeting at a time. The input order is arbitrary. The original text does not define touching meetings. The official solutions treat a meeting as the half-open range [start_i, end_i), so a meeting that ends at time t and a meeting that starts at time t can use the same room.
signals: The question asks for the minimum number of resources (rooms, servers, platforms, cars) so that overlapping jobs never share one resource.
The input is a list of [start, end] intervals in arbitrary order, so a sort by start or by endpoint comes first.
The answer depends only on how many intervals overlap at one time, not on which interval goes where.
n is up to 10^4, so O(n^2) pair checks are slow in Python and O(n log n) sorting is the target.
memory_hook: Start is +1, end is -1, sort the events, and keep the peak.
approach: Event sweep with +1/-1. Turn each meeting into a +1 event at its start and a -1 event at its end, sort the events, and walk them while you track the running count and its maximum.
rebuild_steps: For each meeting, append (start, 1) and (end, -1) to a list of events.
Sort the events. At equal times, -1 comes before 1, so an end frees its room before a start uses it.
Set busy = 0 and most = 0.
Walk the events in order, add each change to busy, and set most = max(most, busy).
Return most.
key_insight: The minimum number of resources equals the maximum number of intervals that overlap at one point. To track that count as time moves forward, you only need the earliest finishing time among the active intervals, and a min-heap gives it in O(log n).
optimal_note: The record's solution_code sorts meetings by start and keeps a min-heap of room end times. It has the same O(n log n) time and O(n) space. Use the heap when you must know which room frees first, for example to assign room ids or to delay meetings as in Meeting Rooms III. For a plain room count, the event sweep is enough.
ladder: Brute force over time points: O(n * M) where M is the maximum end time time, O(1) space (too slow)
Brute force over start points: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort by start plus min-heap of end times: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Two sorted arrays (start and end sweep): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Event sweep with +1/-1: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Difference array over time: O(n + M) where M is the maximum end time time, O(M) space
pitfalls: Tie rule: a meeting that ends at t frees its room for a meeting that starts at t. Use <= in the heap check, and in an event sweep put end events before start events at equal times.
The input is not sorted. Sort by start time before you use the heap.
Sorting by end time instead of start time breaks the heap approach. A meeting placed earlier can take the room that a meeting with an earlier start needs, and the count gets too high.
solution:
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def minMeetingRooms(self, intervals: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        events = []
        for start, end in intervals:
            events.append((start, 1))   # a meeting begins: one more room busy
            events.append((end, -1))    # a meeting ends: one room frees
        events.sort()  # at equal times, (t, -1) sorts before (t, 1)
        busy = 0
        most = 0
        for _, change in events:
            busy += change
            most = max(most, busy)
        return most

title: Graph Valid Tree
statement: You have a graph of n nodes labeled from 0 to n - 1. You get the integer n and a list edges, where edges[i] = [ai, bi] is an undirected edge between nodes ai and bi. Return true if the edges make up a valid tree, and false otherwise. A valid tree is a graph that is connected and has no cycle. Every node from 0 to n - 1 is part of the graph, even if no edge touches it. There are no self-loops and no repeated edges.
signals: The question asks if an undirected graph has a global shape, such as one tree, a forest or one connected piece. It does not ask for a path or a distance. This points to one full traversal or to union-find.
The input is a node count n plus an unordered edge list. This points to an adjacency list for a traversal, or to union-find directly over the raw edges.
The word tree means two properties at once: connected and acyclic. Plan to check both, or check one of them plus the edge count.
Each edge either merges two groups or closes a loop, and the edge order does not matter. This points to union-find.
memory_hook: A tree has n - 1 edges and reaches everyone.
approach: Edge count plus one flood fill. A tree on n nodes has exactly n - 1 edges, so reject any other count. Then run one iterative DFS from node 0. Return true only if it reaches all n nodes.
rebuild_steps: If len(edges) != n - 1, return False.
Build adj = [[] for _ in range(n)]. Add each edge in both directions.
Set seen = {0} and stack = [0].
While the stack is not empty, pop a node.
For each neighbor of that node that is not in seen, add it to seen and push it on the stack.
After the loop, return len(seen) == n.
key_insight: A graph on n nodes is a tree when any two of these three facts hold: it has n - 1 edges, it is connected, it has no cycle. So check the cheap fact (the edge count) and then one traversal fact (connectivity). Turn a structural question into a count plus one linear scan.
ladder: Enumerate paths between every pair: O(n^2 * P), where P is the number of simple paths that backtracking explores for one pair. P is exponential in dense graphs. time, O(n + E) space (too slow)
Bridge test by definition: O(E * (n + E)) time, O(n + E) space (too slow)
DFS with parent tracking: O(n + E) time, O(n + E) space
Edge count plus one traversal (chosen): O(n + E). After the guard, E = n - 1, so the work is O(n). time, O(n + E), which is O(n) after the guard space
Union-find: O(E * alpha(n)) with path compression and union by rank, O(E log n) with path compression only time, O(n) space
pitfalls: n = 1 with no edges is a valid tree. The edge check 0 == 1 - 1 passes and the traversal visits one node.
An edge count of n - 1 alone is not enough. A cycle plus an isolated node also has n - 1 edges.
Connectivity alone is not enough. A connected graph can contain a cycle.

title: Missing Number
statement: You get an array nums of n distinct integers. Each integer is in the range [0, n]. The range [0, n] has n + 1 values, so exactly one value in that range is not in nums. Return that missing value. The missing value can be 0, n, or any value between them.
constraints: All the numbers of nums are unique.
follow_up: Could you implement a solution using only O(1) extra space complexity and O(n) runtime complexity?
signals: The input is a known contiguous range of values with a small number of values removed. You know the full expected set before you read the input.
Exactly one value is unknown. One aggregate equation (a sum or an XOR) is enough to find one unknown.
The values are distinct, so each expected value appears zero times or one time. Pairing expected values with actual values cancels everything except the gap.
The problem asks for O(n) time and O(1) extra space. This rules out a hash set and sorting. It points to a running aggregate or to in-place index marking.
memory_hook: Expected sum minus actual sum.
approach: Gauss sum difference. The full range 0..n has a known sum, n * (n + 1) // 2. Subtract the actual sum of nums. The difference is the missing value.
rebuild_steps: Set n = len(nums). The full range is 0..n.
Compute expected = n * (n + 1) // 2, the sum of 0..n.
Compute actual = sum(nums).
Return expected - actual.
key_insight: When you know the complete expected collection, combine it with the actual collection through an invertible aggregate. Everything that appears in both cancels, and only the difference remains. XOR is its own inverse, so x ^ x = 0 removes every matched value. The order of the values does not matter, and the result cannot overflow.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses XOR cancellation: start res = n, then do res ^= i ^ nums[i] for each index. It has the same O(n) time and O(1) extra space. XOR cannot overflow in fixed-width languages such as C++ or Java. XOR is also the pattern for the Single Number family, where every value appears twice except one. Use XOR when you need a bit manipulation answer, or when the language has fixed-width integers and n is large. In Python, the sum version is equally valid.
ladder: Linear search per candidate: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort and compare to index: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Hash set: O(n) time, O(n) space
Gauss sum difference: O(n) time, O(1) space
XOR cancellation (chosen): O(n) time, O(1) space
Cyclic sort (index as hash): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the value n. The indices cover only 0..n-1, so you must seed the accumulator with n. Without the seed, [0,1] returns 0 instead of 2.
The missing value can be 0. For [1] the answer is 0. Check that the code does not treat 0 as 'not found'.
In the sort approach, return n when every index matches its value.

title: Alien Dictionary
statement: A new alien language uses the English alphabet, but the order of the letters is unknown. You get a list of strings words from the dictionary of this language. The claim is that words is sorted lexicographically by the rules of the alien language. Lexicographic order works as usual: at the first position where two strings differ, the string with the letter that comes earlier in the alien order is smaller. If the first min(a.length, b.length) letters do not differ, the shorter string is smaller. If the claim is false and no order of letters makes the given arrangement sorted, return the empty string. Otherwise, return a string of the unique letters of the alien language, sorted in lexicographically increasing order by its rules. Each letter that appears in words must appear in the answer exactly once, also when no comparison constrains it. If more than one valid order exists, return any of them.
constraints: words[i] consists of only lowercase English letters.
signals: The input is already sorted by an unknown rule, and you must recover the rule. Each adjacent pair leaks a precedence fact.
The output is an ordering of items that must respect pairwise 'a comes before b' facts. This is a topological order of a directed graph.
The problem says to return an empty or invalid result when the facts contradict each other. Contradiction means a directed cycle.
The problem says 'return any of them'. A partial order has many linear extensions, so any topological order is acceptable.
memory_hook: Compare neighbors: a longer word before its prefix fails, else the first difference gives one edge. Kahn gives the order. A short order means a cycle.
approach: Adjacent pairs plus Kahn's topological sort. Compare each word with the next one: a longer word before its own prefix is invalid, and the first differing letters give one edge. Then run the standard Kahn template and return the empty string if some letter never gets placed.
rebuild_steps: Make graph = {letter: set()} for every letter of every word, and indegree = 0 for each.
For each adjacent pair w1, w2: if w1 is longer and starts with w2, return the empty string.
Walk zip(w1, w2) to the first a != b, add edge a -> b once (raise indegree[b]), then break.
Queue every letter with indegree 0; pop, append to order, lower each successor, queue it at 0.
Return the joined order if it holds every letter, else the empty string.
key_insight: A sorted list of sequences reveals the hidden order only through the first position where neighbors differ. Each such position gives one precedence edge, and the hidden order is any topological order of those edges. A cycle or a longer word placed before its own prefix means no order exists.
optimal_note: The algorithm and complexity are the same as solution_code. The only change is the form of the prefix rule: a separate startswith check before the inner loop, instead of a for-else after it.
ladder: Brute force over all letter permutations: O(U! * C), where U <= 26 is the number of unique letters and C is the total number of characters time, O(U) space (too slow)
All pairs of words to build the graph, then topological sort: O(n^2 * L + U^2), where n is the number of words and L is the maximum word length time, O(U^2) space
Adjacent pairs plus Kahn's BFS topological sort (optimal, chosen): O(C + U + E), which is O(C) because U <= 26 and E <= n - 1 time, O(U + E) space
Adjacent pairs plus DFS post-order topological sort (NeetCode reference): O(C + U + E) time, O(U + E) including the recursion stack space
pitfalls: Adding edges for every differing position instead of only the first one creates false constraints and false cycles.
Forgetting the prefix rule: ["abc", "ab"] must return the empty string, but no edge shows the problem.
Forgetting letters that never appear in any edge. Every letter that appears in any word, including the last word, must be in the output.

title: Encode and Decode Strings
statement: Design an algorithm that encodes a list of strings to one string and decodes that string back to the original list. Implement the encode and decode methods of a Codec class. Machine 1 (the sender) calls encode and sends the encoded string over the network to Machine 2 (the receiver). Machine 2 creates its own Codec object and calls decode on that string, so decode can use only the encoded string. The decoded list must equal the original list exactly, including order, empty strings and the number of items. Each string can contain any of the 256 valid ASCII characters, so no character is safe to use as a plain delimiter. You must not use any serialize methods, such as eval.
constraints: strs[i] contains any possible characters out of 256 valid ASCII characters.
follow_up: Could you write a generalized algorithm to work on any possible set of characters?
signals: You must pack many variable-length items into one flat string or stream and recover them exactly.
Items can contain any character, so every candidate delimiter can also appear inside the data.
The task bans built-in serialize methods (such as eval), so you must design the framing yourself.
The round trip must keep empty items and the exact item count, so each item needs its own boundary information, not only a gap between items.
memory_hook: Write length, hash, string; read length, then jump.
approach: Length prefix with a marker. Write each string as its length, then '#', then the string. Decode reads the digits up to the next '#', then takes exactly that many characters and jumps past them.
rebuild_steps: Encode: return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs).
Decode: set res = [] and i = 0. Loop while i < len(s).
Find the end of the header: j = s.index("#", i). The digits s[i:j] give length = int(s[i:j]).
Set start = j + 1. Append s[start:start + length] to res. Do not search inside this payload.
Set i = start + length to jump to the next header. Return res after the loop.
key_insight: When the data can contain any symbol, do not search the data for a boundary. Put the length of each item before the item, so the reader knows exactly how far to jump. A header that uses a restricted alphabet (digits) and ends with a marker is unambiguous even when the payload contains that marker.
ladder: Join with a plain delimiter: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Delimiter outside the input alphabet: O(n) time, O(n) space
Escaping with a terminator: O(n) time, O(n) space
Length prefix with a marker (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
Fixed-width length header: O(n) time, O(n) space
Header of all lengths, then all payloads: O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: A bare delimiter join fails when the delimiter appears inside a string, for example ["a#b"] and ["a", "b"].
Splitting the whole encoded string on '#' in decode breaks when a payload contains '#'. Find only the marker that ends the current header, then slice by length.
Lengths can have more than one digit. Read all digits up to the marker, not one character.
solution:
from typing import List


class Codec:
    def encode(self, strs: List[str]) -> str:
        """Encodes a list of strings to a single string."""
        # Each item becomes "<length>#<payload>".
        return "".join(f"{len(s)}#{s}" for s in strs)

    def decode(self, s: str) -> List[str]:
        """Decodes a single string to a list of strings."""
        res = []
        i = 0
        while i < len(s):
            j = s.index("#", i)          # end of the length header
            length = int(s[i:j])
            start = j + 1
            res.append(s[start:start + length])
            i = start + length           # jump over the payload
        return res

title: Walls and Gates
statement: You get an m x n grid rooms. Each cell holds one of three values. The value -1 is a wall or an obstacle. The value 0 is a gate. The value INF means an empty room.
