INF is 2^31 - 1 = 2147483647. You may assume that the distance to a gate is less than 2147483647. Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate. If it is impossible to reach a gate, the room keeps the value INF. The statement does not say it directly, but the example shows that a move goes one step up, down, left or right, and that a path cannot pass through a wall. Modify rooms in place and return nothing. Walls and gates keep their values.
signals: The task asks for the distance from every cell to the nearest member of a set of special cells (gates, sources, zeros, rotten items).
Moves are unit steps in four directions on a grid, so the graph is unweighted and BFS gives shortest paths.
There are many query cells and possibly many sources, so one search per cell or per source repeats work.
The grid can hold tens of thousands of cells (here 250 x 250 = 62,500), so a search per cell is too slow and the target is linear work in the number of cells.
memory_hook: Push all gates first, then BFS and fill only INF rooms.
approach: Multi-source BFS from all gates. Put every gate in one queue at distance 0, then run a plain grid BFS and write parent distance + 1 into each room that still holds INF.
rebuild_steps: Set INF = 2**31 - 1 and read rows and cols.
Scan the grid and append every gate (value 0) to a deque.
While the queue is not empty, popleft a cell (r, c).
List the four neighbors (r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1) and (r, c - 1).
For each neighbor, check that it is in bounds and holds INF.
Write rooms[r][c] + 1 into that neighbor and append it to the queue.
Return nothing. Rooms that BFS never reaches keep INF.
key_insight: When every cell needs its distance to the nearest of several sources, do not search from each cell. Start one BFS with all sources in the queue at distance 0. This acts like a single virtual source joined to all real sources, so the first time BFS reaches a cell gives its nearest-source distance.
ladder: BFS from each empty room: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
BFS from each gate separately: O(g*m*n), worst O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
Repeated relaxation (Bellman-Ford style sweeps): O((m*n)^2) worst case time, O(1) extra space (too slow)
Multi-source BFS from all gates (optimal): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Running a separate BFS from each gate and overwriting values gives wrong answers. Taking the minimum fixes correctness but is too slow when there are many gates.
DFS does not give shortest distances in one pass. It must revisit cells when it finds a shorter path, and it can exceed Python's recursion limit on a 250 x 250 grid.
Mark a cell as visited when you push it, not when you pop it. Otherwise the same cell enters the queue many times.

title: Find the Duplicate Number
statement: You get an array nums of n + 1 integers. Each integer is in the range [1, n] inclusive. Exactly one value repeats, and it can appear two or more times. Every other value appears at most once. Return the repeated value. You must not modify nums. You must use only constant extra space.
constraints: All the integers in nums appear only once except for precisely one integer which appears two or more times.
follow_up: How can we prove that at least one duplicate number must exist in nums? Can you solve the problem in linear runtime complexity?
signals: The array has n + 1 slots and every value is in [1, n]. The pigeonhole principle guarantees a repeat.
Every value is a valid index into the same array. You can read the array as a function i -> nums[i], which is a linked list or graph.
The rules forbid changes to the input and forbid extra memory. This removes sorting, hash sets and in-place sign marking.

The task asks for a node that two different nodes point to. A walk that starts at a node with no incoming edge must enter a cycle, and the cycle entrance always has two incoming edges. When only one node can have two incoming edges, the entrance is that node.
memory_hook: Index points to value: tortoise and hare from 0, then reset one to 0, walk together, and meet at the duplicate.
approach: Floyd cycle detection on the array read as a linked list. Index i points to index nums[i], index 0 is the head, and the cycle entrance is the duplicate.
rebuild_steps: Read nums as a linked list: the next node of index i is nums[i], and the head is index 0.
Set slow = nums[0] and fast = nums[nums[0]]. Both pointers now start after their first move.
While slow != fast, move slow one step with slow = nums[slow] and fast two steps with fast = nums[nums[fast]].
Set start = 0. While start != slow, move start and slow one step each.
Return slow. The cycle entrance is the value that two indices point to, so it is the duplicate.
key_insight: When array values are valid indices into the same array, the array is a linked list where index i points to index nums[i]. A value that appears twice is a node with two incoming edges. A walk from a node that nothing points to must enter a cycle, and the cycle entrance has two incoming edges. Only one node has two incoming edges here, so the entrance is the duplicate. Floyd's algorithm finds the entrance in O(1) space.
ladder: Brute force pairs: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort and scan: O(n log n) time, O(n) for a copy space (too slow)
Hash set: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Negative marking: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Binary search on value with counting: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
Bit counting: O(n log n) time, O(1) space
Floyd cycle detection on i -> nums[i]: O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Starting at index 0 matters. If you start at an index inside the cycle, phase 2 can return a node that is not the duplicate.
The first meeting point of slow and fast is not the answer. You must run phase 2 to find the cycle entrance.
Do not check whether slow equals fast before the first move. Both start at 0, so a loop that tests for inequality first never runs. Move first and test after, in a do-while shape.
solution:
class Solution:
    def findDuplicate(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # Read the array as a linked list: index i points to index nums[i].
        # Index 0 is the head, because no value is 0.

        # Phase 1: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps, until they meet.
        slow = nums[0]
        fast = nums[nums[0]]
        while slow != fast:
            slow = nums[slow]
            fast = nums[nums[fast]]

        # Phase 2: restart one pointer at the head.
        # Both move 1 step. They meet at the cycle entrance = the duplicate.
        start = 0
        while start != slow:
            start = nums[start]
            slow = nums[slow]
        return slow

title: Find Median from Data Stream
statement: The median is the middle value in an ordered integer list. If the size of the list is even, there is no middle value, and the median is the mean of the two middle values. For example, for arr = [2,3,4], the median is 3. For example, for arr = [2,3], the median is (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5. Implement the MedianFinder class. MedianFinder() initializes the MedianFinder object. void addNum(int num) adds the integer num from the data stream to the data structure. double findMedian() returns the median of all elements so far. Answers within 10^-5 of the actual answer will be accepted.
constraints: There will be at least one element in the data structure before calling findMedian.
At most 5 * 10^4 calls will be made to addNum and findMedian.
follow_up: If all integer numbers from the stream are in the range [0, 100], how would you optimize your solution? If 99% of all integer numbers from the stream are in the range [0, 100], how would you optimize your solution?
signals: Values arrive one at a time, and queries interleave with insertions. This is an online problem, so you cannot sort once at the end.
The query asks for a value at a rank that moves as the data grows, such as the middle or a percentile. It does not ask for the minimum or the maximum.
Only the elements at the boundary between two halves matter for the answer. The order inside each half does not matter.
Up to 5 * 10^4 interleaved operations rule out a full sort per query. Aim for about O(log n) per insert and O(1) or O(log n) per query.
memory_hook: Push into small, pass its top to large, give one back if large gets bigger.
approach: Use two heaps that face each other. Keep the lower half in a max-heap (small) and the upper half in a min-heap (large). Then the median is always at the tops.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq. Make two lists: small is a max-heap of the lower half (store negated values), and large is a min-heap of the upper half.
addNum: push -num into small.
Pop the top of small, negate it, and push it into large.
If len(large) > len(small), pop the top of large and push its negation into small.
findMedian: if small is bigger, return float(-small[0]).
Otherwise, return (-small[0] + large[0]) / 2.
key_insight: The median depends only on the boundary between the lower half and the upper half. Keep each half in a heap that exposes the side next to the boundary: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half. Then each insert costs O(log n), and each query reads the two tops in O(1).
ladder: Sort on every query: O(1) addNum, O(n log n) findMedian time, O(n) space (too slow)
Sorted list with binary-search insertion: O(n) addNum (O(log n) search plus O(n) shift), O(1) findMedian time, O(n) space
Two heaps (max-heap for lower half, min-heap for upper half): O(log n) addNum, O(1) findMedian time, O(n) space
Balanced order-statistic structure (SortedList, balanced BST, or Fenwick tree over values): O(log n) or O(log range) per addNum and per findMedian time, O(n) or O(range) space
Counting buckets (follow-up for values in [0, 100]): O(1) addNum for values in [0, 100], O(101) findMedian; outlier inserts cost O(k) for k outliers time, O(101) plus outliers space
pitfalls: Forgetting to negate values on both push and pop for the max-heap. This returns the wrong sign or the wrong element.
Pushing num into a heap by size alone, with no comparison to a top and no route through the other heap. This breaks the rule that every lower value is <= every upper value.
Not choosing which heap holds the extra element. findMedian must read the top of the larger heap when the count is odd.

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
statement: Serialization converts a data structure into a sequence of bits or characters, so that you can store it or send it and rebuild it later. Design an algorithm to serialize and deserialize a binary tree. Implement a Codec class with two methods. serialize(root) converts a binary tree to a string. deserialize(data) converts that string back to the original tree structure, with the same shape and the same node values. There is no restriction on how the algorithm works. The examples use the LeetCode level-order list format, with null for a missing child. You do not have to use this format for your string. The code template creates one Codec object to serialize and a different Codec object to deserialize, so the methods must not depend on instance state. The tree has 0 to 10^4 nodes, and each node value is an integer from -1000 to 1000. The statement does not say that values are unique. A tree with more than 2001 nodes must contain repeated values.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [0, 10^4].
signals: The task asks you to convert a structure to a flat string and back without loss. So the encoding must capture the shape as well as the values.
The problem lets you choose the encoding format. You design both sides, so choose the format that makes the decoder simplest.
Values can repeat. So you cannot locate a node by its value, and a pair of traversals such as preorder plus inorder does not identify the tree.
The structure is recursive: a tree is empty, or a value plus two subtrees. This points to a recursive grammar with an explicit marker for the empty case.
memory_hook: Write it level by level like the example list, with N for every null; each real node in the queue takes the next two tokens as its kids.
approach: Level-order BFS with null markers. Serialize with a queue that also holds None children and write N for each None. Deserialize with the same queue loop: each real node takes the next two tokens as its left and right children.
rebuild_steps: Serialize: make an empty list out and a deque that holds root.
While the deque is not empty, pop the left item. If it is None, append N and continue.
Otherwise append str(node.val). Then push node.left and node.right, even when they are None.
Return ','.join(out).
Deserialize: set tokens = iter(data.split(',')). Write make(tok): it returns None for N, else TreeNode(int(tok)).
Set root = make(next(tokens)) and put root in a new deque.
While the deque is not empty, pop the left item. If it is None, continue.
Otherwise set node.left = make(next(tokens)) and node.right = make(next(tokens)). Then push both children.
Return root.
key_insight: A traversal of values alone is ambiguous. Write an explicit marker for every empty child. Then a single preorder sequence is a self-delimiting encoding, and the decoder is the same recursion that reads tokens in the same order the encoder wrote them.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses preorder DFS with null markers. It has the same O(n) time and O(n) space. It is shorter. Its grammar (tree = N or value tree tree) is the base for related problems: verify a preorder serialization (331), serialize a BST (449), and find duplicate subtrees (652). In Python it recurses up to 10^4 deep on a skewed tree, so it needs sys.setrecursionlimit. Learn it when you want the recursive grammar view or when a problem asks for a preorder encoding.
ladder: Values only, or preorder plus inorder without null markers: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Preorder DFS with null markers, pop(0) cursor: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Preorder DFS with null markers, iterator cursor (chosen): O(n) time, O(n) for the string and token list, plus O(h) recursion depth space
Level-order BFS with null markers (LeetCode format): O(n) time, O(n) space
Compact encodings (bracket form or shape bits plus values): O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Omitting null markers: [1,2] and [1,null,2] then give the same string.
Using preorder plus inorder without markers: it fails when values repeat. Here values can repeat, and a tree with more than 2001 nodes must have repeats.
Using list.pop(0) as the cursor makes decoding O(n^2); use an iterator or an index.
solution:
from collections import deque


# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode(object):
#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.left = None
#         self.right = None

class Codec:

    def serialize(self, root):
        """Encodes a tree to a single string."""
        out = []
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                out.append("N")            # null marker keeps the shape
                continue
            out.append(str(node.val))
            queue.append(node.left)        # queue holds None children too
            queue.append(node.right)
        return ",".join(out)

    def deserialize(self, data):
        """Decodes your encoded data to tree."""
        tokens = iter(data.split(","))

        def make(tok):
            return None if tok == "N" else TreeNode(int(tok))

        root = make(next(tokens))
        queue = deque([root])
        while queue:
            node = queue.popleft()
            if node is None:
                continue                   # a null has no children to read
            node.left = make(next(tokens))     # next two tokens are its children
            node.right = make(next(tokens))
            queue.append(node.left)
            queue.append(node.right)
        return root


# Your Codec object will be instantiated and called as such:
# ser = Codec()
# deser = Codec()
# ans = deser.deserialize(ser.serialize(root))

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
statement: You get an integer array nums. Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. A subsequence keeps the original relative order of the chosen elements but can skip elements. The chosen elements do not need to be adjacent. Strictly increasing means each chosen element is greater than the previous chosen element, so equal values cannot both be in the subsequence. Return only the length, not the subsequence.
follow_up: Can you come up with an algorithm that runs in O(n log(n)) time complexity?
signals: The word subsequence means you choose elements in order and can skip elements. This points to DP over the index where the chosen sequence ends.
The answer is the longest or best chain where each new element must relate to the previous chosen element (greater, divisible, nests inside). Make the DP state end at an index.
n is about a few thousand, so O(n^2) pair checks are acceptable. A follow-up that asks for O(n log n) hints at binary search over a sorted helper array.
Only the length is asked, not the sequence itself. Then a compressed state is enough, such as the best tail value for each length.
memory_hook: Smallest tail per length: bisect_left, then replace or append.
approach: Patience sorting with one tails list. Keep the smallest last value for each chain length. For each x, bisect_left finds the first tail >= x. Then x replaces that tail, or you append x when no tail is >= x.
rebuild_steps: Import bisect_left from bisect.
Make an empty list tails. tails[k] is the smallest last value of an increasing chain of length k + 1.
Loop over each value x in nums.
Set pos = bisect_left(tails, x). This is the first tail that is >= x.
If pos == len(tails), append x, because x extends the longest chain.
Else set tails[pos] = x, because x is a smaller tail for length pos + 1.
Return len(tails). Use bisect_left, not bisect_right, so equal values do not chain.
key_insight: Among all increasing chains of the same length, only the one with the smallest last value matters, because it is the easiest to extend. Keep one best tail per length. These tails stay sorted, so binary search finds where each new value fits.
ladder: Brute force over all subsequences: O(2^n * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized recursion (index, previous index): O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
O(n^2) DP by ending index: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Patience sorting with binary search (optimal): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Fenwick tree or segment tree over values: O(n log V) time, O(V) space
pitfalls: Using bisect_right instead of bisect_left counts non-decreasing subsequences. Then [7,7,7] wrongly returns 3 instead of 1.
Returning f[n-1] instead of max(f). The LIS does not need to end at the last index.
Treating tails as the real subsequence. It only has the correct length. To rebuild the sequence, store parent indices.

title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock with Cooldown
statement: You get an array prices where prices[i] is the price of a stock on day i. Find the maximum profit. You may complete as many transactions as you like. A transaction is one buy and one later sell of one share. You cannot hold more than one share at a time, so you must sell before you buy again. After you sell, you cannot buy on the next day (a one-day cooldown). You may also make no transaction, so the answer is never negative.
signals: The problem asks for an optimal value over a sequence of step-by-step decisions (buy, sell, wait).
A rule restricts what you may do next based on what you did before (cooldown after a sell, hold at most one item).
The past matters only through a small status (holding or not, cooling down or not), not through the full history.
n is at most 5000. This rules out exponential search. A linear or quadratic DP fits.
memory_hook: Walk the days backward. Free waits or buys, holding waits or sells, and a sale skips tomorrow.
approach: Use a bottom-up decision table on (day, holding). Walk the days from last to first. For each day, store the best future profit when you own no share and when you own one share. Selling jumps to day i + 2. This jump is the cooldown.
rebuild_steps: Let n = len(prices). Make two lists free and holding of length n + 2, filled with 0 (after the last day there is nothing to earn).
Loop i from n - 1 down to 0 and let p = prices[i].
free[i] = max(free[i + 1], holding[i + 1] - p): wait, or buy today.
holding[i] = max(holding[i + 1], free[i + 2] + p): wait, or sell today and skip tomorrow.
Return free[0], because day 0 starts with no share.
key_insight: Model the constraint as a status, not as history. The cooldown becomes a separate state (just sold) that cannot move directly to holding. Then each day is a fixed set of transitions between a few best-value states.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses three rolling variables (hold, sold, rest) and runs forward in O(1) extra space. The time is the same O(n). It needs the -inf base, simultaneous tuple assignment and the answer max(sold, rest). Use it when memory must be O(1) or when you want the compact state machine form. For n <= 5000 the O(n) table is far inside the limits, so the extra memory trick is not needed here.
ladder: Brute force decision tree: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on (day, holding): O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up tabulation with two states and a lag: O(n) time, O(n), or O(1) with rolling variables space
Three-state machine with rolling variables (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Updating hold, sold and rest one by one makes later updates read new values. Use tuple assignment or temporary variables.
Buying from sold instead of rest ignores the cooldown and gives too much profit.
Starting hold at 0 instead of -inf (or -prices[0]) pretends you own a free share.
solution:
class Solution:
    def maxProfit(self, prices: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(prices)
        # free[i]: best profit from day i on when you own no share.
        # holding[i]: best profit from day i on when you own one share.
        # Two extra zero cells: after the last day there is nothing to earn.
        free = [0] * (n + 2)
        holding = [0] * (n + 2)
        for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
            p = prices[i]
            free[i] = max(free[i + 1], holding[i + 1] - p)     # wait or buy
            holding[i] = max(holding[i + 1], free[i + 2] + p)  # wait or sell (selling skips tomorrow)
        return free[0]

title: Burst Balloons
statement: You are given n balloons, indexed from 0 to n - 1. Each balloon has a number painted on it. The array nums gives these numbers. You must burst all the balloons. If you burst balloon i, you get nums[i - 1] * nums[i] * nums[i + 1] coins. If i - 1 or i + 1 is out of bounds of the array, treat it as a balloon with 1 painted on it. Return the maximum coins that you can collect by bursting the balloons wisely. Example 1 shows that i - 1 and i + 1 mean the neighbors that are still present when balloon i bursts.
signals: You remove elements of a sequence one at a time, and the score of a removal depends on the neighbors that are adjacent at that moment.
The order of operations matters and you must optimize over all orders. A greedy rule has no obvious proof, and n! orders are too many.
The input is a sequence of a few hundred items (n <= 300). This budget allows O(n^3). That fits a DP over all ranges [l, r] with a split point.
Choosing the first operation leaves the two sides coupled, but choosing the last operation leaves them independent. That asymmetry signals reverse-time interval DP.
memory_hook: Pick the balloon that pops last. It sees only the two walls.
approach: Use interval DP on the last balloon to burst. Pad the row with 1 at both ends. Let dp[l][r] be the best score for the balloons strictly between walls l and r. Try each k between the walls as the last balloon to burst. At that moment, k sees only the walls l and r.
rebuild_steps: Pad the row: vals = [1] + nums + [1]. Set n = len(vals).
Make an n by n table dp of zeros. dp[l][r] is the best coins for the balloons strictly between walls l and r.
Loop length from 2 to n - 1. Inside it, loop l from 0 to n - length - 1 and set r = l + length. Short ranges come first, so both subranges are ready.
Set edge = vals[l] * vals[r], the product of the two walls. Set best = 0.
For each k in range(l + 1, r), let k burst last: coins = dp[l][k] + edge * vals[k] + dp[k][r]. If coins is larger than best, set best = coins.
After the k loop, store best in dp[l][r].
Return dp[0][n - 1]. This is the range between the two sentinel walls.
key_insight: When an action on one element changes who its neighbors are, do not choose the first action in a range. Choose the last one. The last element stays alive while the rest of the range is cleared, so it separates the range into two independent subranges. When it finally acts, its neighbors are exactly the fixed range boundaries.
ladder: Brute force over all burst orders: O(n! * n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized search over the set of remaining balloons: O(2^n * n^2) time, O(2^n * n) space (too slow)
Top-down interval DP on the last balloon (memoized recursion): O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
Bottom-up interval DP on the last balloon (optimal): O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
pitfalls: Splitting on the first balloon burst gives wrong answers, because its neighbors become adjacent and the two sides interact.
Using original neighbors nums[k - 1] and nums[k + 1] instead of the range walls vals[l] and vals[r] for the last burst.
Mixing open and closed ranges. In this formulation l and r are walls that never burst, and k runs strictly between them.

title: Coin Change
statement: You get an integer array coins. Each value in coins is a coin of a different denomination. You also get an integer amount, which is a total amount of money. Return the fewest number of coins that you need to make up that amount. If no combination of the coins can make up that amount, return -1. You can assume that you have an infinite number of each kind of coin.
signals: The task asks for the fewest items that reach an exact target sum. This points to a min DP over target values.
Each item is reusable without limit. So the state needs only the remaining target, not the set of items already used.
The target is small (10^4) but item values are huge. Index the DP by the target, not by item value.
The item values are arbitrary, so a greedy choice is not safe. You must compare all choices, and the choices share subproblems.
memory_hook: Pick the last coin: dp[a] = 1 + min of dp[a - coin], with dp[0] = 0.
approach: Bottom-up DP over amounts (fix the last coin). dp[a] is the fewest coins for amount a, and dp[a] = min(dp[a - c] + 1) over every coin c <= a, filled from a = 1 up to amount.
rebuild_steps: Make dp of size amount + 1. dp[a] means the fewest coins for amount a. Set dp[0] = 0 and every other cell to inf.
Loop a from 1 to amount in increasing order.
For each coin c with c <= a, set dp[a] = min(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1).
After the loops, return dp[amount], or -1 if it is still inf.
key_insight: When items are reusable and only the total matters, the state is just the remaining target. Fix the last item chosen, and the rest is the same problem on a smaller target. So the best answer for a target is one plus the best answer for the target minus some item.
ladder: Plain recursion (brute force): O(n^(amount/m)), m = smallest coin time, O(amount/m) space (too slow)
Greedy, largest coin first: O(n log n + amount) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(amount * n) time, O(amount) space
Bottom-up DP over amounts (unbounded knapsack, chosen): O(amount * n) time, O(amount) space
BFS over amounts: O(amount * n) time, O(amount) space
pitfalls: Greedy by largest coin fails on non-canonical coin sets such as [1,3,4] with amount 6.
amount = 0 must return 0, not -1.
The sentinel must exceed every real answer. The largest real answer is amount (all ones), so amount + 1 is safe and amount is not.

title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
statement: You have a graph of n nodes. You get an integer n and an array edges. Each edges[i] = [ai, bi] means that there is an edge between ai and bi in the graph. Return the number of connected components in the graph. Note: the title says that the graph is undirected. The nodes have the labels 0 to n - 1.
signals: The input is a node count plus an undirected edge list, and the question asks how many groups exist.
The question asks about connectivity only, not about distances, path lengths or edge order.
The words connected, components, groups, provinces, networks, islands or clusters appear.
The relation is symmetric and transitive. If a links to b and b links to c, then a and c are in the same group.
memory_hook: Count how many times you must start a new flood.
approach: Flood fill and count the starts (iterative DFS with a visited list). Loop over all nodes, and each time you find an unvisited node, add one to the count and mark its whole component with a stack.
rebuild_steps: Make graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]. For each edge (a, b), append b to graph[a] and append a to graph[b].
Make seen = [False] * n and components = 0.
Loop over each start node in range(n). Skip the node when seen[start] is True.
Otherwise add one to components. Mark start as seen and put it on a new stack.
While the stack is not empty, pop a node. For each neighbor of that node that is not seen, mark the neighbor as seen and push it.
After the loop over all start nodes, return components.
key_insight: Count components as n minus the number of edges that join two different groups. Every node starts as its own group. An edge that connects two different groups merges them and removes exactly one group. An edge inside one group closes a cycle and changes nothing. Union-Find answers the question 'same group already?' in near constant amortized time.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code uses Union-Find with path halving and union by size. It starts at n and subtracts one for each edge that joins two different roots. It needs no adjacency list, uses O(n) memory, and works when edges stream in one at a time. Use it when you must report the count after each new edge, or when the problem asks about redundant edges or a valid tree. For one count over a fixed edge list, both run in about O(n + m) time.
ladder: Transitive closure matrix: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
Search from every node: O(n * (n + m)) time, O(n + m) space (too slow)
Repeated min-label propagation: O(n * m) time, O(n) space (too slow)
DFS or BFS with a shared visited set: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
Union-Find with path compression and union by size (chosen): O(n + m * alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
Union-Find, count distinct roots at the end (NeetCode reference): O((n + m) log n) amortized time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Isolated nodes are components. Start the count at n, and do not count only nodes that appear in edges.
Edges are undirected. With an adjacency list, add both directions.

Recursive DFS on a 2000-node path needs about 2000 nested calls. That exceeds the CPython default recursion limit of 1000 and raises RecursionError. Use an iterative stack, BFS, Union-Find, or raise the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit.

title: Longest Increasing Path in a Matrix
statement: Given an m x n integer matrix, return the length of the longest increasing path in the matrix. From each cell you can move in four directions: left, right, up, or down. You may not move diagonally or move outside the boundary (wrap-around is not allowed). Increasing means strictly increasing: each next cell must hold a larger value than the current cell. The statement does not say strictly, but Example 1 shows it. With equal steps allowed, Example 1 would give 7 cells instead of 4. The length counts cells, so one cell alone is a path of length 1. The path can start and end at any cell.
signals: The problem asks for the longest path in a graph or grid. Longest simple path is hard in general, so look for a property that removes cycles.
Every allowed move must strictly increase (or decrease) a value. A strict order along edges means the move graph is a directed acyclic graph.
The path has no fixed start or end. You need the best answer over all start cells, so compute one value per cell and reuse it.
Moves go in all four directions. No simple row-by-row fill order exists, so the order must come from the values themselves: memoized recursion, sorting by value, or topological order.
memory_hook: Biggest first: each cell is 1 plus its best bigger neighbor.
approach: Sort cells by value, bottom-up DP. Visit cells from the largest value to the smallest, and set each cell to 1 plus the best answer of its strictly larger neighbors, which are already final.
rebuild_steps: Read rows and cols. Make a table best with 1 in every cell, because one cell alone is a path of length 1.
Build a list of (value, r, c) for all cells and sort it in reverse order, so the largest value comes first.
For each cell in that order, check the 4 neighbors with bounds 0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols.
If a neighbor value is strictly larger, set best[r][c] = max(best[r][c], 1 + best[nr][nc]).
Return the largest value in best.
key_insight: A strict order along every move makes the move graph acyclic. Then the best path from a node does not depend on how you reached the node. So longest path becomes a DAG DP: f(node) = 1 + max f(successor), and memoization solves each node once.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code is a memoized DFS in O(m*n) time. This solution takes O(m*n log(m*n)) time and O(m*n) space because of the sort. At 200 x 200 the sort alone costs about 0.04 s of CPU time, and the whole solution costs less than 0.15 s, so the gain does not matter here. The DFS needs a recursion limit above m*n because a snake grid gives a 40000-cell path. Use the memoized DFS when you want the shortest code and the path depth is small. Use Kahn's algorithm when you need strict O(m*n) time with no recursion.
ladder: Brute-force DFS from every cell: O(m*n * 3^L) where L is the longest path length; exponential time, O(L) recursion depth, which is O(m*n) in the worst case space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on the implicit DAG (top-down DP): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) for the cache and the recursion stack space
Sort cells by value, bottom-up DP: O(m*n log(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
Kahn topological sort by layers: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Using >= instead of >. Equal neighbors create cycles, which cause infinite recursion or wrong answers. Example 1 has equal 9s and 6s.
Adding a shared visited set to the DFS. It is not needed. If the result depends on the path so far, a cache keyed by cell gives wrong answers.
Starting only at (0, 0) or only at the smallest cell. The answer is the max over every start cell.

title: Reconstruct Itinerary
statement: You get a list of airline tickets. Each ticket tickets[i] = [from_i, to_i] gives the departure airport and the arrival airport of one flight. Reconstruct the itinerary in order and return it. All tickets belong to one man who departs from "JFK", so the itinerary must begin with "JFK". If more than one valid itinerary exists, return the itinerary that has the smallest lexical order when read as a single string. For example, the itinerary ["JFK", "LGA"] has a smaller lexical order than ["JFK", "LGB"]. You may assume that all tickets form at least one valid itinerary. You must use all the tickets once and only once.
signals: The task says to use every edge (ticket, pair, domino, connection) exactly once. This points to an Eulerian path, not a vertex search.
Vertices can repeat in the answer but edges cannot. Track used edges, not visited vertices.
Each item links an end of one item to the start of the next item. Model items as edges between endpoint values.
The start vertex is fixed and a valid answer is guaranteed. You can run Hierholzer from that start with no existence check.
memory_hook: Take the smallest ticket, write the airport down when stuck, then reverse.
approach: Hierholzer DFS with post-order append. Walk from JFK and always take the smallest unused ticket. When an airport has no unused tickets, append it to the route. Reverse the route at the end.
rebuild_steps: Build graph = defaultdict(list) from sorted(tickets, reverse=True), so each list ends with the smallest destination.
Create an empty route list.
Define visit(airport): while graph[airport] has tickets, call visit(graph[airport].pop()). The pop removes the smallest ticket, so each ticket is used once.
After the while loop, append airport to route (post-order, the airport is stuck).
Call visit("JFK") and return route[::-1].
key_insight: In an Eulerian path walk, the first vertex where you get stuck must be the final vertex of the path. So build the answer backward: append a vertex when it has no unused edges, then reverse. Any detour that the greedy walk skipped gets spliced in before the dead end, so greedy choice of the smallest edge never needs to be undone.
ladder: Brute force over ticket orders: O(E! * E) time, O(E) space (too slow)
Backtracking DFS with sorted adjacency: O(E^d) worst case, d = max out-degree time, O(E) space (too slow)
Hierholzer DFS with post-order (optimal): O(E log E) time, O(E) space
Hierholzer with min-heaps per airport: O(E log E) time, O(E) space
Iterative Hierholzer with an explicit stack: O(E log E) time, O(E) space
pitfalls: Forward greedy that appends airports as it walks gets stuck in a dead end and leaves tickets unused.
Appending the airport before its loop (pre-order) gives a wrong order. Append after the loop.
Forgetting to reverse the post-order list returns the itinerary backward.

title: Counting Bits
statement: You get an integer n. Return an array ans of length n + 1. For each i with 0 <= i <= n, ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in the binary representation of i. Do not use a built-in popcount function (for example __builtin_popcount in C++).
follow_up: It is very easy to come up with a solution with a runtime of O(n log n). Can you do it in linear time O(n) and possibly in a single pass?
signals: The output is a value for every integer from 0 to n, not for one number. Answers for small numbers can build answers for larger numbers.
The value is a property of the binary form of a number. Removing one bit (shift right, clear lowest set bit, or remove highest bit) gives a smaller number with a known answer.
The follow-up asks for O(n) when a per-item O(log n) method is obvious. This means each answer must come from an earlier answer in O(1).
The problem bans the built-in popcount and asks for linear time. A separate loop per number is then too slow, so the answers must share work through a recurrence.
memory_hook: Drop the last bit, look it up, add the bit back.
approach: DP on the right shift. The number i >> 1 is i without its last bit, and its answer is already in the table, so ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1).
rebuild_steps: Make a table ans = [0] * (n + 1); ans[0] = 0 is the base case.
Loop i from 1 to n in increasing order.
Drop the last bit: i >> 1 is smaller than i, so ans[i >> 1] is already filled.
Add the dropped bit back: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1), with parentheses around i & 1.
Return ans.
key_insight: A bit operation that removes one known bit from i gives a smaller number. So the answer for i is the stored answer for that smaller number plus the removed bit.
ladder: Count bits of each number separately: O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
Built-in popcount (not allowed by the statement): O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space
DP on the right shift (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
DP on the lowest set bit: O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
DP on the highest set bit (NeetCode offset): O(n) time, O(1) extra (O(n) output) space
pitfalls: The array has length n + 1, not n. It includes 0 and n.
Handle n = 0. The answer is [0], and the loop must not run.
Write (i & 1) in parentheses. In Python, + binds tighter than &, so ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 is wrong.

title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: You get an integer array nums and an integer k. Return the k elements that occur most often in nums. You can return the answer in any order. k is at least 1 and at most the number of distinct values in nums. The answer is guaranteed to be unique, so there is no tie at the boundary between the k-th and the (k+1)-th most frequent value.
constraints: k is in the range [1, the number of unique elements in the array].
It is guaranteed that the answer is unique.
follow_up: Your algorithm's time complexity must be better than O(n log n), where n is the array's size.
signals: The task asks for the k most frequent, k largest, or k best items, not a full ranking.
The output order is free, so you only need to select a set, not sort it.
The ranking key is a count, and a count is an integer between 1 and n. A bounded integer key allows bucket sort or counting sort.
A follow-up demands better than O(n log n). This rules out a full sort and points to a heap, bucket sort, or quickselect.
memory_hook: Bucket values by count, read buckets top down, take the first k.
approach: Count, then bucket sort by frequency and take the first k. Put each value into buckets[count], read the buckets from the highest count down into one list, and return the first k items of that list.
rebuild_steps: Count every value with count = Counter(nums).
Make len(nums) + 1 empty buckets with a list comprehension, because a count can be as large as n.
For each (num, freq) in count.items(), append num to buckets[freq].
Start an empty list by_frequency.
Loop freq from len(nums) down to 1. Extend by_frequency with buckets[freq].
Return by_frequency[:k].
key_insight: When the ranking key is a small bounded integer, do not compare keys. Use the key as an array index. A frequency is always between 1 and n, so an array of n + 1 buckets sorts the values by frequency in linear time.
optimal_note: The algorithm is the same bucket sort in O(n) time and O(n) space. The record's solution_code adds an early exit. It appends one value at a time and returns as soon as it has k values, so it skips the remaining low buckets. This saves only a constant factor. Use it if you want to stop the work early. The answer does not change.
ladder: Brute force: count each value by rescanning: O(n * m + m log m), m = number of distinct values time, O(m) space (too slow)
Hash map count + sort by frequency: O(n + m log m) time, O(m) space
Hash map count + min-heap of size k: O(n + m log k) time, O(m + k) space
Hash map count + bucket sort by frequency (optimal, standard): O(n) time, O(n) space
Hash map count + quickselect: O(n) average, O(n + m^2) worst case time, O(m) space
pitfalls: Do not bucket by value. Make one bucket per possible frequency, from 0 to n.
The bucket array needs size n + 1, because one value can occur n times. Size n causes an IndexError.
Do not build the buckets with [[]] * (n + 1). That creates n + 1 references to one shared list.
solution:
from collections import Counter
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def topKFrequent(self, nums: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
        count = Counter(nums)

        # buckets[f] holds the values that occur exactly f times.
        buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
        for num, freq in count.items():
            buckets[freq].append(num)

        # Read the buckets from the highest frequency down.
        # This lists the values from most frequent to least frequent.
        by_frequency = []
        for freq in range(len(nums), 0, -1):
            by_frequency.extend(buckets[freq])

        return by_frequency[:k]

title: Design Twitter
statement: Design a simplified version of Twitter. Users can post tweets and follow or unfollow another user. A user can see the 10 most recent tweets in the user's news feed. Implement the Twitter class. Twitter() initializes your twitter object. void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId) composes a new tweet with ID tweetId by the user userId. Each call to this function uses a unique tweetId. List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId) retrieves the 10 most recent tweet IDs in the user's news feed. Each item in the news feed must be posted by users who the user followed or by the user themself. Tweets must be ordered from most recent to least recent. void follow(int followerId, int followeeId): the user with ID followerId starts to follow the user with ID followeeId. void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId): the user with ID followerId stops following the user with ID followeeId.
constraints: All the tweets have unique IDs.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to postTweet, getNewsFeed, follow, and unfollow.
signals: The query asks for the k most recent or k best items, and k is a small fixed number.
The candidates come from many sources, and each source already keeps its items in sorted order.
Items arrive over time and are appended, so each per-source list is sorted by time for free.
Ranking is by recency, but the IDs carry no time order. This points to a global counter as a timestamp.
memory_hook: Stamp each tweet with a global clock. Merge the timelines with a heap: one cursor per user, pop the newest, push that user's previous tweet, stop at ten.
approach: Heap k-way merge with one cursor per user. Stamp each tweet with a global counter and append it to its author's list. For a feed, put the newest tweet of you and each followee in a max-heap, pop the newest 10 times, and after each pop push the next older tweet of that same user.
rebuild_steps: State: a counter time = 0, tweets = defaultdict(list) that holds (time, tweetId) per user, and following = defaultdict(set) per user.
postTweet: append (time, tweetId) to tweets[userId]. Then add 1 to time.

getNewsFeed seed: start an empty list heap. For each uid in following[userId] | {userId}, read user_tweets = tweets.get(uid). If it has tweets, append (-time, tweetId, uid, i) for its last index i. Then heapify the list.
getNewsFeed merge: while the heap is not empty and the feed has fewer than 10 items, pop the top and append its tweetId to the feed.
After each pop, if i > 0, read tweets[uid][i - 1] and push (-time, tweetId, uid, i - 1).
Return the feed list.
follow: if followerId is not followeeId, add followeeId to following[followerId].
unfollow: discard followeeId from following[followerId]. discard does not raise an error for a missing item.
key_insight: The feed is a merge of several lists that are already sorted by time, and you need only the first 10 results. A heap that holds one cursor per list gives the next global item in O(log F), where F is the number of lists. So the read work depends on the number of sources and the output size, not on the total data size.
ladder: Global tweet log scan: O(1) post, follow, unfollow; O(T) getNewsFeed in the worst case, T = total tweets time, O(T + E), E = follow edges space (too slow)
Collect all relevant tweets and sort: O(N log N) per getNewsFeed, N = tweets of the user and followees time, O(T + E) plus O(N) per call space (too slow)
Last 10 per user, then select top 10: O(10F log 10) = O(F) per getNewsFeed, with up to 10F candidates; O(1) for other operations time, O(T + E) plus O(10F) per call space (too slow)
Heap k-way merge over per-user sorted lists (chosen): O(1) post, follow, unfollow; O(F + 10 log F) getNewsFeed, F = number of followees time, O(T + E) total; O(F) heap per call space
heapq.merge with reversed lists: O(F + 10 log F) per getNewsFeed time, O(F) per call space
Fan-out on write (push model): O(followers) post; O(10) getNewsFeed; O(F + 10 log F) rebuild on follow or unfollow time, O(T + E + 10U), U = users space
pitfalls: Order by post time, not by tweetId. Tweet IDs are unique but not increasing with time.
Include the user's own tweets in the feed, even when the user follows nobody.
Do not add userId to its own follow set inside getNewsFeed. It changes the follow graph as a side effect. Use a temporary set union.

title: Sum of Two Integers
statement: Given two integers a and b, return the sum of the two integers without using the operators + and -.
signals: The statement forbids the normal arithmetic operators. This points to building the arithmetic from bitwise operators.
The task asks for a basic arithmetic operation under an operator ban. Think of how a hardware circuit or the long-hand method computes it, one bit column at a time.
The inputs can be negative. This means two's complement matters, and in Python you must emulate a fixed word width with a mask.
The values fit in a fixed word width such as 32 bits. A loop over the bit positions then runs a constant number of times.
memory_hook: XOR is the sum, AND shifted left is the carry. Repeat until no carry, mask to 32 bits, and fix the sign with ~(a ^ MASK).
approach: XOR sum plus shifted AND carry, masked to 32 bits. XOR adds each column without carry, AND shifted left by one gives the carry, and you repeat until the carry is zero, then convert bit 31 back to a negative sign.
rebuild_steps: Set MASK = 0xFFFFFFFF to emulate a 32-bit int.
Loop while b != 0.
In one tuple assignment, set a to (a ^ b) & MASK and b to ((a & b) << 1) & MASK. The tuple form makes both parts use the old a.
After the loop, return a if a <= 0x7FFFFFFF.
Otherwise return ~(a ^ MASK), which equals a minus 2^32 without the minus operator.
key_insight: Addition splits into two independent parts: a carry-free sum (XOR) and a carry (AND shifted left by one). Their sum equals the original sum, so you repeat the split until the carry is zero.
ladder: Built-in shortcut (sum([a, b]) or operator.add): O(1) time, O(1) space
Unit steps with bitwise increment and decrement: O(|b| * 32) time, O(1) space
Ripple-carry adder bit by bit: O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
XOR plus shifted AND carry loop with a 32-bit mask (optimal): O(32) = O(1) time, O(1) space
Sign case analysis without a mask (common reference form): O(log(max(|a|, |b|))) time, O(log(max(|a|, |b|))) recursion space
pitfalls: Without a mask, the loop never ends in Python when one operand is negative and the true sum is zero or positive. The carry shifts left without limit. Examples: a = -1, b = 1 and a = -3, b = 5. A case such as a = -3, b = 1 ends, so a few tests can hide the bug.
Returning a - 2**32 to restore the sign uses the forbidden minus operator. Use ~(a ^ mask) or a | ~mask instead.
If you mask only the carry and not a ^ b, a can stay a negative Python int with infinite sign bits. The final sign test then gives a wrong answer. Example: a = -1, b = 1 returns -2^32 instead of 0.

title: Combination Sum IV
statement: You get an array nums of distinct positive integers and a positive integer target. Return the number of possible combinations of numbers from nums that add up to target. You can use each number any number of times. Different orders count as different combinations, so (1, 2) and (2, 1) are two separate ways. In other words, count the ordered sequences whose sum is exactly target. The test cases make sure that the answer fits in a 32-bit integer.
constraints: All the elements of nums are unique.
follow_up: What if negative numbers are allowed in the given array? How does it change the problem? What limitation we need to add to the question to allow negative numbers?
signals: The problem asks for the number of ways to reach an exact total, not for the list of ways. Counting points to DP, not backtracking.
Items can be reused without limit. This is an unbounded knapsack shape.
The statement says that different orders count as different. Order matters, so you count sequences, not multisets.
The target is small (at most 1000) and the values are positive integers. A table indexed by the running sum is cheap.
memory_hook: Ways to make a total: try every last number, add the ways for what is left.
approach: Bottom-up DP over the total, split by the last number. ways[total] is the sum of ways[total - last] over every number last that fits, with ways[0] = 1.
rebuild_steps: Make a list ways of size target + 1 filled with 0.
Set ways[0] = 1, because picking nothing is one way to make 0.
Loop total from 1 to target in the outer loop.
In the inner loop, try each number last in nums as the last pick.
If last <= total, add ways[total - last] to ways[total].
Return ways[target].
key_insight: To count ordered sequences that reach a total, condition on the last step. The count for total s is the sum of the counts for s - x over every allowed step x. The future depends only on the remaining amount, so a 1-D table over the amount replaces the exponential search. The loop order decides what you count: amount outside counts orderings, items outside counts multisets.
ladder: Brute-force enumeration (DFS over sequences): O(n^(target / min(nums))) time, O(target / min(nums)) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS on remaining sum: O(n * target) time, O(target) space
Bottom-up DP over the sum (sum outer, nums inner): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
Bottom-up DP with sorted nums and early break: O(n log n + n * target) time, O(target) space
pitfalls: The title says 'combination', but the problem counts ordered sequences. Example 1 shows (1, 1, 2), (1, 2, 1) and (2, 1, 1) as three answers.
Swapping the loops (items outside, amounts inside) gives Coin Change II. It returns 4 instead of 7 on example 1.
dp[0] must be 1, not 0. With 0, every entry stays 0.

title: Partition Equal Subset Sum
statement: You get an integer array nums. Return true if you can split the elements into two subsets so that the sum of the elements in each subset is equal. Otherwise return false. Every element goes into exactly one subset.
signals: The task asks if you can split items into two groups with equal sums. This is the same as asking if one subset reaches half of the total.
Each item is used at most once, and you only choose take or skip. This is a 0/1 knapsack decision.
The values are small positive integers and the count is small. So the total sum is small (here at most 20000), and a table indexed by sum is cheap.
The answer is yes or no about reachability, not an optimum. A boolean DP over reachable sums fits.
memory_hook: Odd total means no. Otherwise grow the set of reachable sums and ask if half the total is in it.
approach: Set of reachable sums. Start with {0} for the empty subset. For each number, add that number to every old sum and merge the results into the set. At the end, check if half of the total is in the set.
rebuild_steps: Compute total = sum(nums). If total is odd, return False.
Start with sums = {0}, the sum of the empty subset.
For each x in nums, do sums |= {s + x for s in sums}. Skip keeps the old sums, take adds x to them. The comprehension reads only the old sums, so x is used once.
Return total // 2 in sums.
key_insight: Equal partition is a disguise for subset sum to half the total. Subsets that reach the same sum are interchangeable for the future, so you track which sums are reachable, not which subsets exist.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code stores the same reachable sums in a boolean list of size total / 2 + 1 and updates it in place. It must loop j from target down to x so that dp[j - x] still holds the value from before x. It also caps sums at the target and can return early when dp[target] becomes true. Use it when you need the classic 0/1 knapsack table, or when you need a counting or min/max version, for example target sum or coin change, because a set cannot store a count per sum. Both versions are O(n * total). In CPython both take under 0.2 s of CPU time at the maximum size.
ladder: Brute force over all subsets: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on (index, remaining): O(n * target) time, O(n * target) space
2-D bottom-up 0/1 knapsack table: O(n * target) time, O(n * target) space
Set of reachable sums (intuitive pick): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
1-D boolean DP with reverse sum loop (chosen): O(n * target) time, O(target) space
Bitset shift: O(n * target / w) time, O(target / w) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the odd total check. An odd total can never split evenly.
Looping j upward in the 1-D table. Then dp[j - x] can already include x, so one element is counted many times.
Forgetting dp[0] = true. Without the empty subset base case no sum becomes reachable.

title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
statement: There is an m x n rectangular island. The Pacific Ocean touches the left and top edges of the island. The Atlantic Ocean touches the right and bottom edges of the island. The island is a grid of square cells. You get an m x n integer matrix heights. heights[r][c] is the height above sea level of the cell at coordinate (r, c). The island receives a lot of rain. Rain water can flow from a cell to a neighbor directly north, south, east or west if the neighbor's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height. Water can flow from any cell next to an ocean into that ocean. Return a 2D list of grid coordinates result, where result[i] = [ri, ci] means that rain water can flow from cell (ri, ci) to both the Pacific and the Atlantic oceans. Note: the official text does not fix an output order. The examples list the cells in row-major order.
signals: The question asks which cells or nodes can reach a fixed target set, such as a border, an exit or a gate.
Many sources share a few fixed targets. A separate search from each source repeats the same work.
A local rule between neighbors sets the move direction, such as height less than or equal. You can test the same rule backward from the target side.
The answer needs cells that meet two or more reachability conditions at the same time. This points to one search per condition and an intersection.
memory_hook: Water flows down, so flood uphill from each ocean and keep the cells both floods reach.
approach: Use a reverse flood fill from each ocean. Seed a stack and a reached set with all border cells of one ocean. Step only to neighbors that are at least as high. Return the cells that both floods reach.
rebuild_steps: Read rows = len(heights) and cols = len(heights[0]).
Write flood_uphill(starts). Set reached = set(starts) and stack = list(starts).
While the stack is not empty, pop a cell (r, c).
For each of the 4 neighbors, check that it is inside the grid, is not in reached, and has height >= heights[r][c].
If all checks pass, add the neighbor to reached and push it. Return reached when the stack is empty.
Set pacific = flood_uphill(the whole top row plus the whole left column).
Set atlantic = flood_uphill(the whole bottom row plus the whole right column).
Return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(pacific & atlantic)].
key_insight: When many sources ask whether they can reach a small fixed target set, reverse the edges and search once from all targets together. One reverse search answers the question for every source at the same time.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code uses the same reverse search with the same O(m*n) time and O(m*n) space. It uses a collections.deque as a BFS queue instead of a list as a stack. It builds the result with a row-major scan of the grid instead of sorted(pacific & atlantic). The visit order does not change the reached sets, so both versions return the same cells in the same order.
ladder: Brute force: downhill search from every cell: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
Memoized downhill search per cell: O(m*n) with SCC condensation time, O(m*n) space
Reverse multi-source BFS from each ocean (optimal): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Reverse DFS from each ocean (NeetCode style): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Using the wrong comparison in the reverse search. Move to a neighbor only if its height is >= the current cell's height, not <=.
Using strict > instead of >=. Water flows to cells of equal height, so equal neighbors must be included.

Seeding only part of a border. The Pacific search starts from the whole top row and the whole left column. The Atlantic search starts from the whole bottom row and the whole right column. Then the top-right and bottom-left corners, and every cell of a single-row or single-column grid, belong to both oceans with no special case.
solution:
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def pacificAtlantic(self, heights: List[List[int]]) -> List[List[int]]:
        rows, cols = len(heights), len(heights[0])

        def flood_uphill(starts):
            # Water flows down or level, so search backward from the ocean:
            # climb to neighbors that are at least as high.
            reached = set(starts)
            stack = list(starts)
            while stack:
                r, c = stack.pop()
                for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                    if (
                        0 <= nr < rows
                        and 0 <= nc < cols
                        and (nr, nc) not in reached
                        and heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]
                    ):
                        reached.add((nr, nc))
                        stack.append((nr, nc))
            return reached

        top_and_left = [(0, c) for c in range(cols)] + [(r, 0) for r in range(rows)]
        bottom_and_right = [(rows - 1, c) for c in range(cols)] + [
            (r, cols - 1) for r in range(rows)
        ]
        pacific = flood_uphill(top_and_left)
        atlantic = flood_uphill(bottom_and_right)
        return [[r, c] for r, c in sorted(pacific & atlantic)]

title: Longest Repeating Character Replacement
statement: You get a string s and an integer k. In one operation, you choose any character of s and change it to any other uppercase English letter. You can do this operation at most k times. Return the length of the longest substring that contains only the same letter after the operations. A substring is contiguous. You do not have to use all k operations.
constraints: s consists of only uppercase English letters.
signals: The task asks for the longest contiguous substring or subarray that satisfies a condition.
A budget of at most k changes, deletions or flips limits how many bad elements a window can hold.
The validity test of a window depends only on counts inside the window, so you can update it in O(1) when one element enters or leaves.
Validity is monotone: if a window is valid, every shorter window inside it is also valid. So you can shrink from the left without losing a valid answer.
memory_hook: Window length minus top count must be at most k.
approach: Sliding window with exact max frequency. Grow the window one letter to the right. While window length minus the count of its most common letter is more than k, shrink the window from the left. Get that top count with max over the at most 26 letter counts.
rebuild_steps: Import Counter from collections. Make a Counter for the window, and set left = 0 and best = 0.
For each right, ch in enumerate(s), add one to count[ch].
While (right - left + 1) - max(count.values()) > k, subtract one from count[s[left]] and add one to left.
After the while loop the window is valid, so set best = max(best, right - left + 1).
After the for loop, return best.
key_insight: Reframe the cost of a window as a count expression: the minimum number of changes to make a window uniform is its length minus the count of its most frequent element. Then the problem is the longest window with length - max_freq <= k, a classic variable sliding window with a monotone validity condition.
optimal_note: The optimal solution keeps max_freq as a running maximum that never goes down, so it does not scan the counts. This removes the factor of 26 and gives O(n). A stale max_freq can be too high, so the window can stay at a length that is not valid now. That length is never more than the length of a valid window found before, so the answer stays correct. The answer grows only when a letter count goes above the old max_freq. You need this trick only for a large alphabet, where a scan of all counts is too slow, or when the task requires strict O(n).
ladder: Brute force over all substrings: O(26 * n^2) time, O(26) space (too slow)
Binary search on the answer length: O(26 * n log n) time, O(26) space
One sliding window per target letter: O(26 * n) time, O(1) space
Sliding window with exact max frequency: O(26 * n) time, O(26) space
Sliding window with non-decreasing max frequency (optimal): O(n) time, O(26) space
pitfalls: Do not count the number of distinct letters. The cost is length - max_freq, not the number of other letter types.
Do not fix the target letter as the first letter of the window. The best letter can be any letter in the window.
If you return right - left + 1 at the end instead of tracking best, it works only because the window never shrinks with the stale max_freq. With exact max recomputation, you must track best.
solution:
from collections import Counter


class Solution:
    def characterReplacement(self, s: str, k: int) -> int:
        count = Counter()
        left = 0
        best = 0
        for right, ch in enumerate(s):
            count[ch] += 1
            # Changes needed = window length - count of its most common letter.
            while (right - left + 1) - max(count.values()) > k:
                count[s[left]] -= 1
                left += 1
            best = max(best, right - left + 1)
        return best

title: Non-overlapping Intervals
statement: You get an array intervals where intervals[i] = [start_i, end_i]. Return the minimum number of intervals that you must remove so that the remaining intervals do not overlap. Intervals that only touch at a point do not overlap. For example, [1, 2] and [2, 3] do not overlap. Every interval has start_i < end_i.
signals: The task asks for the minimum number of items to remove so that the rest satisfy a pairwise compatibility rule. Rewrite it as the maximum number of items to keep.
The items are intervals on a line and the conflict is overlap. This is the classic activity selection or interval scheduling setup.
Every interval has the same value, and only the count of kept intervals matters. Equal values make the earliest-end greedy safe. Different values need DP.
The input size is up to 10^5, so the target is O(n log n) or better. That points to sort plus one linear pass.
memory_hook: Sort by end, keep what fits, remove the rest.
approach: Greedy, sort by end. Keep the interval that finishes first, skip every interval that starts before the last kept end, and return n minus the kept count.
rebuild_steps: Sort the intervals by their end value.
Set kept = 0 and prev_end = negative infinity.
For each start, end: if start >= prev_end, the interval fits. Touching intervals fit, so use >= and not >.
When it fits, add one to kept and set prev_end = end.
Return len(intervals) - kept.
key_insight: Minimum removals equals n minus the maximum set you can keep. To keep the most non-overlapping intervals, always keep the one that ends first. An early end leaves the most room for the rest, and an exchange argument shows this choice is never worse.
ladder: Brute force over subsets: O(2^n * n log n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
DP like longest increasing subsequence: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Weighted-scheduling DP with binary search: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Greedy, sort by end (optimal, standard): O(n log n) time, O(n), because sort with a key function stores n keys and Timsort can use a merge buffer of up to n/2 items space
Greedy, sort by start (NeetCode variant): O(n log n) time, O(n) in the worst case for the Timsort merge buffer space
pitfalls: Using start > prev_end instead of start >= prev_end. Touching intervals do not overlap, so they must be kept.
Sorting by start and then always keeping the current interval on overlap. On overlap you must keep the interval with the smaller end, so set prev_end to the smaller of the two ends.
Counting overlapping pairs instead of removals. One long interval can overlap many short ones but needs only one removal.

title: Target Sum
statement: You get an integer array nums and an integer target. Put exactly one symbol, '+' or '-', before each integer in nums, then concatenate all the integers to build an expression. For example, for nums = [2, 1], a '+' before 2 and a '-' before 1 give the expression "+2-1". Return the number of different expressions that you can build that evaluate to target. Two expressions are different when the sign at one or more positions is different, so +0 and -0 count as two expressions.
signals: Each item gets one of two choices (plus or minus, take or skip), and the question asks how many choice sequences hit an exact total.
The answer is a count of ways, not a single best value, so the DP adds counts instead of taking a max or min.
The sum of all values is small (here at most 1000), so a table indexed by partial sum is cheap.
The limit n <= 20 allows 2^n enumeration only in a fast language. In Python, plain 2^n recursion takes seconds per test. The small bound on the sum makes a DP over sums the safe choice.
memory_hook: Plus or minus each number, cache on (index, running sum).
approach: Memoized DFS on (index, running sum). Try '+' and '-' for each number. Count the paths that end at target. Cache each (i, running_sum) pair so that equal prefixes are solved only once.
rebuild_steps: Inside findTargetSumWays, define ways(i, running_sum): the number of ways to sign nums[i:] so that the final sum equals target.
Base case: at i == len(nums), return 1 if running_sum == target, else 0.
Branch: return ways(i + 1, running_sum + nums[i]) + ways(i + 1, running_sum - nums[i]).
Import cache from functools and put @cache on ways. Because ways is an inner function, each call of findTargetSumWays gets a new cache.
Return ways(0, 0).
key_insight: A plus/minus sign assignment is the same as picking a subset: the plus group P satisfies P - N = target and P + N = total, so P = (total + target) / 2. Counting sign assignments becomes counting subsets with a fixed sum, which is a standard 0/1 knapsack count.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code rewrites the signs as a subset. The '+' group must sum to P = (total + target) / 2. It then counts subsets with sum P in one 1-D array, dp[s] += dp[s - num], with s going from high to low. It has the same O(n * total) time. It uses O(total) memory, no recursion and no hashing, so it is faster by a constant factor. Use it when n is large enough to make recursion depth a risk, or when the problem asks for O(total) space. It is also the bridge to Partition Equal Subset Sum and Last Stone Weight II.
ladder: Brute force recursion over signs: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Memoized DFS on (index, running sum): O(n * total) time, O(n * total) space
Bottom-up layered counts of reachable sums: O(n * total) time, O(total) space
Subset-sum reduction with 1-D 0/1 knapsack count (optimal): O(n * total) time, O(total) space
Meet in the middle: O(2^(n/2)) time, O(2^(n/2)) space
pitfalls: Zeros: +0 and -0 are different expressions, so each zero doubles the count. The inner loop must include s = num so that num = 0 gives dp[s] += dp[s].
Negative target: check abs(target) > total, not only target > total. Otherwise P can be negative and the array size breaks.
Parity: if total + target is odd, return 0 before building the array.

title: Coin Change II
statement: You get an integer array coins of distinct coin values and an integer amount. Return the number of combinations of coins that sum to exactly amount. A combination is unordered: 1+2 and 2+1 are the same combination. You can use each coin value an unlimited number of times. If no combination makes the amount, return 0. For amount 0 the answer is 1, because the empty combination counts. The final answer is guaranteed to fit in a signed 32-bit integer.
constraints: All the values of coins are unique.
signals: The problem asks for the number of ways to reach a target sum, so you count with a sum-of-ways DP and do not enumerate.
The word combinations means order does not matter, so you must fix one canonical order of choices to avoid counting the same multiset twice.
Each item has an infinite supply, which points to the unbounded knapsack pattern.

The target sum is a small integer (at most 5000) and there are at most 300 item types, so a table of item types times sums (about 1.5 million cells) is cheap. A small numeric target suggests a DP indexed by the sum.
memory_hook: Coins outside, amounts going up inside: ways[a] += ways[a - coin].
approach: 1-D counting DP, coins outside, amounts inside (unbounded knapsack). Keep ways[a] for every amount, and add one coin type at a time: ways[a] += ways[a - coin], with a going up from coin to amount.
rebuild_steps: Make ways = [0] * (amount + 1) and set ways[0] = 1 for the empty combination.
Loop over each coin in the outer loop, so each combination is built in one fixed coin order.
Loop a from coin up to amount in the inner loop, so the same coin can repeat.
Add ways[a - coin] to ways[a]: old ways[a] skips the coin, ways[a - coin] adds one more of it.
Return ways[amount].
key_insight: To count unordered combinations, process the item types in a fixed order in the outer loop. Then every multiset has exactly one build order and is counted once. Unlimited copies mean the 'take one more' transition stays on the same item, so in a 1-D array you sweep the target upward and read values that already include the current item.
ladder: Brute force: enumerate a count for each coin: O(product of (amount / c_i + 1)), exponential time, O(m) recursion depth space (too slow)
Memoized DFS take-or-skip (NeetCode): O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space (too slow)
2-D DP that sums over the copy count: O(m * n + n^2 log m) time, O(m * n) space (too slow)
2-D bottom-up DP: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
1-D rolling DP (optimal): O(m * n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: If you put the amount loop outside and the coin loop inside, you count ordered sequences. For amount = 3 and coins = [1,2] you get 3 instead of 2.
If the inner loop runs in descending order, each coin is used at most once (0/1 knapsack), and the result is wrong.
dp[0] must be 1. For amount = 0 the answer is 1, not 0.
solution:
class Solution:
    def change(self, amount: int, coins: List[int]) -> int:
        # ways[a] = number of combinations that make a, using the coins seen so far
        ways = [0] * (amount + 1)
        ways[0] = 1  # one way to make 0: take nothing
        for coin in coins:  # one coin type at a time: each combination is built once
            for a in range(coin, amount + 1):  # go up: this coin can repeat
                ways[a] += ways[a - coin]  # ways without coin + ways that add one more coin
        return ways[amount]

title: Diameter of Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. Return the length of the diameter of the tree. The diameter is the length of the longest path between any two nodes in the tree. The length of a path is the number of edges on it, not the number of nodes. The path does not have to pass through the root. A tree with one node has diameter 0.
constraints: The number of nodes in the tree is in the range [1, 10^4].
signals: The statement asks for the longest path between any two nodes of a tree. Such a path goes up to one highest node and then goes down, so each node is a possible bend point.
The statement says the path may or may not pass through the root. This tells you that the answer can sit at any node, so you need a running global best, not only the value at the root.
The value at a node depends on results from both children, such as heights. This points to a postorder (bottom-up) DFS.
The node count goes up to 10^4 and the tree can be skewed. Recomputing heights for every node is O(n^2), so each node must be visited a constant number of times.
memory_hook: At each node, record left height + right height as a candidate for best, and pass 1 + the bigger height up. Deep tree: list parents first, then walk backward.
approach: Bottom-up heights from a parents-first list. Collect the nodes with a stack so that each parent comes before its children, then walk the list backward. At each node, add the two child heights as a candidate path and store 1 + the larger height for the parent.
rebuild_steps: Make order = [] and stack = [root].
While the stack is not empty, pop a node. If the node is not None, append it to order and push node.left and node.right. Every parent now comes before its children in order.
Make height = {None: 0} and best = 0. The None key gives a missing child the height 0.
Loop over reversed(order). Both children of each node then already have a height.
Read left = height[node.left] and right = height[node.right].
Set best = max(best, left + right). This sum is the edge count of the path that bends at node.
Store height[node] = 1 + max(left, right).
After the loop, return best.
key_insight: Every path in a tree has a unique highest node where it bends. The longest path that bends at a node is the sum of the two longest downward chains from that node. Compute these chains bottom-up, record the two-sided sum as a candidate at each node, and pass only the one-sided chain up to the parent.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code is the recursive form of the same idea: height(node) returns 1 + max of the child heights and updates a nonlocal best with left + right. It is shorter and uses O(h) extra space instead of O(n). Both are O(n) time. Use the recursive form when the tree depth is small or the judge raises the recursion limit. For a skewed tree with 10^4 nodes it needs sys.setrecursionlimit above 10^4 in CPython.
ladder: All-pairs BFS on the undirected tree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Separate height call at every node: O(n^2) worst case on a skewed tree, O(n log n) on a balanced tree time, O(h) space (too slow)
Single postorder DFS that returns height and updates a global best: O(n) time, O(h), where h is the tree height, up to O(n) for a skewed tree space
Iterative postorder with an explicit stack: O(n) time, O(n) space
Two traversals (farthest-node trick): O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Returning the left height plus the right height at the root only. This fails when the longest path does not pass through the root, for example [1,2,null,3,4,5,null,null,6] with answer 4.

Mixing nodes and edges. If height counts nodes and height(None) = 0, then left + right is already the edge count. If height counts edges, height(None) must be -1 and the candidate becomes left + right + 2.
Returning the two-sided value (left + right or left + right + 1) to the parent. The parent can only extend one branch, so return 1 + max(left, right).
solution:
class Solution:
    def diameterOfBinaryTree(self, root: Optional[TreeNode]) -> int:
        # 1. List the nodes so that every parent comes before its children.
        order = []
        stack = [root]
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            if node:
                order.append(node)
                stack.append(node.left)
                stack.append(node.right)

        # 2. Walk the list backward, so both children are done before the parent.
        height = {None: 0}  # nodes on the longest downward chain
        best = 0
        for node in reversed(order):
            left = height[node.left]
            right = height[node.right]
            best = max(best, left + right)  # edges of the path that bends here
            height[node] = 1 + max(left, right)
        return best

title: Permutation in String
statement: You get two strings s1 and s2. Return true if s2 contains a permutation of s1. Otherwise, return false. In other words, return true if one of the permutations of s1 is a substring of s2. A permutation is a rearrangement of all the characters of a string. A substring is a contiguous part of a string.
