constraints: s1 and s2 consist of lowercase English letters.
signals: The statement says permutation or anagram of a pattern. Order does not matter, so only the letter counts matter.
The target is a contiguous substring whose length is fixed by the pattern. This points to a fixed-size sliding window.
The window property is a comparison of two multisets. Letter counts support one add and one remove in O(1), so the state can slide instead of being rebuilt.
The alphabet is small and fixed (26 lowercase letters). A count array of size 26 is the window state, and a full compare of two states costs O(26).
memory_hook: Slide a window of len(s1) over s2 and compare its letter counts to s1's counts.
approach: Fixed sliding window with two count arrays. Keep the letter counts of s1 and the letter counts of the last k letters of s2, and return true when the two arrays are equal.
rebuild_steps: Set k = len(s1) and make two lists of 26 zeros: need and window.
Count each letter of s1 into need with ord(ch) - ord('a').
Loop r, ch over enumerate(s2) and add ch to window.
If r >= k, remove s2[r - k] from window, so the window holds only the last k letters.
If window == need, return True.
After the loop, return False.
key_insight: A permutation is identified only by its letter counts. Every candidate substring has the same length as the pattern. So slide a fixed-size window and update its counts with one letter in and one letter out. Do not rebuild the counts for each window.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code keeps one diff array and an integer bad that counts the letters with unequal counts. Only the entering letter and the leaving letter can change bad, so each step is O(1) instead of O(26). This removes the alphabet factor. Use it when the alphabet is large or unknown, for example Unicode letters in a dict. Also use it when the task asks for O(n) time that does not depend on the alphabet size. For 26 letters and n up to 10^4, the two-array compare is already fast.
ladder: Try every permutation of s1: O(k! * n * k) time, O(k! * k) space (too slow)
Sort every window: O((n - k + 1) * k log k) time, O(k) space (too slow)
Recount every window: O((n - k + 1) * k) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Fixed sliding window with two count arrays: O(k + 26 * n) time, O(1) space
Fixed sliding window with a mismatch counter (optimal): O(k + n) time, O(1) space
Multiset rolling hash: O(k + n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: s1 is longer than s2: return false. Code that fills the first window by index can go out of range.
Comparing sets of letters instead of counts: 'aab' and 'ab' have the same set, but they are not permutations.
Off-by-one when removing: the leaving letter is s2[r - k], and you remove it only when r >= k.

title: Subtree of Another Tree
statement: You get the roots of two binary trees, root and subRoot. Return true if some subtree of root has the same structure and the same node values as subRoot. Otherwise return false. A subtree of a tree is one node of that tree together with all of its descendants. The whole tree also counts as a subtree of itself. So a match must cover every descendant down to the leaves. A match of only the top part of a subtree does not count.
constraints: The number of nodes in the root tree is in the range [1, 2000].
The number of nodes in the subRoot tree is in the range [1, 1000].
signals: The question asks if one structure occurs inside another structure. This is pattern search, like substring search, but on trees.
The phrase 'a node and all of its descendants' means the match must end at the same leaves. A match of only the top part is not enough.
The node counts are small (2000 and 1000). Their product is 2 * 10^6, so an exact check at every node fits.

The check at one fixed start node is an 'are two trees identical' question (Same Tree). When a bigger question needs that equality check at every position, reuse the equality helper inside an outer traversal.
memory_hook: Try every node as a start, and ask Same Tree at each one. Both loops pop, skip the empty case, check, and push the children.
approach: DFS with a Same Tree check at every node, written with two explicit stacks. The outer stack visits every node of root as a possible start. At each start, a stack of node pairs checks if the tree there is identical to subRoot.
rebuild_steps: Write same_tree(a, b). Put the pair (a, b) in a list named pairs.
While pairs is not empty, pop a pair (x, y).
If x and y are both None, continue. This pair matches.
If only one of them is None, or x.val != y.val, return False.
Push the left pair (x.left, y.left) and the right pair (x.right, y.right).
After the loop, return True. Every pair matched.
In isSubtree, put root in a list named stack.
While stack is not empty, pop a node. If the node is None, continue.
If same_tree(node, subRoot) is True, return True.
Push node.left and node.right.
After the loop, return False. No start node matched.
key_insight: A question of the form 'does pattern P occur inside structure S' splits into two parts. One part is an exact equality check that starts at a fixed position. The other part enumerates every position in S where P can start. For trees, the positions are the nodes, and the equality check is the Same Tree recursion.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses the same idea with recursion. same() recurses down both trees together, and isSubtree() recurses down root. It is shorter, and it is the usual textbook answer. Its base case 'return p is q' is a compact form of the two None rules. Both forms take O(n * m) time. The recursion depth of solution_code equals the height of root, so a skewed root of 2000 nodes makes it about 2000 levels deep. This is above the default CPython limit of 1000, so it raises RecursionError without sys.setrecursionlimit. A judge that raises the limit accepts it. Use the recursive form when the tree is shallow or when you want the shortest code.
ladder: Brute force: encode every subtree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
DFS with a same-tree check at every node (standard): O(n * m) time, O(h), where h is the height of root, up to O(n) space
Preorder serialization with null markers plus string search: O(n + m) time, O(n + m) space
Canonical subtree ids (Merkle hashing): O(n + m) expected time, O(n + m) space
pitfalls: A match of only the top part of subRoot is wrong. The candidate must have no extra descendants, as Example 2 shows. The base case 'both None' enforces this.
In same(), return False when exactly one node is None. A base case like 'if not q: return True' accepts a partial match.
Do not stop at the first node whose value equals subRoot.val. Values repeat, so a failed match at one node does not rule out a match deeper in the tree.

title: Task Scheduler
statement: You get an array tasks of CPU tasks. Each task is an uppercase letter from A to Z. You also get an integer n. Each CPU interval either runs one task or stays idle. You can run the tasks in any order. Two tasks with the same label must have a gap of at least n intervals between them. Return the minimum number of CPU intervals needed to complete all tasks, idle intervals included.
constraints: tasks[i] is an uppercase English letter.
signals: The problem asks for a minimum total time to schedule jobs that have a cooldown or minimum gap between repeats of the same kind.
Only the count of each job kind matters, not the input order, so you can compress the input to a frequency table.
The alphabet is small (26 kinds), so a heap or a scan over kinds costs a constant per step.
At each step you pick one available item, and the item with the most remaining copies is the safest pick. A repeated 'pick the largest available' choice points to a max-heap.
memory_hook: Fill each window of n + 1 with the most frequent different tasks. Only the last window has no idle tail.
approach: Round-by-round max-heap greedy. Each round is one cooldown window of n + 1 slots. You fill the window with the most frequent different tasks. A full window costs n + 1. The last round costs only the tasks that ran.
rebuild_steps: Count the tasks. Put the negated counts in a list and heapify it, so the heap gives the largest count first. Set time to 0.
While the heap is not empty, start a round with an empty list named ran.
Pop up to n + 1 counts and stop early if the heap is empty. Add 1 to each count to run one copy, and append it to ran.
Push back each count in ran that is not zero.
If the heap still has work, add n + 1 to time. Else add len(ran), because this is the last round.
After the loop, return time.
key_insight: The most frequent item is the bottleneck in a cooldown schedule. Always run the available item with the most remaining copies, and hold used items in a FIFO queue until their cooldown ends. Idle time appears only when every remaining item is cooling. The total length is (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties, where m is the top count. If the other items fill all gaps, no idle occurs and the length equals the number of tasks.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code runs the same greedy one interval at a time. It keeps a FIFO queue of cooling tasks with their ready times and jumps over idle runs. That event-simulation form extends directly to tasks with different cooldowns, because the queue then becomes a min-heap keyed by ready time. The round method can also print a valid schedule if the heap holds (negated count, label) pairs and full rounds get idle padding. The closed form max(N, (m - 1) * (n + 1) + ties) is O(N) with no heap, and it is the fastest to type once you trust it. All three cost O(N log 26) or less on these constraints.
ladder: Exhaustive search over schedules: O(exponential in number of kinds and counts) time, O(number of states) space (too slow)
Step-by-step greedy with a linear scan: O(T * 26), where T is the answer, up to about 1e6 time, O(26) space (too slow)
Max-heap plus cooldown queue simulation (chosen): O(N log 26) = O(N) time, O(26) space
Closed-form counting (greedy frames): O(N) time, O(26) space
pitfalls: The gap is n intervals between runs, so a task run at time t can run again at time t + n + 1, not t + n. An off-by-one error here changes the answer whenever a task must wait.
With n = 0 the cooldown ends immediately. The task must return to the heap in the same iteration, so check the queue after you push to it.
Forgetting to negate counts makes heapq pick the least frequent task, which creates extra idle time.
solution:
import heapq
from collections import Counter
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def leastInterval(self, tasks: List[str], n: int) -> int:
        heap = [-count for count in Counter(tasks).values()]  # max-heap of counts
        heapq.heapify(heap)
        time = 0
        while heap:
            # One round = one cooldown window of n + 1 slots.
            # Run the most frequent different tasks in it.
            ran = []
            while heap and len(ran) < n + 1:
                ran.append(heapq.heappop(heap) + 1)  # run one copy
            for count in ran:
                if count:  # copies remain
                    heapq.heappush(heap, count)
            # A full window if work remains, else only the tasks that ran.
            time += n + 1 if heap else len(ran)
        return time

title: Palindromic Substrings
statement: Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it. A string is a palindrome when it reads the same backward as forward. A substring is a contiguous sequence of characters within the string.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
signals: The task asks to count or find substrings that are palindromes.
The target pieces are symmetric around a middle point. So each one grows outward from that middle one matching pair at a time.
The string length is at most about 1000 to 3000. So O(n^2) work is fine and O(n^3) work is risky.
The answer counts positions, not distinct texts. So each (start, end) pair that is a palindrome adds one.
memory_hook: Every palindrome has a middle: expand from each middle, odd and even, and count each match.
approach: Expand around center with a helper. For each index i, call expand(i, i) for odd-length palindromes and expand(i, i + 1) for even-length palindromes, and add one for each matching pair as the two ends move outward.
rebuild_steps: Set n to len(s).
Define expand(left, right). Set count to 0.
While left >= 0, right < n and s[left] == s[right], add one to count. Then move left down by one and right up by one.
Return count from expand.
Set total to 0. Loop i over every index of s.
Add expand(i, i) for odd-length palindromes centered on s[i].
Add expand(i, i + 1) for even-length palindromes centered between s[i] and s[i + 1].
Return total.
key_insight: A palindrome is defined by its center and its radius. Growing outward from a fixed center gives one new palindrome per matching pair. The first mismatch ends all longer candidates at that center. So each center costs one step per palindrome it produces plus at most one failed check. The total work is O(n + answer), which is O(n^2) in the worst case.
optimal_note: The algorithm and the complexity are the same: O(n^2) time and O(1) extra space. The record code puts both center types into one loop over 2n - 1 centers with left = c // 2 and right = left + c % 2. This is only a compact form. Use it when you want one loop and no helper. For n of 10^5 or more, use Manacher's algorithm for O(n) time.
ladder: Brute force: O(n^3) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Interval DP table: O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
Expand around center: O(n^2) time, O(1) space
Manacher's algorithm: O(n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Forgetting even-length centers misses palindromes such as "aa" and "abba".
Counting distinct palindromic texts instead of positions gives the wrong answer for "aaa" (it gives 3 instead of 6).
Checking bounds after indexing raises IndexError or wraps with a negative index. Check left >= 0 and right < n before comparing characters.

title: Valid Parenthesis String
statement: You get a string s that contains only three types of characters: '(', ')' and '*'. Return true if s is valid, else return false. These rules define a valid string. Any left parenthesis '(' must have a corresponding right parenthesis ')'. Any right parenthesis ')' must have a corresponding left parenthesis '('. A left parenthesis '(' must come before its corresponding right parenthesis ')'. A '*' can act as a single right parenthesis ')', a single left parenthesis '(', or an empty string. Each '*' makes its own choice. So s is valid if at least one choice for all the '*' characters gives a valid string.
signals: The input is a bracket sequence, so validity reduces to a running balance that never goes negative and ends at zero.
A wildcard symbol can take one of several values, and the question asks whether at least one assignment works.
Each wildcard changes a counter by a run of consecutive amounts, here -1, 0 or +1. This keeps the set of reachable counter values contiguous.
The answer is only true or false, so you do not need to build the assignment. You only need to prove that one exists.
memory_hook: Range of open counts: fail if the most goes below zero, clamp the fewest at zero, and end with fewest == 0.
approach: Range of open counts (lo, hi). Keep the fewest and the most unmatched '(' that are possible after each character, and at the end check that zero open is possible.
rebuild_steps: Set lo = hi = 0, the fewest and the most unmatched '(' so far.
Loop over each character c of s.
For '(' add 1 to both. For ')' subtract 1 from both.
For '*' subtract 1 from lo and add 1 to hi, because it can close or open.
If hi < 0, return False, because even all '*' as '(' cannot cover the ')'.
Set lo = max(lo, 0), because an open count is never negative.
After the loop, return lo == 0, because then zero open brackets is possible.
key_insight: When each uncertain choice changes a counter by -1, 0 or +1, the set of reachable counter values stays a contiguous range. So you can replace an exponential set of choices with two numbers: the minimum and the maximum reachable value.
ladder: Brute force over all wildcard assignments: O(3^k * n), k = number of '*' time, O(n) space (too slow)
Interval DP over substrings: O(n^3) time, O(n^2) space
Memoized DFS over (index, open count): O(n^2) time, O(n^2) space
Two stacks of indices: O(n) time, O(n) space
Two-pass balance check: O(n) time, O(1) space
Greedy range of open counts (optimal): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to clamp lo at zero: '(*)(' then returns true, but the answer is false.
Forgetting the early return when hi < 0: ')*' then returns true, because later characters raise hi again, but the answer is false.
Testing hi at the end instead of lo. The final test asks whether zero is in [lo, hi]. Since lo is clamped at zero and hi >= 0, that test is lo == 0. For '(', hi is 1 and the answer is false.
solution:
class Solution:
    def checkValidString(self, s: str) -> bool:
        lo = hi = 0  # fewest and most unmatched '(' we could have now
        for c in s:
            if c == "(":
                lo += 1
                hi += 1
            elif c == ")":
                lo -= 1
                hi -= 1
            else:  # '*' may close one, open one, or do nothing
                lo -= 1
                hi += 1
            if hi < 0:  # too many ')' even if every '*' opens
                return False
            lo = max(lo, 0)  # an open count can never be negative
        return lo == 0  # zero open brackets is reachable

title: Redundant Connection
statement: In this problem, a tree is an undirected graph that is connected and has no cycles. You get a graph that started as a tree with n nodes labeled from 1 to n, with one additional edge added. The added edge has two different vertices chosen from 1 to n, and it was not an edge that already existed. The graph is an array edges of length n, where edges[i] = [ai, bi] means that there is an edge between nodes ai and bi. Return an edge that you can remove so that the resulting graph is a tree of n nodes. If there are multiple answers, return the answer that occurs last in the input.
signals: The input is an undirected edge list and the question asks which edge creates a cycle or breaks the tree property.
The graph has n nodes and n edges, so it is a tree plus exactly one extra edge and has exactly one cycle.
The answer depends on the order of the edges in the input, which suggests processing edges one by one and stopping at the first conflict.
Each step asks the same question: are these two nodes already connected? Repeated connectivity queries under edge insertions point to union-find.
memory_hook: Same root already? That edge closes the cycle.
approach: Plain union-find over edges in input order. Add edges one by one, and return the first edge whose two endpoints already have the same root.
rebuild_steps: Make parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1)). There are n = len(edges) nodes, labeled 1 to n. Each node starts as its own root. Index 0 is not used.
Write find(x): while parent[x] != x, set parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] and move x up. Return x.
Loop for a, b in edges and compute root_a = find(a) and root_b = find(b).
If the roots are equal, return [a, b]. This edge closes the cycle.
Else set parent[root_a] = root_b to join the two groups.
After the loop, return []. The loop always returns first, because the input has exactly one cycle.
key_insight: When you add edges to an undirected graph one at a time, an edge creates a cycle exactly when its two endpoints are already in the same connected component. Union-find answers that question in near-constant time. The first edge that fails this test is also the last cycle edge in input order, because a cycle closes only when its last edge arrives.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code adds union by size: it keeps a size array and attaches the smaller tree under the larger one. Together with path halving, this makes each operation almost O(1) in the worst case, O(n alpha(n)) total. Without union by size, path halving alone still gives O(log n) amortized per operation, which is far below the limit for n <= 1000. Add union by size when inputs are very large or when an interviewer asks for the tight bound.
ladder: Remove each edge and test for a tree: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Incremental DFS reachability check: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Find the cycle, then pick the last cycle edge: O(n) time, O(n) space
Union-find over edges in input order (optimal, standard): O(n alpha(n)) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Nodes are labeled 1 to n. Size the parent array n + 1, or subtract 1 from each label.
Do not union before you compare roots. Compare find(a) and find(b) first, then merge.
Compare roots, not direct parents. The test parent[a] == parent[b] misses connections deeper in the tree.

title: Max Area of Island
statement: You get an m x n binary matrix grid. A cell with value 1 is land. A cell with value 0 is water. An island is a group of land cells that connect 4-directionally (up, down, left, right). Diagonal cells do not connect. All four edges of the grid are surrounded by water. The area of an island is the number of cells with value 1 in that island. Return the maximum area of an island in grid. If there is no island, return 0.
signals: The input is a 2D grid of cells, and cells connect to their 4 neighbors. Treat the grid as an implicit graph.
The problem talks about groups, regions, islands or blobs of same-valued cells. These are connected components.
The question asks for a property of each component (size, perimeter, shape) and then a max, min or total over components. Or it asks for the number of components.

The grid can hold up to a few thousand cells, and one component can cover all of them. A traversal that visits each cell once fits. A recursive traversal can get as deep as the cell count, so plan for an explicit stack in Python.
memory_hook: Scan for land. Sink on push, count on pop, keep the max.
approach: Scan and flood fill with a stack. Scan every cell. When you find land, call a helper that flood fills that island with an explicit stack. The helper sinks each cell to 0 when it pushes the cell, counts each pop and returns the count. Keep the largest count.
rebuild_steps: Get rows and cols from the grid.
Write island_size(r, c). Sink grid[r][c] to 0, put (r, c) on a stack, and set size to 0.
While the stack is not empty, pop a cell and add 1 to size.
For each of the 4 neighbors, check that it is in bounds and equals 1. Then sink it to 0 and push it.
When the stack is empty, return size.
Set best to 0. Scan every cell. When a cell equals 1, set best to max(best, island_size(r, c)).
Return best.
key_insight: An island is a connected component of an implicit grid graph. Flood fill each component exactly once from its first unvisited cell, and count cells as you visit them. Marking cells visited makes the whole scan linear, because no cell starts or joins a second traversal.
optimal_note: The intuitive solution uses the same algorithm as solution_code. It only moves the flood fill into a helper function. Both run in O(m*n) time and use O(m*n) extra space for the stack in the worst case.
ladder: Fresh search from every land cell: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space (too slow)
Recursive DFS flood fill (NeetCode reference): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Iterative DFS or BFS flood fill with in-place sinking (chosen): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Union-find with component sizes: O(m*n * alpha(m*n)) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Recursive DFS can reach depth m*n = 2500. That exceeds the default CPython recursion limit of 1000, and a plain interpreter raises RecursionError. Some online judges raise the limit, so the code can pass there and still fail locally. Use an explicit stack, or call sys.setrecursionlimit.
If you mark a cell only when you pop it, the same cell can enter the stack twice. Then you must skip already-marked cells on pop, or the area counts that cell twice. Marking on push avoids this.
Diagonal neighbors do not connect. Use exactly 4 directions.

title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
statement: Design a class KthLargest. The story frames the values as test scores in a university admissions office, and the kth highest score acts as a dynamic cut-off mark. The constructor KthLargest(k, nums) receives an integer k and an initial list of integer scores nums. The method add(val) adds the integer val to the stream. It then returns the kth largest value among all values so far, which are the initial nums plus every added value. The kth largest is the kth element of the list of all values sorted in descending order. Duplicates count separately, so it is not the kth distinct value. k stays fixed for the object. Values are only added and never removed. nums can be empty and k can equal nums.length + 1, so the object can hold fewer than k values before the first add. After each add, at least k values exist.
signals: The question asks for the kth largest or kth smallest value, not for the whole sorted order.
Values arrive one at a time and a query follows each arrival, so the answer must update online.
The collection only grows. Nothing is deleted, and no window slides.
k is fixed for the lifetime of the structure, so a container of fixed size k is enough.
memory_hook: Keep the top k in a min-heap. Every value goes through add: push, pop if over k, return the root.
approach: Min-heap of size k with one gate for every value. The constructor feeds each initial number through add. add pushes the value. If the heap then holds more than k values, add pops the smallest value. add returns the root.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq. Store k and start an empty list top_k that acts as a min-heap.
In the constructor, call self.add(num) for each num in nums.
In add, heappush the value onto top_k.
If len(top_k) > k, heappop to remove the smallest value.
Return top_k[0], which is the smallest of the k largest values.
key_insight: When you only insert and need the kth largest, the answer never decreases. So a value below the current kth largest can never become the answer again, and you can discard it. Keep a min-heap of exactly k values. The heap holds the k largest values, and its root is the smallest of them. A new value must beat the root to enter, and the root is the answer.
optimal_note: Same technique and same per-add cost of O(log k). Only the constructor differs. The record's solution_code copies nums, calls heapify in O(n), and pops until the size is k. That build costs O(n + (n - k) log n). The intuitive version costs O(n log k) for the build. At the maximum input size both builds take a few milliseconds, so the difference does not matter here. Use the heapify form only when the initial list is very large and k is close to n.
ladder: Sort on every add: O(N log N) per add, where N is the number of values so far. Timsort on a list that stays sorted drops this to about O(N), which is still too slow in total. time, O(N) space (too slow)
Sorted list with binary insertion: O(n log n) build, O(N) per add time, O(N) space
Quickselect on every add: O(N) average per add, O(N^2) worst case time, O(N) space (too slow)
Min-heap of size k (optimal, standard): O(n + (n - k) log n) build, O(log k) per add time, O(n) during build because of the copy, then O(k) space
Fenwick tree over the value range: O(n log V) build, O(log V) per add, where V = 20001 time, O(V) space
pitfalls: Do not use a max-heap of all values. Popping k times per query costs O(k log N) and destroys the data.
A max-heap of size k is wrong for kth largest. Its root is the largest kept value, not the kth largest.
k can equal len(nums) + 1. The heap then holds k - 1 values after the constructor. Do not read heap[0] in the constructor, and do not assume the heap is full before the first add.

title: Binary Search
statement: You get an array of integers nums that is sorted in ascending order, and an integer target. Write a function that searches for target in nums. If target exists, return its index. Otherwise, return -1. You must write an algorithm with O(log n) runtime complexity.
constraints: All the integers in nums are unique.
nums is sorted in ascending order.
signals: The input is sorted, so one comparison at a middle position tells you which half cannot hold the answer.
The statement demands O(log n) time. This rules out any scan and points to halving the search range.
You must find the position of one value in a static sorted sequence, or report that it is absent.
The values are unique, so any match is the answer and the loop can stop on it. With duplicates, use a boundary search instead.
memory_hook: Closed range, check the middle, drop the half that cannot hold target.
approach: Iterative binary search on a closed range. Keep [lo, hi] as the part of the array that can still hold target, check the middle, and drop the half that cannot hold it.
rebuild_steps: Set lo = 0 and hi = len(nums) - 1, so [lo, hi] covers the whole array.
Loop while lo <= hi, because the range still has at least one element.
Set mid = (lo + hi) // 2 and return mid if nums[mid] == target.
If nums[mid] < target, set lo = mid + 1. Otherwise, set hi = mid - 1.
After the loop the range is empty, so return -1.
key_insight: In a sorted range, one comparison with the middle element proves that a whole half cannot contain the target. Discard that half and repeat, so the search range shrinks by half each step.
ladder: Linear scan: O(n) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Hash map from value to index: O(n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Iterative binary search on a closed range: O(log n) time, O(1) space
Lower-bound binary search (half-open or bisect_left): O(log n) time, O(1) space
Recursive binary search: O(log n) time, O(log n) space
pitfalls: Using lo < hi with a closed range skips the last candidate when lo == hi. Then a one-element array misses its target.
Setting lo = mid with a closed range loops forever when hi == lo + 1, because mid then equals lo.
Setting hi = mid with the condition lo <= hi loops forever when lo == hi.
solution:
class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
        lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1          # closed range [lo, hi] can hold target
        while lo <= hi:                     # range is not empty
            mid = (lo + hi) // 2
            if nums[mid] == target:
                return mid
            if nums[mid] < target:          # mid and everything left are too small
                lo = mid + 1
            else:                           # mid and everything right are too big
                hi = mid - 1
        return -1                           # range is empty, target is absent

title: Daily Temperatures
statement: You get an integer array temperatures. temperatures[i] is the temperature on day i. Return an array answer of the same length. answer[i] is the number of days after day i until a strictly warmer temperature occurs. Thus answer[i] = j - i for the smallest j > i with temperatures[j] > temperatures[i]. An equal temperature does not count as warmer. If no later day is warmer, answer[i] is 0.
signals: For each element, the task asks for the nearest later element that is greater (or smaller). This is the next-greater-element pattern.
The answer is a distance or an index of that nearest element, not a value computed over a whole range.
The array length goes up to about 10^5. A scan from every index costs O(n^2), so you need a single pass.
An element that is greater than an earlier element resolves that earlier element for good. Resolved elements never matter again, so a stack can discard them.
memory_hook: Today pops every colder waiting day and writes the gap.
approach: Use a monotonic stack of waiting days and scan from left to right. The stack holds the indices of the days that still wait for a warmer day. Each new day pops every strictly colder waiting day and writes the gap. Then the new day waits on the stack too.
rebuild_steps: Make answer = [0] * len(temperatures) and an empty list called waiting. The list holds day indices.
Loop over today, temp in enumerate(temperatures).
While waiting is not empty and temperatures[waiting[-1]] < temp, pop the top index into day and set answer[day] = today - day.
After the while loop, push today onto waiting.
Return answer. Days that still wait at the end keep 0.
key_insight: Each new element is the answer for every earlier pending element that is smaller than it. So keep the pending elements in a monotonic stack. The new element pops and resolves the smaller ones from the top, and then it waits on the stack itself.
ladder: Brute force scan: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space (too slow)
Nearest-index table by temperature value: O(n * 71) time, O(71) extra space
Monotonic stack, left to right: O(n) time, O(n) space
Monotonic stack, right to left: O(n) time, O(n) space
Jump pointers with the answer array: O(n) amortized time, O(1) extra space
pitfalls: Equal temperatures are not warmer. Pop only when the stored temperature is strictly lower than the current one in the left-to-right version. In the right-to-left version, pop when the stored temperature is lower or equal.
Store indices, not only temperatures. The answer is a distance, so you need the index.
Days left on the stack at the end have no warmer day. Initialize the answer to zeros so they stay 0.

title: Network Delay Time
statement: You get a network of n nodes, labeled from 1 to n. You also get times, a list of travel times as directed edges times[i] = (u_i, v_i, w_i). Here u_i is the source node, v_i is the target node, and w_i is the time a signal takes to travel from source to target. You send a signal from a given node k. Return the minimum time it takes for all n nodes to receive the signal. If it is impossible for all n nodes to receive the signal, return -1.
signals: The problem asks for the earliest arrival time or the minimum total cost from one source over weighted edges.
Edges come as (from, to, weight) triples, and all weights are non-negative.
Something spreads from a start node along all edges at once. Each node then receives it at its shortest-path distance.
The question asks when all nodes are reached. The answer is then the maximum of the shortest distances, not their sum.
memory_hook: The first pop of a node is its arrival time.
approach: Dijkstra with a min-heap and lazy deletion. Pop the closest node. Make it final on its first pop. Push each unfinished neighbor with the new distance. If all n nodes are final, return the largest final distance. Else return -1.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq and defaultdict. Build graph = defaultdict(list). For each directed edge (u, v, w), append (v, w) to graph[u].
Start with dist = {} and heap = [(0, k)].
While the heap is not empty, pop (d, node). If node is in dist, continue.
Set dist[node] = d. Push (d + w, nxt) for each neighbor nxt that is not in dist.
Return max(dist.values()) if len(dist) == n, else return -1.
key_insight: When something spreads from a source along all weighted edges at once, each node is reached at its shortest-path distance. The time to reach every node is the maximum of these distances. With non-negative weights, Dijkstra finds them in increasing order.
ladder: DFS over paths with pruning: O(V!) worst case (exponential) time, O(V + E) space (too slow)
Floyd-Warshall: O(V^3) time, O(V^2) space
Bellman-Ford: O(V * E) time, O(V) space
SPFA (queue-based Bellman-Ford): O(V * E) worst case time, O(V + E) space
Dijkstra with array scan: O(V^2 + E) time, O(V + E) space
Dijkstra with binary heap and lazy deletion (chosen): O(E log E) = O(E log V) time, O(V + E) space
pitfalls: Nodes are labeled 1 to n. Size arrays n + 1 or subtract 1 from labels.
Edges are directed. Do not add the reverse edge.
Make a node final when it pops, not when it is pushed. A later push can carry a smaller distance.

title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement: You get an integer array cost. cost[i] is the cost of step i on a staircase. When you pay the cost of the step you stand on, you can climb one step or two steps. You can start on step 0 or on step 1 without paying anything to get there. The top of the floor is the position just past the last step, at index n = cost.length. Return the minimum total cost to reach the top.
signals: The problem asks for a minimum or maximum total over a sequence of choices.
Each move goes forward along a line by a small fixed set of step sizes, such as 1 or 2.
The best result at a position depends only on a few earlier positions, so subproblems overlap.
Moves only go forward, so the positions have no cycles and a left-to-right fill order works.
memory_hook: To stand on step i, come from one back or two back, and pay the step you leave.
approach: Bottom-up dp array. dp[i] is the cheapest cost to stand on step i, and the last move into i came from one step back or two steps back, so take the cheaper of the two.
rebuild_steps: Set n = len(cost). The top is index n, one past the last step.
Make dp = [0] * (n + 1).
Leave dp[0] and dp[1] at 0 because both starts are free.
Loop i from 2 to n inclusive.
Set from_one_back = dp[i-1] + cost[i-1] and from_two_back = dp[i-2] + cost[i-2].
Set dp[i] to the smaller of the two.
Return dp[n].
key_insight: The cheapest way to reach a position depends only on the cheapest ways to reach the positions that can move into it. So you take the minimum over the last move and you never need to remember the full path.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code runs the same recurrence but keeps only the last two dp values in prev2 and prev1. This cuts the extra space from O(n) to O(1). Time stays O(n). You need it only when the task asks for constant extra space. With n up to 1000, the array costs almost nothing.
ladder: Plain recursion: O(2^n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up dp array: O(n) time, O(n) space
Bottom-up with two rolling variables: O(n) time, O(1) space
In-place suffix dp (NeetCode style): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: The top is index n, one past the last step. Returning dp[n-1] or the cost of the last step is wrong.
Choose one state definition and keep it. Either dp[i] excludes cost[i] (you pay when you leave) or dp[i] includes cost[i]. Mixing the two adds or drops one cost.
Both starting steps are free. Setting dp[1] = cost[0] is a common off-by-one bug.

title: Partition Labels
statement: You get a string s of lowercase English letters. Split s into contiguous parts, in order, so that the parts concatenate back to s. Each letter must appear in at most one part. Make as many parts as possible. Return a list of the part sizes, in order from left to right. For example, "ababcc" splits into ["abab", "cc"]. The splits ["aba", "bcc"] and ["ab", "ab", "cc"] are invalid because a letter appears in two parts.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
signals: The task splits a sequence into contiguous segments so that each value stays inside one segment.
The task asks for the maximum number of segments, so every legal cut must be taken.
Each value forces a span from its first to its last occurrence, which is an implicit interval.
A value's last occurrence decides how far its segment must reach, so one pass that stores last positions gives O(1) lookups.
memory_hook: Each letter drags the cut to its last spot; cut when you catch up.
approach: Greedy scan with last occurrence. Store the last index of each letter. Scan left to right, push the part end out to the furthest last index seen, and cut when the index reaches that end.
rebuild_steps: Build last = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(s)}. Later keys overwrite earlier ones, so each letter keeps its last index.
Set sizes = [] and start = end = 0.
For each i, c in enumerate(s), set end = max(end, last[c]).
If i == end, append end - start + 1 to sizes and set start = i + 1.
Return sizes.
key_insight: A segment that contains an element must extend to that element's last occurrence. So track the furthest required end while you scan, and cut as soon as the scan index catches up with it.
ladder: Brute force over all cut sets: O(2^n * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Check each gap with prefix and suffix letter sets: O(n^2) naive, O(26 * n) with prefix counts time, O(n) or O(26 * n) space
Merge letter intervals: O(n + k log k), k <= 26 time, O(k) space
Greedy scan with last occurrence (optimal): O(n) time, O(k), k <= 26 space
pitfalls: Using the first occurrence instead of the last occurrence gives cuts that split a letter.
Setting end to the current letter's last index, instead of the running maximum, cuts too early.
The part size is i - start + 1, not i - start. An off-by-one error here shifts every size.

title: Swim in Rising Water
statement: You get an n x n integer matrix grid. The value grid[i][j] is the elevation of cell (i, j). Rain starts and the water level rises over time. At time t the water level is t, so every cell with elevation at most t is under water. You can swim from a cell to a 4-directionally adjacent cell only if the elevations of both cells are at most t. You can swim any distance in zero time. You must stay inside the grid. You start at the top-left cell (0, 0). Return the minimum time until you can reach the bottom-right cell (n - 1, n - 1).
signals: You may use a route only when every cell on it is at most some level. So the cost of a route is its single highest cell, not a sum. This is a bottleneck (minimax) path.
The question asks for the earliest time, or the smallest threshold, at which two points become connected.
A threshold rises and cells only become usable, never unusable. Feasibility is monotone in the threshold, so binary search on the answer works.
Movement is 4-directional between grid cells. The grid is an implicit graph, so you do not build an edge list.
memory_hook: Dijkstra, but the path cost is the highest cell, so use max instead of plus.
approach: Use Dijkstra with max instead of plus. The heap key of a cell is the highest elevation on the path to it. This key is the earliest time that you can reach the cell. Pop the entry with the smallest key. The first pop of a cell gives its final key, so mark the cell visited at that point. Push each unvisited neighbor with the key max(t, neighbor elevation). When you pop the bottom-right cell, its key is the answer.
rebuild_steps: Set n = len(grid). Put (grid[0][0], 0, 0) in a min-heap. Make an empty visited set.
While the heap is not empty, pop the smallest entry (t, r, c). The value t is the highest elevation on the best path to (r, c).
If (r, c) is already in visited, skip the entry. It is an older copy with a key that is not smaller.
Add (r, c) to visited. Its key t is now final.
If (r, c) is the bottom-right cell, return t.
For each of the 4 neighbors (nr, nc) that is inside the grid and not in visited, push (max(t, grid[nr][nc]), nr, nc).
After the loop, return -1. The loop always returns earlier, because every cell is reachable.
key_insight: When a path cost is the maximum weight on the path, Dijkstra still works if you replace addition with max. Max never decreases along a path, so the first time the heap pops a node, its bottleneck value is final. Equivalently, the answer is the smallest threshold at which start and end fall into the same connected component.
optimal_note: The record solution_code uses the same algorithm with the same O(n^2 log n) time. It marks a cell when the cell is first pushed. That is correct here only because the cost to enter a cell depends on the cell alone, so the first push key is already final. The intuitive code marks a cell when the cell is popped. This is the general Dijkstra rule. It can push one cell up to 4 times, but it still uses less than 0.01 s of CPU time at n = 50. The mark-on-push form gives wrong answers on edge-weighted variants such as Path With Minimum Effort.
ladder: Linear scan over t with BFS: O(n^4) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
Binary search on answer with BFS or DFS: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
Dijkstra with max-path cost (min-heap): O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
Union-find in elevation order (Kruskal style): O(n^2 * alpha(n^2)) with path compression and union by size or rank time, O(n^2) space
pitfalls: The start cell counts. The answer is at least grid[0][0], so seed the heap with grid[0][0], not 0.
The end cell counts. The answer is at least grid[n-1][n-1]. Return the popped key of the target, not the key of its neighbor.

Return when the target is popped, not when it is pushed, unless you know the push key is final. Here the push key is final because the entry cost depends only on the cell, but returning on pop is the safe Dijkstra habit.

title: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops
statement: There are n cities, numbered 0 to n - 1. Directed flights connect some of them. flights[i] = [from_i, to_i, price_i] means one flight goes from city from_i to city to_i and costs price_i. You get three integers src, dst and k. Return the cheapest total price to travel from src to dst with at most k stops. A stop is an intermediate city, so at most k stops means at most k + 1 flights. If no such route exists, return -1. All prices are positive. There are no multiple flights between the same two cities. No flight goes from a city to itself. src and dst are different.
signals: The problem asks for a minimum-cost path in a weighted directed graph.
A second limit caps the number of edges or hops on the path (at most k stops, at most k moves, within k steps).
The cheapest path overall can break the hop limit, so a plain shortest-path answer is not enough.
The hop limit is small (below n) and the edge list is small, so k + 1 passes over all edges are cheap.
memory_hook: k + 1 rounds: relax every flight from last round's copy.
approach: Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds. Each round relaxes every flight once, reads the old prices and writes into a copy, so round i gives the cheapest cost with at most i flights.
rebuild_steps: Set prices to infinity for every city and set prices[src] = 0.
Loop k + 1 times, because k stops means k + 1 flights.
At the start of each round, copy prices into next_prices.
For each flight (u, v, cost), skip the flight if prices[u] is still infinity.
Otherwise, if prices[u] + cost is less than next_prices[v], set next_prices[v] to prices[u] + cost. Read only from prices and write only to next_prices.
After the round, set prices = next_prices.
Return prices[dst], or -1 if it is still infinity.
key_insight: A hop limit turns shortest path into a layered problem. Bellman-Ford round i gives the best cost with at most i edges, but only when each round reads a frozen copy of the previous round. So you run exactly k + 1 rounds and stop.
ladder: Brute force DFS over all walks: O(d^(k+1)) where d is the max out-degree time, O(k) recursion depth space (too slow)
Level-by-level BFS with per-level best costs: O(k * (n + E)) time, O(n + E) space
Bellman-Ford limited to k + 1 rounds (chosen): O(k * (n + E)) time, O(n) space
Dijkstra on state (node, edges used): O(k * E * log(k * E)) time, O(k * E) space
Memoized DFS / 2D DP: O(k * (n + E)) time, O(k * n) space
pitfalls: Off by one: k stops means k + 1 edges, so run k + 1 rounds, not k.
Updating prices in place lets one round use several edges. The answer can then break the stop limit (for example, with k = 0 and edge 0->1 listed before 1->2, round 1 reaches 2 through 1).
Plain Dijkstra with one best cost per node is wrong. A cheap arrival with many stops can block a costlier arrival with fewer stops that still reaches dst.

title: Hand of Straights
statement: Alice has some cards. Each card has an integer value. You get the integer array hand, where hand[i] is the value on the i-th card, and an integer groupSize. Alice wants to rearrange all the cards into groups. Each group must have exactly groupSize cards. The cards in each group must be groupSize consecutive values (for example x, x+1, ..., x+groupSize-1). Every card must be used exactly once. Duplicate values are allowed and each copy is a separate card. Return true if such a rearrangement exists, and false otherwise.
signals: The task asks you to partition all items into groups of fixed size with a rigid internal shape, such as consecutive values.
Order of the input does not matter, so only the multiset of values matters. This points to a frequency map.
Values are large (up to 10^9) but the count is small (10^4). Sort the distinct values or use a heap instead of an array indexed by value.
A yes or no feasibility question about covering every item exactly once often has a forced choice at an extreme element, such as the smallest.
memory_hook: Smallest card left starts a straight. Pull its next cards one by one.
approach: Smallest card left starts a straight, one card at a time. Walk the sorted hand. Skip a card if its count is 0, because an earlier straight used it. Otherwise, the card is the smallest card left, so it must start a straight. Remove one copy of each value card, card+1, ..., card+groupSize-1. If one of these values has no copy left, return False.
rebuild_steps: If len(hand) % groupSize is not 0, return False.
Build count = Counter(hand).
For each card in sorted(hand), skip it if count[card] == 0, because an earlier straight used it.
Otherwise, the card starts a straight. Loop value over range(card, card + groupSize).
Inside that loop, return False if count[value] == 0. Else do count[value] -= 1.
After the outer loop, return True.
key_insight: The smallest remaining element has no smaller neighbor, so it can only be the start of a group. Its placement is forced, and a forced choice never needs backtracking. Commit to it greedily, remove its whole group, and repeat.
optimal_note: The optimal solution_code walks only the distinct values and subtracts all copies of a value at once (count[card] -= need). It does the same work in fewer loop steps when the hand has many duplicates. Both are O(n log n) time and O(n) space, and both run in about 0.01 s at n = 10^4. You do not need the batch form for these constraints. Use it when the hand has many copies of each value or when you already work on (value, count) pairs.
ladder: Exhaustive search over groupings: Exponential time, O(n) space (too slow)
Sort the list and remove groups from a list: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Min-heap of distinct values with a count map (NeetCode): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Counter plus sorted distinct values, batch subtract (chosen): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Sorted distinct values with a sliding count of open groups: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Forgetting the early check len(hand) % groupSize. The greedy stays correct without it, but the check rejects impossible inputs in O(1).
Starting a group from an arbitrary value instead of the smallest remaining value. Only the smallest value has a forced role.
Walking the sorted hand card by card and not skipping a card whose count is already 0. An earlier group already used that card. Starting a group from it gives a wrong false.

title: Car Fleet
statement: There are n cars at different miles on a road. All cars travel toward mile target. You get two integer arrays, position and speed, both of length n. Car i starts at mile position[i] and drives at speed[i] miles per hour. A car cannot pass another car. It can catch up to a car ahead and then drive next to it at the speed of the slower car. A car fleet is a single car or a group of cars that drive next to each other. The speed of a fleet is the minimum speed of any car in the fleet. If a car catches up to a fleet exactly at mile target, it counts as part of that fleet. Return the number of car fleets that arrive at the destination.
signals: Objects move in one direction on a line and cannot overtake. A slow object ahead blocks every faster object behind it.
The question asks how many groups form, not when or where they form. This means you can avoid a time simulation.
Each object has a simple independent outcome, such as a finish time. Interaction only clamps that outcome by the object ahead.
Positions and attributes come as parallel unsorted arrays with unique positions. This points to zip and sort by position.
memory_hook: Front car first: a car that arrives later than the fleet ahead starts a new fleet.
approach: Sort the cars from the car closest to the target to the farthest car. Compute the solo arrival time of each car. A car starts a new fleet only when its solo arrival time is greater than the arrival time of the fleet just ahead. Otherwise it catches that fleet and joins it.
rebuild_steps: Zip position and speed and sort in reverse, so the car closest to the target comes first.
Set fleets = 0 and fleet_time = 0.0, the arrival time of the fleet just ahead.
For each car, compute arrive = (target - pos) / spd, its time on an empty road.
If arrive > fleet_time, add 1 to fleets and set fleet_time = arrive.
Else the car catches the fleet ahead at or before the target, so do nothing.
Return fleets.
key_insight: A car can never pass the car ahead, so its real arrival time is the maximum of its own solo arrival time and the real arrival time of the car ahead. Replace the motion with one number per car, the solo time to the target. Then scan from the front and count the cars whose solo time is strictly greater than every solo time before it. The first car and each strict new maximum start a new fleet.
optimal_note: The optimal code uses the same sort and the same comparison, but it pushes each new fleet time onto a stack and returns the stack size. The stack only ever uses its top, so it is the running maximum in another form. Both are O(n log n) time. The stack form helps when you must keep each fleet, for example to return the fleet sizes or arrival times.
ladder: Event-driven simulation: O(n^2) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Leader check per car: O(n^2) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Sort by position plus monotonic stack of arrival times: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Sort plus one running maximum: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Bucket by position instead of sorting: O(n + target) time, O(target) space
pitfalls: Scanning from the farthest car instead of the car closest to the target gives wrong counts. Blocking flows from front to back.
Using >= to start a new fleet is wrong. Equal arrival times mean the cars meet at the target, which counts as one fleet.
Comparing with the solo time of the car directly ahead is wrong. Compare with the fleet time, which is the running maximum. A fast car between two slow cars must not reset the threshold.
solution:
from typing import List


class Solution:
    def carFleet(self, target: int, position: List[int], speed: List[int]) -> int:
        cars = sorted(zip(position, speed), reverse=True)  # front car first
        fleets = 0
        fleet_time = 0.0  # arrival time of the fleet just ahead
        for pos, spd in cars:
            arrive = (target - pos) / spd  # time if the road were empty
            if arrive > fleet_time:  # arrives later than the fleet ahead: new fleet
                fleets += 1
                fleet_time = arrive
            # else: it catches the fleet ahead and joins it
        return fleets

title: Koko Eating Bananas
statement: Koko loves to eat bananas. There are n piles of bananas, and the i-th pile has piles[i] bananas. The guards have gone and will come back in h hours. Koko can decide her bananas-per-hour eating speed k. Each hour, she chooses some pile of bananas and eats k bananas from that pile. If the pile has less than k bananas, she eats all of them instead and does not eat any more bananas during that hour. Koko likes to eat slowly but still wants to finish eating all the bananas before the guards return. Return the minimum integer k such that she can eat all the bananas within h hours.
signals: The question asks for the minimum (or maximum) value of a parameter, such as a speed, rate or capacity, that still meets a limit.
You can check one candidate value fast, but no direct formula gives the answer.
Feasibility is monotone: if a value works, every larger value also works.
The candidate range is very large (here up to 10^9), so a linear scan is too slow. A binary search needs only about log2 of the range checks, here about 30.
memory_hook: Guess a speed, count the hours, and binary search for the first speed that fits.
approach: Binary search on the answer (speed). Total hours never increase as the speed grows, so search [1, max(piles)] for the first speed whose total hours fit in h.
rebuild_steps: Write hours_needed(k) = sum of ceil(p / k), as (p + k - 1) // k.
Set lo = 1 and hi = max(piles), because hi always works.
Loop while lo < hi and take mid = (lo + hi) // 2.
If hours_needed(mid) <= h, set hi = mid, because mid can be the answer.
Else set lo = mid + 1, because mid is too slow.
Return lo, which is the first speed that fits.
key_insight: When a problem asks for the smallest parameter that makes a task feasible, and feasibility is monotone in that parameter, do not try to compute the answer directly. Binary search over the parameter values. Use a fast feasibility check as the comparison.
ladder: Linear scan over speeds: O(n * max(piles)) time, O(1) space (too slow)
Binary search on the answer (speed): O(n * log(max(piles))) time, O(1) space
Binary search with tighter bounds: O(n * log(max(piles))) time, O(1) space
bisect_left with key over a range: O(n * log(max(piles))) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Floor division instead of ceiling division undercounts hours. A partial pile still costs a full hour.
Float division followed by math.ceil works within these limits, but it can give wrong results for values near 2^53. Integer ceiling division is safer.
Starting lo at 0 causes division by zero. The minimum speed is 1.

title: K Closest Points to Origin
statement: You get an array points where points[i] = [xi, yi] is a point on the X-Y plane, and an integer k. Return the k points that are closest to the origin (0, 0). Distance is the Euclidean distance sqrt((x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2). You may return the answer in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique, except for its order.
signals: The task asks for the k smallest, k largest, k closest, or k most frequent items. This points to a size-k heap or to quickselect.
The output order does not matter. A full sort does more work than the task needs.
You rank items by a score that you compute from each item, such as a distance or a count. This points to a heap or a sort keyed on (score, item).
The score is only compared, never reported. You can rank by a cheaper monotone transform of it, such as the squared distance.
memory_hook: Sort by x*x + y*y, keep the first k.
approach: Sort by squared distance, then slice. Sort all points from closest to farthest with the key x*x + y*y, and return the first k points.
rebuild_steps: Write a key function that returns x * x + y * y for a point. Do not take the square root.
Call sorted(points, key=squared_distance). This gives a new list from closest to farthest and does not change the input.
Return the slice [:k] of that sorted list.
Check: the answer can be in any order, and the problem guarantees a unique set, so ties at the edge do not matter.
key_insight: To keep the k smallest items, keep a heap of size k ordered by the opposite criterion. The root is the worst item you keep, so each new item needs one comparison with the root to decide if it gets in.
optimal_note: The record solution_code keeps a bounded max-heap of size k with negated keys in heapq. It costs O(n log k) time and O(k) memory instead of O(n log n) time and O(n) memory. It never needs all points at once, so it also works on a stream or on data that does not fit in memory. Use it when k is much smaller than n, when the points arrive one by one, or when the interviewer asks to beat the full sort. Quickselect gives average O(n) when the interviewer asks for more.
ladder: Sort by squared distance: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Min-heap of all points, pop k (NeetCode): O(n + k log n) time, O(n) space
Bounded max-heap of size k: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
Quickselect on squared distance: O(n) average, O(n^2) worst case time, O(1) extra with an in-place iterative loop, O(log n) average stack if recursive space
heapq.nsmallest: O(n log k) time, O(k) space
pitfalls: Do not use a min-heap of size k for the k smallest items. The root would be the best item, so you would evict the wrong one. Use a max-heap with negated keys.
Do not take the square root or use math.hypot. It is slower and brings float rounding. Squared integer distance gives the same order.

The heapq functions heappush, heappop and heapreplace build a min-heap. Python 3.14 adds max-heap functions, but older versions and most judges do not have them. Push the negated key, and negate it again when you read the real value.

title: Time Based Key-Value Store
statement: Design a time-based key-value data structure. It stores multiple values for the same key at different timestamps. It returns the value of a key at a given timestamp. Implement the TimeMap class. TimeMap() initializes the object of the data structure. set(key, value, timestamp) stores the key with the value at the given timestamp. get(key, timestamp) returns a value from an earlier set call with timestamp_prev <= timestamp. If more than one such value exists, it returns the value with the largest timestamp_prev. If no such value exists, it returns the empty string "".
constraints: key and value consist of lowercase English letters and digits.
All the timestamps timestamp of set are strictly increasing.
signals: The query asks for the latest entry at or before a given point. This is a floor query: find the largest item <= x.
Inserts arrive in increasing order of the search field. An append-only list then stays sorted for free.
Up to 2 * 10^5 calls, and one key can hold about 10^5 sets. A linear scan per query can then reach about 10^10 steps, so each query must be logarithmic.
The data groups by an exact key, and order matters only inside each group. Use a hash map from key to a sorted list.
memory_hook: Two lists per key: times and values. bisect_right counts times <= t, so take the value one left.
approach: Parallel lists with bisect_right. Each key keeps a list of timestamps and a matching list of values. For get, i = bisect_right(times, t) is the count of timestamps <= t. The answer is the value at index i - 1, or the empty string when i is 0.
rebuild_steps: Import bisect_right from bisect and defaultdict from collections.
Make two defaultdict(list) maps: key to timestamps and key to values.
In set, append the timestamp and the value to the lists of that key. Increasing timestamps keep the list sorted.
In get, read the timestamp list with dict.get(key, []) so a missing key adds no entry.
Compute i = bisect_right(times, timestamp). This is the count of timestamps <= timestamp.
Return values[key][i - 1] if i > 0, else return the empty string.
key_insight: Split the query into an exact part and an ordered part. Use a hash map for the exact part. Keep each group sorted on the ordered part. Here the order is free because inserts arrive in increasing order. Then a question of the form latest value at or before t is a floor search, and binary search answers it in O(log k).
optimal_note: The record solution writes the binary search by hand on (timestamp, value) pairs. It has the same O(log k) get and O(1) set. Use the hand-written form when bisect is not available or when the interviewer asks you to write the search. Its template is: while lo <= hi, on a match save the value and move lo = mid + 1, else move hi = mid - 1. If set timestamps can arrive out of order, neither form works alone; use bisect.insort or an ordered map.
ladder: Brute force: log of all sets with linear scan: O(1) amortized per set, O(n) per get where n is the total number of sets time, O(n) space (too slow)
Hash map of lists with linear scan from the end: O(1) amortized per set, O(k) per get where k is the number of sets on that key time, O(n) space (too slow)
Hash map of sorted lists with binary search (optimal, standard): O(1) amortized per set, O(log k) per get where k is the number of sets on that key time, O(n) space
Parallel lists with bisect_right: O(1) amortized per set, O(log k) per get time, O(n) space
Ordered map per key (TreeMap floorKey or SortedDict): O(log k) per set, O(log k) per get time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Return "" for a key that was never set. Use dict.get or a membership check so the lookup does not raise KeyError.
Return "" when the query timestamp is smaller than the first stored timestamp of that key.
Search for the last timestamp <= t, not the first timestamp >= t. After a match, keep moving right to find a later one.
solution:
from bisect import bisect_right
from collections import defaultdict


class TimeMap:

    def __init__(self):
        self.times = defaultdict(list)   # key -> timestamps, increasing
        self.values = defaultdict(list)  # key -> values, same order as times

    def set(self, key: str, value: str, timestamp: int) -> None:
        # set timestamps strictly increase, so append keeps times sorted
        self.times[key].append(timestamp)
        self.values[key].append(value)

    def get(self, key: str, timestamp: int) -> str:
        times = self.times.get(key, [])     # .get does not add a missing key
        i = bisect_right(times, timestamp)  # i = count of times <= timestamp
        return self.values[key][i - 1] if i > 0 else ""

title: Rotting Oranges
statement: You get an m x n grid. Each cell holds one of three values: 0 is an empty cell, 1 is a fresh orange, 2 is a rotten orange. Every minute, each fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent (up, down, left, right) to a rotten orange becomes rotten. All oranges that touch a rotten orange at the start of a minute rot during that minute at the same time. Empty cells and the grid edges stop the spread. Diagonal cells do not count as adjacent. Return the minimum number of minutes until no cell holds a fresh orange. If some fresh orange can never rot, return -1. If there are no fresh oranges at the start, return 0.
signals: A state spreads to neighboring cells one step per unit of time. Spread over time on a grid means BFS levels.
The spread starts from many cells at the same time. Many simultaneous sources mean one BFS with all sources in the queue at distance 0.
The question asks for the minimum time or steps, and every move costs the same. Unweighted shortest path means BFS, not DFS.
The answer is the time when the last cell is reached. That is the maximum shortest distance over all targets, so it equals the number of BFS levels after the source level.
memory_hook: All rotten in the queue, count the fresh, one level is one minute, stop when fresh is zero.
approach: Multi-source BFS by levels with a fresh counter. Put every rotten orange in one queue and count the fresh oranges, then rot one ring of neighbors per minute until no fresh orange is left or the queue is empty.
rebuild_steps: Get rows and cols. Scan the grid once. Push each rotten cell into a deque and count each fresh cell.
Set minutes to 0. List the 4 direction offsets: down, up, right, left.
Loop while the queue is not empty and fresh is more than 0. The fresh check stops the loop before an extra empty minute.
In each pass, pop exactly len(queue) cells, so one pass is one minute.
For each popped cell, check the 4 neighbors. If a neighbor is in bounds and fresh, set it to 2, decrease fresh and push it.
After the pass, add 1 to minutes.
Return minutes if fresh is 0, else return -1.
key_insight: When a process starts from many cells at once and spreads one step per unit of time, the time a cell is reached equals its shortest distance to the nearest source. Put all sources in one BFS queue at distance 0. This is the same as a BFS from one virtual source that connects to all of them. The total time is the number of BFS levels needed to reach the last target.
ladder: Minute-by-minute grid simulation: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space
BFS from each fresh orange to the nearest rotten orange: O((m*n)^2) time, O(m*n) space
Multi-source BFS by levels with a fresh counter (optimal): O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
Multi-source BFS with time stored per cell: O(m*n) time, O(m*n) space
pitfalls: Off-by-one: a loop that runs until the queue is empty also processes the last level, which rots nothing, and counts one extra minute. Stop when the fresh count reaches 0, or subtract one minute at the end and keep the result at 0 or more.
No fresh oranges at the start must return 0. This includes a grid with no oranges at all, as in [[0]], and a grid with only rotten oranges and empty cells, as in [[0,2]].
Fresh oranges with no rotten orange at all must return -1, because the queue starts empty.

title: Last Stone Weight
statement: You get an array of integers stones, where stones[i] is the weight of the i-th stone. On each turn, choose the two heaviest stones and smash them together. Let their weights be x and y with x <= y. If x == y, both stones are destroyed. If x != y, the stone of weight x is destroyed and the stone of weight y gets the new weight y - x. The game ends when at most one stone remains. Return the weight of the last remaining stone, or 0 if no stones remain.
signals: The process repeatedly takes the largest (or smallest) elements of a changing collection.
Each step removes items and may insert a new item computed from them, so the order changes after every step.
The statement says simulate a game or process until one or zero items remain.
The rules define the answer step by step, and no shortcut formula is visible. Simulate the process directly and use a structure with fast extract-max.
memory_hook: Negate into a heap, smash the top two, push back only a nonzero difference.
approach: Max-heap simulation. Put negated weights in a heap, pop the two heaviest stones, push back their difference when it is not zero, and stop when fewer than two stones remain.
rebuild_steps: Import heapq. Python heapq is a min-heap, so store each weight as a negative number.
Make heap = [-s for s in stones] and call heapq.heapify(heap).
Loop while len(heap) > 1, because a smash needs two stones.
Pop y = -heapq.heappop(heap) as the heavier stone. Then pop x = -heapq.heappop(heap) as the lighter stone.
If y != x, push -(y - x) back into the heap. If y == x, push nothing, because both stones are destroyed.
After the loop, return -heap[0] if the heap is not empty. Else return 0.
key_insight: When a process repeatedly removes the current maximum items and inserts new items derived from them, keep the items in a heap so each extract and insert costs O(log n) instead of a re-sort or rescan.
ladder: Sort every turn: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n) space
Linear scan for the two largest every turn: O(n^2) time, O(1) extra space
Sorted list with binary insertion: O(n^2) worst case because insort shifts elements time, O(n) space
Max-heap simulation (optimal, standard): O(n log n) time, O(n) space
Bucket counting by weight: O(n + W), where W is the maximum weight time, O(W) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to negate when pushing the difference back, which inserts a positive value into a heap of negatives.
Pushing a zero when the stones are equal. The answer stays correct here because zeros sink to the bottom, but each zero adds a useless turn and can break variants that count stones or turns.
Reading heap[0] when the heap is empty raises IndexError. Return 0 when no stone remains.

title: Longest Common Subsequence
statement: You get two strings text1 and text2. Return the length of their longest common subsequence. If no common subsequence exists, return 0. A subsequence of a string is a new string that you get when you delete zero or more characters and keep the relative order of the remaining characters. The characters do not need to be contiguous. For example, "ace" is a subsequence of "abcde". A common subsequence is a subsequence of both strings. Return only the length, not the subsequence.
constraints: text1 and text2 consist of only lowercase English characters.
signals: Two sequences are given and the answer measures how well they align or match.
The word subsequence means the kept elements can skip positions but must keep their order.
The problem asks for a length or count, not for every matching subsequence.
Both lengths are up to about 1000, so an O(m * n) table of about 10^6 cells is the intended budget.
memory_hook: Last chars match: go diagonal plus one. Else take the best of up and left.
approach: Bottom-up 2-D table on prefix lengths. dp[i][j] is the LCS length of text1[:i] and text2[:j], and each cell comes from its upper-left, upper and left neighbors.
rebuild_steps: Let m and n be the two lengths. Make a (m+1) by (n+1) table of zeros with a list comprehension. Row 0 and column 0 are the empty prefixes.
Loop i from 1 to m and j from 1 to n.
Compare text1[i-1] with text2[j-1], because cell (i, j) holds prefixes of length i and j.
On a match, set dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1] + 1.
Else set dp[i][j] = max(dp[i-1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
Return dp[m][n].
key_insight: Compare the last elements of two prefixes. If they match, pair them together. If they do not match, at least one of them is not in the answer, so drop either one and keep the better result. This turns the problem into a grid of prefix pairs where each cell depends only on three smaller neighbors.
ladder: Brute force over subsequences: O(2^m * (m + n)) time, O(m) space (too slow)
Plain recursion on (i, j): O(2^(m+n)) time, O(m + n) space (too slow)
Top-down memoized DFS: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Bottom-up 2-D table on prefix lengths: O(m * n) time, O(m * n) space
Rolling rows: O(m * n) time, O(min(m, n)) space
Hunt-Szymanski style reduction to LIS: O(m + n + r * log n) where r is the number of matching pairs time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Do not confuse subsequence with substring. Longest common substring resets the cell to 0 on a mismatch, and its answer is the max over all cells, not dp[m][n].
Use a table of size (m+1) by (n+1) so the empty-prefix border removes index checks. Then compare text1[i-1] with text2[j-1], not text1[i] with text2[j].
Do not build the table with [[0] * (n + 1)] * (m + 1). All rows are the same list object.

title: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree
statement: You get the root of a binary tree. A node X is good if no node on the path from the root to X has a value greater than X's value. The path includes the root and X itself. Equal values do not break the rule, so a node whose value equals the path maximum is good. The root is always good. Return the number of good nodes in the tree.
constraints: The number of nodes in the binary tree is in the range [1, 10^5].
signals: The condition on a node depends on all its ancestors (the root-to-node path), not on its subtree.
The path condition reduces to one summary value: no ancestor is greater means the node value is at least the path maximum.
The answer counts nodes over the whole tree. One traversal that checks each node in O(1) gives O(n).
Up to 10^5 nodes rules out re-walking the path for each node on a skewed tree, which is O(n^2).
memory_hook: Carry the path max down; count a node when it is at least the max.
approach: Iterative DFS that carries the path maximum. Each stack entry holds a node and the biggest value above it on the path, so the node is good when its value is at least that maximum.
rebuild_steps: Start a stack with (root, root.val) and set count to 0. The root compares with its own value, so it counts as good.
Loop while the stack is not empty and pop (node, path_max).
If node is None, continue.
If node.val >= path_max, add 1 to count.
Set path_max = max(path_max, node.val) and push (node.left, path_max) and (node.right, path_max).
Return count after the loop.
key_insight: A condition over the whole root-to-node path often collapses to one running aggregate, such as a maximum, minimum, sum or bitmask. Each parent computes the aggregate for its children in O(1) and passes it down. Then each node is checked in O(1).
ladder: Brute force with explicit path: O(n * h), O(n^2) worst case on a skewed tree time, O(h) space (too slow)
Recursive top-down DFS carrying the path maximum: O(n) time, O(h) call stack, O(n) on a skewed tree space
Iterative DFS with a stack of (node, path_max) pairs: O(n) time, O(h) for the stack, O(n) worst case space
BFS with a queue of (node, path_max) pairs: O(n) time, O(w), the maximum tree width, up to O(n) space
pitfalls: Use >= and not >. A node equal to the path maximum is good, and the root must count.
Update the path maximum before you pass it to the children, not after you return from them.
Do not use one shared global maximum. Each branch needs its own value. Pass the value as a parameter or store it in the stack entry.

title: Min Cost to Connect All Points
statement: You get an array points that holds integer coordinates of points on a 2D plane, where points[i] = [xi, yi]. The cost to connect two points [xi, yi] and [xj, yj] is the Manhattan distance between them: |xi - xj| + |yi - yj|, where |val| is the absolute value of val. Return the minimum cost to make all points connected. All points are connected if there is exactly one simple path between any two points.
signals: The task asks for the minimum total cost to connect all items, with no requirement on path lengths between pairs. This points to a minimum spanning tree.
The phrase 'exactly one simple path between any two points' defines a tree. A tree that touches all nodes is a spanning tree.
Every pair of items has a cost from a formula, such as a distance. The graph is complete and implicit, so you can compute an edge weight when you need it and store no edges.
The node count is about 10^3. So O(n^2) work (about 10^6 steps) fits, but an edge list or heap with about 10^6 entries is slow in Python.
memory_hook: Keep a dict of outside points: pop the nearest, then let it lower the others.
approach: Prim with a dict of outside points. Keep cost[v], the cheapest edge from each outside point v to the tree. Each round, pop the point with the smallest cost, add that cost to the total, and let the new point lower the costs of the points that are still outside.
rebuild_steps: Make cost = {v: inf for every point}, set cost[0] = 0 and total = 0.
While cost is not empty, pick u = min(cost, key=cost.get).
Add cost.pop(u) to total, so u moves into the tree.
For each v still in cost, compute the Manhattan distance d from u to v.
If d < cost[v], set cost[v] = d.
When the dict is empty, return total.
key_insight: Connecting everything at minimum total cost is a minimum spanning tree, and the cut property makes greedy growth safe. When the graph is complete, use array-based Prim: keep one best-cost value per node and scan it, so the work is O(V^2) and no edge list is stored.
optimal_note: The record's solution_code is the same dense Prim. It keeps an in_tree list and finds the next point with a manual argmin loop over all n points. This version removes tree points from a dict instead. Both run in O(n^2) time with O(n) memory, and both use about 0.2 s of CPU time at n = 1000. The list form is easy to port to a language that has no dict pop. Heap Prim and Kruskal take O(n^2 log n) time, so they are slower here. Only the O(n log n) octant sweep is asymptotically faster, and you need it only when n is near 10^5 or larger.
ladder: Brute force over edge subsets: O(C(n^2/2, n-1) * n) time, O(n^2) space (too slow)
Kruskal with union-find: O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
Lazy Prim with a min-heap (NeetCode reference): O(n^2 log n) time, O(n^2) space
Dense Prim with a best-distance array: O(n^2) time, O(n) space
Manhattan MST with octant sweep: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
pitfalls: Do not confuse MST with shortest paths. Dijkstra minimizes the distance from one source, not the total edge weight.
