With n = 1, the answer is 0. Make sure the code does not look for an edge that does not exist.
Building the full adjacency list stores about 10^6 entries. It works but is slow and uses much memory in Python, so prefer to compute distances on the fly.

title: Minimum Interval to Include Each Query
statement: You get a 2D integer array intervals. Each intervals[i] = [left_i, right_i] is an inclusive interval. The size of an interval is the number of integers it contains: right_i - left_i + 1. You also get an integer array queries. The answer to query j is the size of the smallest interval i with left_i <= queries[j] <= right_i. If no interval contains queries[j], the answer is -1. Return an array of the answers, in the original order of queries.
signals: Many point queries against a fixed set of intervals, and all queries are known in advance. The answer to one query does not depend on the other queries. This permits offline processing: you can answer the queries in any order.
Both input sizes are up to 10^5, so a scan of all intervals per query (10^10 checks) is too slow. You need about O((n + m) log(n + m)) total work.
Each query asks for the best (minimum or maximum) item among the items that are active at a point. Think of a sweep line with a priority queue of active items.

Each item becomes usable at a start value and becomes useless forever after an end value, and the sorted queries only move forward. This points to a pointer that releases items into a heap, plus lazy removal of expired items at the top.
memory_hook: Sweep sorted queries, push started intervals by size, pop ended tops, read the top.
approach: Offline sweep with a min-heap and lazy deletion. Visit the queries from small to large, push every interval that has started as (size, right), pop the top while it has already ended, and read the top size.
rebuild_steps: Sort intervals by left, and sort the query indices by query value.
Make ans = [-1] * m, an empty heap, and an interval pointer i = 0.
For each query q in sorted order, move i forward while intervals[i] has left <= q, and push (right - left + 1, right) for each of these intervals. Do not reset i between queries.
Pop the heap top while its right < q, because that interval ended and never comes back.
If the heap is not empty, write the top size into ans at the original index of the query.
Return ans.
key_insight: When all queries are known in advance, sort them and sweep. Items enter an active set when the sweep passes their start. Items that expire never come back, so a heap with lazy deletion of expired tops gives the best active item in O(log n) amortized time.
ladder: Brute force per query: O(n * m) time, O(1) extra besides the output space (too slow)
Offline sweep with min-heap and lazy deletion (standard): O(n log n + m log m) time, O(n + m) space
Smallest interval first with union-find over sorted queries: O(n log n + m log m + (n + m) * alpha(m)) time, O(n + m) space
Coordinate compression with segment tree range min: O(m log m + n log m) time, O(m) space
pitfalls: Returning answers in sorted order instead of the original order. Keep the original index with each query.
Duplicate query values. A dict keyed by value works, but sorting indices handles duplicates with no special case.
Popping by left instead of right. An interval leaves only when right < q; left <= q is already guaranteed for everything in the heap.

title: Merge Triplets to Form Target Triplet
statement: A triplet is an array of three integers. You get a 2D integer array triplets, where triplets[i] = [ai, bi, ci] is the i-th triplet. You also get an integer array target = [x, y, z], the triplet you want to obtain. You may apply this operation any number of times, possibly zero: choose two 0-indexed indices i and j with i != j, and update triplets[j] to [max(ai, aj), max(bi, bj), max(ci, cj)]. Only triplets[j] changes; triplets[i] stays the same. For example, if triplets[i] = [2, 5, 3] and triplets[j] = [1, 7, 5], triplets[j] becomes [2, 7, 5]. Return true if you can make target appear as an element of triplets. Otherwise return false.
signals: The operation combines elements with max (or min, OR, AND, gcd). These operators are associative, commutative and idempotent, so order and repetition of operations do not matter.
The operation is irreversible: values only grow (or only shrink). An element that passes the target in one coordinate can never come back.
The question asks 'is it possible after any number of operations'. Think about the set of reachable results, not about the sequence of moves.
n is up to 10^5 but each element has a small fixed size. This points to one linear pass with O(1) work per element.
memory_hook: Drop any triplet that overshoots, max the rest, compare with target.
approach: Filter and merge (greedy). Throw away every triplet that is bigger than the target in any coordinate. Merge all the other triplets with a running coordinate-wise max and check that the result equals the target.
rebuild_steps: Unpack the target into x, y, z and set best_a, best_b, best_c to 0.
Loop over each triplet as a, b, c.
Skip the triplet unless a <= x and b <= y and c <= z.
For a safe triplet, update each best value with max.
After the loop, return [best_a, best_b, best_c] == target (compare a list with the list target).
key_insight: With a monotone, idempotent combine such as max, any element that overshoots the target in one coordinate is poison and must be excluded. Every other element is harmless, so combine all of them and check whether the result hits the target exactly.
ladder: Simulate all operation sequences (BFS over array states): Exponential in n. Each triplet always equals the max of a subset that contains it, so up to 2^(n(n-1)) array states, each with O(n^2) moves. time, O(number of states) space (too slow)
Enumerate subsets: O(2^n * n) time, O(n) space (too slow)
Greedy filter and merge all safe triplets: O(n) time, O(1) space
Greedy coverage set (NeetCode version): O(n) time, O(1) space
pitfalls: Using a triplet that holds a needed value but overshoots another coordinate. Max can never undo the overshoot, so such a triplet is unusable.
Checking only that each target value appears somewhere, without the filter. Example: [[2,2,3],[1,1,2]] with target [2,2,2] returns a wrong true.
Writing the filter with or instead of and, or with < instead of <=. A coordinate equal to the target is allowed and is in fact required.

title: Detect Squares
statement: Design a data structure for a stream of points on the X-Y plane. add(point) stores the point [x, y]. Duplicate points are allowed, and each copy counts as a different point. count(point) returns the number of ways to choose three stored points so that these three points and the query point form an axis-aligned square with positive area. An axis-aligned square has four equal sides, and each side is parallel to the x-axis or the y-axis. The query point is not added to the structure. Implement DetectSquares() which starts empty, void add(int[] point), and int count(int[] point).
constraints: At most 3000 calls in total will be made to add and count.
signals: The task counts shapes that must include one given query point. The query anchors the shape, so only a few free parameters remain.
The shape is axis-aligned. All corners then come from two x values and two y values, so one diagonal corner fixes the other corners.
Duplicate points count as different choices. Store a frequency per point and multiply the frequencies instead of storing a set.
The task is a design problem with cheap inserts and repeated queries. Keep a hash map that each query reads without a rebuild.
memory_hook: Pick the diagonal, the other two corners are forced, multiply the counts.
approach: Diagonal corner with a point counter. Keep a Counter of point copies. For a query, try each distinct stored point as the diagonal corner. If it makes a square, the other two corners are forced. Add the product of the three counts.
rebuild_steps: Store a Counter that maps (x, y) to its copies. add does points[tuple(point)] += 1.
In count, unpack the query as qx, qy and set total to 0.
Loop over points.items() to get each distinct point (x, y) and its copies.
Skip the point unless x != qx and abs(x - qx) == abs(y - qy). Only then is it the diagonal corner of a real square.
Add copies * points.get((x, qy), 0) * points.get((qx, y), 0) to total. Return total.
key_insight: Fix the query corner, then enumerate the single free parameter that determines the whole shape, here the diagonal corner. The other corners are forced, so a hash-map lookup replaces a search. With duplicates, the number of ways is the product of the counts of the forced corners.
optimal_note: Same algorithm as solution_code. Only the names and the .get lookups differ. Time is O(1) per add and O(d) per count, where d is the number of distinct stored points.
ladder: Brute force over triples: O(1) add, O(n^3) count time, O(n) space (too slow)
Enumerate pairs, look up the fourth corner: O(1) add, O(n^2) count time, O(n) space (too slow)
Enumerate the diagonal corner with a point counter (optimal, standard): O(1) add, O(d) count where d is the number of distinct points time, O(d) space
Enumerate the vertical side through a column index: O(1) add, O(k) count where k is the number of distinct points in the query's column (at most 1001) time, O(d) space
pitfalls: Forgetting to exclude zero-area squares. Skip the diagonal when x == px (then y == py too).
Accepting rectangles. The diagonal must satisfy |x - px| == |y - py|.
Using a set instead of counts. Duplicates are distinct choices, so multiply the frequencies.
